The following article is reprinted from the Railway Supplie Journal (London, April 2nd. 1887) In the course of our visit, as interesting as it was instruc- tive, in August last, to the Lancaster Agricultural Show., we were particularly impressed with the essentially healthy and vigorous physique of the calves shown, and were informed that this excellence arose from the animals having been fattened on the " Lancaster Calf Food," which we subsequently learned is manufactured by Messrs. Carruthers and Co., ot Laneaster, who for a century have maintained a deservedly good reputa- tion for the excellence of their productions, and who for upwards of 25 years have devoted special atten- tion to the manufacture of food for cattle and calves. Their feeding principle from the that has been to provide for all the wants of the animal, economy ht rearing young stock with sound and wellileveloped frazzles, and after- wards maintaining the system in 1 state of health and vigour, and many who have used Messrs. Carruthers and Ct).'s manu- factures through all these years testify that this subjeet has been fully realised, their stock having been vronderfully ex- empt from disease or loss. The Lancaster Calf Food, as its name imports, is prima facie intended for the rearing of calves, sodas a milk substitute is unsurpassed. It is a veritable inultain in parro, embracing,as it does, all the contituents for a highly nourishing food. It contains oil and fatty matter, aud albumenoids, starch, sugar, and mucilage. This will sufB- - account for the ease with which it can be digested after having been formed Into a suitable gruel. Calves can be. rear/at with it from three days old to twelve months without the ad- dition of milk, although for young calves it is usual to add skim milk for the first few weeks. Not only is the Calf Food suitable for calves, but it is especially valuable for all animals that may be ailing. Its nourishing qualities. are suited admirably for rearing young pigs, and improving the condition of horses, whilst in dairy cows it producee the richest milk. Mixed with oatmeal in the proportion of two to one, it is unsurpassed for its fattening powers, both. in increase of weight and quality of meat. The price charged by Messrs. Carruthers is very small, for it is only 138. per cwt., carriage paid to any railway station, so that taking into aceount ita many undeniable virtues, it would surely be a waste of thne to look for a cheaper or snore nutritious provender for stock. That the component parts are most judiciously blended with a view to answering the purposes of its manufacture Is suffi- ciently evidencedby the report of Mr. Alfred Simpson, F.C.S., at whose hands the food underwent the crucial test of analysis, and that its general excellence is practical, and not based only upon theory is shown by the testimonials, almost innumer- able, that have been sent without solicitation to Messrs. Car- nithers and Co. from stock meters and others interested in thecattle trade throughout the country.! -LIBRE CALVt'S 1887. .1 At the Lancaster and other Agricultural Shows held in the district in August and September, 1887, upwards of 201st and 2nd societies' prizes were awarded to calves fed on " Tut: LANCASTER CALe FOOD," manufactured by CARRUTHERS & CO., LANCASTER.

THE HOOAM OV A LANCASHIRE MON. Aw've tramped a good deal through mi own native land, Aw've anchored mi booat on a far foreign strand, Bin cast among riches, an' poverty too, Bed wark, an' bin wantin' for summat to do; Aw've slept in a palace, an' lodged in a tent, An' kept mi e'en oppen wherever aw went, Bud ov o sooarts o' hooams aw could never find one To compare with the hooam ov a Lancashire mon. , Aw remember quite weel heaw aveve oft laid mi deawn I' sal quare lookin' bed i' thad Indian teawn Where aw sowjerd a while, an' mi efforts to skeeom A tidy neet's sleep use' to end in a dreeom Ov a little thacked cot in a little green fowd Where aw lived when aw wor bud a dozen year owd, An' aw sighed when AAP wakkend to find id o gone— Thad hooam where aw grew up a Lancashire mon. There's no place th' waurld hawf so snug or so sweet, When a fella comes back fro his wark ov a nest, As the spot where he meets wi' the joys ov his life—. Zia wee little alder an' hard-warkire wife. In' iv yo be anxious to lam an' to serl Heaw blithe an' contented a toyler can be, Toll find th' best exasnple 'at ever yo con In the hooam ov a steady young Lancashire mon. There's a reet hearty welcome whenever yo co, For Lancashire feelin' hes full room to flow, Id isn'd chooked up wi so mich empty pride, An' hypocrisy ne'er comes to poison id tide; ft Bud clear an' unhindered id rowls on id way, An' strangers 'at's tasted id awlus will say As the kindliest fooak they could ever leet on Were found in the hooam ov a Lancashire mon. Just co at yar Turn's, the kettle hums up o' th' hob, An' his wife sings a song to their Nelly an' Bob, For they're o fain to see him ged hooam to his tay, After drivin' four looms o this dark•lookin' day. Wi' th' childer, its which con bi' t' fost on his knee, Their love for their feyther's untrarnelled an' free, An' his wife, tentin' t' rneyt 'at hoo's fryin' i't' pon, Thinks there's nob'ry so true as her Lancashire mon. Iv yo'll stop till they'n just getten th' childer to bed. Yo'll hear a rare bit o' Ned Waugh sung or read, An' theer yo'll sit sighin' an' laffin bi turns At the wisdom an' wit ov eawr Lancashire Burns. An' when yo've shaked hands wi' a "Good fleet," An' th' cottage behind yo fades slow fro yo'r sect, Yell say "there's some true English happiness yon," An' bi preawd o' th' hooam ov a Lancashire mon! Higher Walton, November, 1887. G. H.

A philosopher, who had married an ignorant girl, used to call her "brown sugar," because, he said, she was sweet, but unrefined. "The times are sadly changed," exclaimed one of the "upper ten," who felt that everything was going wrong, and that he himself in particular was being sadly neg- lected. "in what respect do you find them changed most?" he was asked by a friend. "Oh, that is plain," he said; "no regard is paid nowadays .to people of quality!" "Well, to be sure," said the friend, "It isn't so much the people of quality that we pay attention to nowadays as it is the quality of people." A German banker, travelling by rail in a first-class carriage towards Vienna, had as a fellow-traveller at one of the intermediate stations an old gentleman, who entered into conversation, and proved very pleasant. The banker got out before his companion; and, before, he did so, asked the latter how far he was going. The gentle- man replied to Vienna. "I have a daughter very well married there," said the banker. "I should like to give you a note of introduction to her." "1 have also a daughter very well married there," said the' other. "Would it be to, great a liberty to ask the name?" "My daughter," the gentleman answered, "is married to the Emperor of Austria!" It was the old King of Bavaria. THE BEST WAY or HELPING PEOPLE.—On the principle that "charity to the soul is the soul of charity," we should try to improve people's moral nature rather than aim merely at making them comfortable in their bodies. Surround people with every luxury, and they will be miserable still, unless their hearts and wills are in harmony with the moral laws of the universe. Nero on his throne was far less happy than St. Paul, the aged prisoner of Jesus Christ. A faithful friend can often save much misery by gently reminding us of our fail- ings. In his description of the work of charity a Christian writer includes "wholesome blame." fly far the best way, then, of helping people is to make them capable of helping themselves, and so of improving their surround- ings.— Qu;ver for November. Caller (in newspaper office) : " Twenty years ago I wrote a poem." Editor: "Yes." "I brought it to this office, and you refused to publish it." "Very likely." "I remember that I mentally put you down then as a confounded idiot, who didn't know enough to ache when hurt." "Naturally." "I looked that poem over again the other day, and have come to see you about it." " Aha." "I have come to say that if I looked as green twenty years ago as that poem proves me to have been, I want to thank you because you didn't cut me up and feed me to the cows. Good-day." The editor drew a long chalk mark under the table. It was the first case in all his experience in which 20 years had begotten sense enough to understaed that it is sometimes necessary to be cruel to be kind. LIFE ON THE PLANETS.—Does life exist not merely on the earth, hut on all the planets of the solar system, and also on the planets which may be presumed to revolve round the innumerable suns of the stellar regions? Here, again, we have only conjecture to guide us. With respect to the bodies constituting the solar system, which from their comparative proximity to the earth might be supposed to furnish a solution of this problem, careful observations have heretofore offered no indica- tion whatever of the existence of life upon their aur- faces, But life in some form Or another may notwith- standing exist on those bodiee, We must bear in mind rho ntaints are in all probebiiitv in various stages of dev‘Opmeiii. ft may be reasonably Prafaillned that the planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptißle, 11l consequence of their enormous bulk, have cooled down more slowly than the earth and the other §lflegfr planets of the solar sptem, and aIT thqNfOrc ICS uvatl6o. abodes of animated existence than the latter are. But even in the case 'of the earth, it must be admitted to have revolved millions of years round the sun merely as a fiery orb before life appeared on its surface, and even afterit had cooled down and become the abode of ani- mated existence, it produced, during countless millions of years more, life only in its lowest forms. The exist- ence of man is but of yesterday. This is an instructive lesson. It teaches us that although man exists on the earth's surface, it does not follow that beings of the same order of intelligence as man exist upon all the other planets or even upon any of them. Upon some of the planets life may not have yet come into existence; upon others life may exist, but in a less advanced stage than upon the earth; and the same remark is obviously applicable to the numberless bodies of the starry firma- ment.—Goed Words. Tne BEER OF THE Binzr.—A curious work just pub- lished, "The Beer of the Bible" (Triibner and Co.), maintains that what is spoken of in Exodus xii. 19, as "that which is 'leavened," was in reality the Hebrew beer, a substance resembling the present Arab bread- beer, Boosa, a fermented and eatable paste of the con- sistency of mustard; and that the corresponding words "nothing leavened," in verse 2Q, was an eatable malt product, probably calm sweetened by malt. It then goes on to argue that the identification in the account of the Exodus of a substance so purely Egyptian as is Boosa, and 'which appears to be made in no other part of the world than the valley of the Nile, fully establishes the great ' antiquity of the institution of the Passover, and forms the strongest known argument for the commands to abstain from lea Tan having been written about that time instead of being handed down ()ratty to a compiler of the time of Ezra. The author endeavours to show that "the manufacture of beer was the earliest art of primi- tive man, an art exceeding in antiquity that of the potter or of the wine maker, and certainly that of the baker." There are chapters on this beer, Oriental ferment products, Arab brewing, brewing and baking, and the Passover and unleavened bread, &c.; and in these various remarks on such subjects as the effect of the climate on grain, difference between English and Arab malt, Hebrew system of brewing, boosa as a pepsin, alcoholic scents. &c., Sic. To further elucidate his main question, the author brings forward much that is of general interest in connection with ancient Egyptian history and topography. He gives a short account, with map, of the old Atbara or Nubian Canal (not the Suez Canal of Necho) from the Nile to the Red Sea; a longer chapter, with larger map, of the Exodus route; Egyptian brick-making, with illustrations ; curious traditions, principally Arabian, of the Exodus; and a fine chrono- logical concordance of Egyptian, Jewish, Assyrian, Babylonian, and other events. A likeness is presented ,of the mummy of Rameses H. (called the Great) of the XIX. Dynasty. He was the Sesostris of the Greek writers and the Pharaoh who oppressed the Hebrews, and was suoceeded by his son Meneptah, who was drowned in the Red Sea a.c.1316, and of whom alikeness is also given. It is taken from a photograph of his i statue, n black basalt, in the Boulak Museum, Cairo. In the chapter on the lost Hebrews the question is asked, "What became of the Hebrews who were south of Mem- phis, some of whom were employed in stone-cutting and stone-dragging, 500 miles and more lower down?"

"Doctor," said the friend, stopping him on the streets 4' what do you take for a heavy cold ?" "A fee," replied the doctor, softly, and passed on. Man Milliner: "The bonnet, miss, makes you look twenty years younger." Lady Customer: "How funny! I must appear in it like a girl of ten years." "Excuse me, sir; but haven't we met before? Your face is strangely familiar." "Yes.. madam; our host introduced us to each other just before dinner." " Ah, Iwas positive I had seen you somewhere. I never forget a face.' "Did not the sight of the boundless blue sea, bearing I on its bosom white-winged fleets of commerce, fill you with emotion?" "Yes," replied the traveller, "at first it did.; but after a while it didn't fill me with anything. It sorter emptied me" Seedy Individual: "I would like to get measured for a suit." Fashionable Tailor (suspiciously): "At about what price, sir?" Seedy Individual: "It makes no dif- ference." Fashionable Tailor (as before): "We gene- rally require a deposit from unknown parties." Seedy Individual (calmly): "I do not wish You to make the suit. It haa been so long since I enjoyed this experience, that I simply wished to get measured." It is with Balfours as with Bibles. There are so many of them that it has been found necessary to invent names to distinguish them from each other. One very famous edition of the Bible is known to book collectors as the 'Breeches Bible" because of the word which it employs to translate the term usually rendered "apron." And new, I suppose, the present Irish Secretary will (in com- memoration of the feat at Tullamore) be distinguished from all other Balfours by the title "Breeches Balfour." Under this name he will go down to posterity, and doubt- less the future antiquarian from New Zealand will found upon this the specious and learned theory that the Irish SecretarY was the first to introduce to the barbarian Irish thigaisuent in question.—Truth. DARWIN IVITR. 1111 ;FAMILY AND EIS FRlENDS.—Dar- win's life was one ot :Teat seclusion; but he was not at all absorbed in his work to the exclusion of all other interests. He was a most i:actionate and indulgent father. He writes in a very tender' and touching way tie death of his Little daughter Anne. "I do not Says his son, " that he ever addressed n angry word to any of his children." One day he wad talkaag, patties with one of his sons, and argued with unnsuaa warmth. "Next morning, about 6nyet O'clock, he carne Into my room' sat down on my bed, said he hgtriOt n able to slc'ep for thinking that he had been too angry with me and left me after some affectionate words." He joined in all his children's games, and was once bribed by a promise of sixpence on the part of a baby boy of four to come and play during one of his hours of work. His manner with his friends was charm;ng; his talk was enthusiastic. His generosity to fellow-workers and his freedom from the petty jealousies which so often beset scientific men are too well known to need allusion here. The circumstances of the publication of his "Origin of Species," in their relation to Mr. Wallace, are the best instance, and the reader will find the story fully and finally told in Mr. Francis Darwin's pages. Not only had Darwin time for his friends, but he took much interest in all village affairs and in many philanthropic institutions. The clergyman of Down' who was his close friend for 30 years, tells a story of Darwin which shows how he carried his scrupulous love of truth and openness of mind into all departments of life. They had one day been discussing parish affairs together, and that night Darwin walked over to the parsonage; "he had come to say that on thinking over their conversation he was afraid I might have drawn an erroneous conclusion from something he had said, and be could not go to bed without explaining the matter to me." "I am con- , vinced," adds Mr. Brodie Innes, "that if one day a fact ; had presented itself to him which contradicted his , dearest theories he would have registered the' fact for publication before going to bed." TEA Timm iv TANGIRR.—The repast ended by'a bowl of oranges being set on the table, and when these were removed and the crumbs cleared from the table and floor, tea was brought, accompanied by little sweet cakes. Mahommet lit his pipe, the servant was called, and came in from the kitchen bringing the little Mus- tapha asleep. His mother took him and laid him across bet knees. The servant sat on the floor in the back- ground amongst us. Tea was served to her as to um, and the remainder of the evening passed in chat in which she joined. I may mention that the kettle had been set on a brazier in the courtyard just outside the door; aad that when boiling water was wanted, TitraM had only to stretch is harelthrOtigh the Archway'. As she sat on the 'loot, close to her husband, with Mustapha asleep in his little scarlet jelabeer on her knees, a text of the Koran hanging on the wall near at hand, and the curtain put partially back from the arch showing a glimpse of the stars for a background, the group ina.sde so charming a variation of the Holy Family pictures that Biblical asso- ciations were strong again in our minds. In the mean- time, Mahommet himself made tea, and his manner of doing it deserves a word of description. "A barrel full of nuts will hold many gallons of oil." So I found that a teapot full of sugar will hold a great deal besides. First, then, the teapot was filled with sugar in lumps almost the size of my fist; to this were added bunches of verbena and mint, a small measure of green tea, and, fortunately, a considerable quantity of boiling water. It was poured off almost immediately, a syrup, of course, and highly but more delicately flavoured than the tea of the coffee-house. It was served in very small cups, and no sooner was one teapotful consumed than another was brewed. We were expected to drink all the evening, and Titem wanted to hear about England. "Was Lon- I don as big as Tangier ?" "Well, yes, even bigger." And then some description followed of its streets and its parks, and its river, with ships and bridges in the midst of the town. She seemed much interested, especially by the description of carriages. "And it is a queen, is it not," she inquired, "who rules over all this?" I told the story of Queen Victoria's accession while she was still younger than Titem. At the end she laughed, and said something archly to Mahommet. He also laughed, and we asked for a translation. "She says that she thinks it is time to turn Christian, since among Christians the women rule."—Sunday Magazine. div.head: BIG NUGGETS OF COLD.
div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF COLD.

The luckiest "find" ever made in California was made bv a man named Finney, who "turned up" a solid lump a gold near Downievtlle, in 1866, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 18.00 dols. per ounce, which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget sf pure gold ever discovered. Heretofore the Australian nugget found in the Ballarat gold fields has been considared the largest. It was valued at £15,000. I This man Finney, or "Old Virginia," as he was called, went to Washoe, California, and there he made the great silver discoveries, where the " Comstock " lode was located, and where Virginia City, which was named after him, stands. He died in great poverty. He was cele- brated for his wonderful head of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of golden tints, and which fell in heavy curls over his stalwart shoulders. He was very proud of his head covering, and always carried in his " outfit " a brush, comb, and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his "camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great care. When misfortune overtook him, and he continued "playing in bad luck "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hair, and it became frowsy, began to turn gray, And fall Out, so that a few years before he died he was nearly bald, and his few remaining hairs were quite white. Had he added to his " outfit " Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he lived, for it never fails to strengthen and invigorate the hair, restore its colour, and render it soft, glossy and strong. It can be found at any chemist's or perfumer's in the world. It isthe best and most agreeable hair dress- ing known. Try it.

THE DEATH OF MR. 3. T. CUNLIFFE. INQUEST AND FUNERAL Last week we recorded the sudden death in Lon- don of Mr. J. T.. Cunliffe, leather manufacturer and tanner, of Warrington. On Saturday the inquest as to the death was held at the Windmill Tavern, High-street, Lamboth, London, by Mr. W. Carter, coroner for East Surrey. Inspector Watts, of the Lambeth Division, watched the case on behalf of the police authorities. Mr. Walter Cunliffe, a solicitor in practice at Liverpool, and residing at Bromborough, Cheshire, identified the deceased as his father, who always enjoyed good health, and had not been under medi- cal treatment. WitnesoaSt aaw him alive a fort- night no, and he was then !11, eXcellent health.l The deceased was a very sober and ineSt prudent man, and his life was insured in two or three offices. -Mr. Elijah/Frisby deposed' that he was a leather seller, and resided at 42, St. James's-road, Lough- borough Junction, Brixton. lie had known the de- ceased for the past eighteen years. Last Tuesday evening the deceased, who was staying at tjae National Liberal Club, Northumberland-aveune, came on a visit to witness's house and dined there. He was then quite well, and made no complaint whatever. He remained at the house until half- past ten o'clock,when he left to go toi.oughborough Junction Station for the ptirpose of returning to his club, witness accompanying him to see him off by the train. Having walked about GOO yards from the house, the deceased suddenly coughed, and re- marked the: the wind had caugh his breath. They then walked about twenty yards further, when the deceased again coughed, and appeared as if strug- gling for breath. The deceased exclaimed, "Get me a cab, I. am very bad." Witness secured a cab, and caused the deceased to be driven to Dr. Den- ton's, Loughborough-road. On arriving there, the- deceased was seen in the cab by that gentleman, and who administered to him a draught. The de- ceased, however, who appeared very ill, exclaimed, " I shall die." He was then taken into the surgery and seated on a chair, but he expired three minutes afterwards. In further answer to questions, the witness stated that the deceased was a fine gentle- man and of robust health. ,When they left witness home the deceased made no complaint whatever, and he (the witness) had no apprehension whatever of his death. Dr. Thomas John Denton, residing at 19' 5 Lough- borough-road, Brixton, deposed that last Tuesday night he was called out by the last witness to the deceased, whom he found in a cab and extremely iIL The deceased was Conscious, and exclaimed, "I shall die.' He was evidently suffering from failure of the heart's action, and witness having , given him a draught, caused his removal into the surgery, where he died two or three minutes after- wards. The witness had not made a post mortem examination of the body, but he had no doubt that death was due to syncope, arising in &disease of the heart. The jury eventually returned a verdict in accord- ance with the medical testimony. The funeral of Mr. Cunliffe took place on Satur- day afternoon. Shortly before three o'clock the remains of the deceased arrived at Bank Quay Sta- tion, Warrington, and were conveyed to the hearse which was in waiting. The chief mourners present were Mr. Cunliffe's four sons and his son-in-law, the Rev. Arthur Jones, formerly of Walton, and in addition to these gentlemen there were also present the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. B. B. Pres- cott, Mr. J. Reynolds, and a number of deceased's employes._ The funeral service in the cemetery, where the remains were interred, was conducted by the Rev. A. Jones and Rev. B. B. Prescott. The funeral arrangements were conducted by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, of Bridge-street, Warrington. •

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT!,

The descent on Dublin effected by ,Lord Hartidg- ton and Mr. Gosehen -excites singularly little in- terest There are obvious reasons for this. The main one is the vacuity of the intention which is the basis of the movement, namely, to demonstrate that there are some Irishmen in Dublin and through- out the counties who do not desire to see Home Rule established. It was not necessary to go to Dublin to prove this, and what else the two emis- saries have demonstrated is that the opposition is sectional and numerically insignificant. Of course, the landlords and a considerable proportion of the professional classds, do not desire to see the direc- tion of public affairs in the hands of representa- tives of the people. No one supposed they did. Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen might have been more profitably employed than in eliciting a formal declaration to this effect. Beyond this fundamental weakness of the expedition is the lack of power on the part of either emissary to command attention by platform speeches. -Lord Hartington has now delivered himself, bodyand soul,to work the ends of the Conservative Government. People know beiore hand whet he will say, and thus the attractive ele- ment of surprise is absent from his speeches. As for Mr. Goschen, he suffers the penalty of aU rene- gades. After due deliberation he thought proper to sacrifice a high position of independence to take the shilling and wear the livery of the political op- ponents of a lifetime. After 'protesting he would not give a blank cheque to Lord Salisbury, he passed over the document, and how it may be filled in ia really matter of very slight public interest " The decision reported to have been come to by the Government to defer the'summoning of Parlia- ment till the end of February is fresh evidence of their determination to make the most of the for- tuitous circumstance that kept them in office. The tendency of recent years has been to ante-date rather thanto postpone the usual time for the open- ing of a new session. In the good old times Parlia- ment was invariably summoned to meet somewhere between the 3rd and Bth of February, according as the date fell on a Thursday. Six years ago, when Mr. Gladstone was in power, and Ireland was in a state of disturbance, the new year was scarcely born before Parliament was summoned. It met on the 7th of January, in accordance with Liberal in- stinct, which, in moments of emergency, seeks counsel with the popular assembly. The Conserva- tive instinct is, naturally enough, exactly the other way, and if it were possible for Lord Salisbury and his colleagues to pass through the year without summoning Parliament, they would only too gladly adopt that pleasing expedient. Even if the Minis- terial majority in the House of Commons were im- pregnable, the Government could not face, without embarrassment, the thunderstorm of angry ques- tioning that would arise upon, their successive acts. Mr. 0 Brien's pathetic cry from his prison house, which resounds through the country to-day, would make a formidable text for interrogation if Mr. Balfour were only caught on the Treasury bench. Mr., Balfour will,aecordingly, defer as long as possi- ble his appearance on the Treasury bench, and the period of practically irresponsible Government will be extended to the utmost limits. A good deal of uacertainty still surrounds the exact Mations of Mr. Perna; t9llolrers. with the large sums of MOTiac re'mitted from iiineriett in fur- therance of the national Cause. That the Irish numbers largely profit by the dispensation of the money is broadly alleged in some quarters, and is indignantly denied in others. I had the opportu- , nity the other dayof learning the fact from a mem- ber of the party, whose financial circumstances are such as to place him in the position of a disinter- ested witness. He did not think it nesessary or useful to obscure the fact that a very, considerable portion of the money subscribed for campaigning purposes is paid in the form of a sustentation fund for, numerically, a large section of the Irish meixi- bers. It is, indeed, obvious, -.that the campaign could not be conducted es other, terms. A large number of these gentlemen, before they were launched upon public life avowedly had no visible meansof existence, It is obvious that theycould not, without assistance, pay even the travelling expenses ' dennected with their attendance upon Parliamen- tary duties, much less live t large in 'London for six or seven months of the year. This necessity has been recognised by Mr. Parnell, and there exists a Vegular system of payment, partly in the term of a Weekly allowance, and otherwise in the liberal provision for "expenses." The Chancellor of the Parnellite , Exchequer is Mr. Biggar, who upon pay day, draws whatever cheques are necessary. and hands -them to designated individuals. There is, I find, an undercur- rent of good-humoured complaint that Mr. Biggar is a little niggardly and disposed to dis- pense cheques to the limit of .ClO or -£l5, when in- dividual merit seems to demand recognition coming nearer to the extent of £2O or .£3O. But, on the whole, the work is quietly and effectively done. The fullest confidence is placed in Mr. Biggar's rectitude and business capaeity, and it will be understood that he occupies a position of considerable authority and respect among the rank and file of his col- leagues. As I have said, not all the eighty-six Irish members are in receipt of wages. The fund is ad- ministered much upon the principle which directs the distribution of the pension of ex-Cabinet Ministers. If a member of the Party declares his inability to sustain, without assistance, the posi- tion he is called upon to fill he is provide]. with suitable means. Sir Charles Dilke's second article on the British Army, which is the most important contribution to magazine literature of December, has deepened the sensation created by the introductory article. The statements put forward by Sir Charles are very grave, and the deductions made are well calculated to disturb that equanimity which is a marked feature in the national charac- ter. What makes the article more notable is the deadly detail with which it is crowded. It is not a vague sound of alarm, a muster of general state- ments, such as form the staple of speeches on the subject of British defence delivered to empty benches, by the colonels and the admirals in the House of Commons, what time the army and navy estimates are in committee. Sir Charles Dilke has always been noted as one of the most careful and responsible Parliamentary debaters. His article in the December " Fortnightly " bristles with refer- ence to specific sources of information, many avail- able for reference. Such reference Sir Chas. Dilke challenges. and in military circles, just now, there is an animatee movement in search of corroboration or contradiction. The death of Lord Dalhousie, following so swiftly on the death of his wife, has struck the public faney with a keen emotion of sympathy. The end of their homeward journey from America is the churchyard, where they he in the same grave, re- calling the story told in the old ballad. Lady Nancie was laid in the cold churchyard, Lord Lovel was laid in the choir, And out of her bosom there grew a red rose, And out of his bosom a brier. The last time I saw a,dy Dalhousie she was stand- ing at the top of the stairs at Dover House, review- ing the brilliant company that had assembled for the official "At Home" of herself and her husband, then the newly-appointed Secretary for Scotland. She Was in, the full materity of her beauty, in the highest spirits, and, apparently, in perfect health. In a particularly brilliant season this assembly at Dover House was long talked of as the most successful. To Lady Dalhousie had oc- curred the happy thought of drawing upon the re- sources of the Wqr Office, for the loan of some of the disused military stores. The walls of the re-

ception rooms in Dover House were decorated with coats of arms, with helmets, spears, and banners. The effect was as striking as it was novel. Lady Dalhousie recEived with almost girlish delight the congratulations that poured in upon her. This was little more than twelve months ago, and now the red rose and the brier have been planted in a Scot- tish churchyard. Lord Dalhousie, for a short time known as Lord Ramsay, always looked more like a simple sailor than a per of the realm and a rising minister of state. He was a singularly conscien- tious man, and actually thought, being called tothe position of a hereditary legislator, it behoved him to scorn •delights and spend laborious days in master- ing the questions of the day. His untimely death is a marked loss to the House of Lords, which can ill spare men of his stamn :t PIO altelOttird of the private affairs of Mr. Bor- -IRM, but lately member for St. !Austell and Under Secretary to the Local Government Board in Mr. Gladstone's last Ministry, has come with great shock upon the general public. Every one was surprised when last summer Mr. Borlase's application for the Chiltern Hundreds was announced. Mr. Gladstone personally requested him,to reconsider his decision. But at an interview with the Liberal whip, Mr. Bor- lase made it clear that he had no option in the mat- ter, and that it was with difficulty some brief period of delay was arranged. Then came the sequel of the bankruptcy,' and the sale of the effects at Laregan, including the priceless library. How a comparatively young man of good family, of ample means, with his foot well planted on the ladder of political advancement, found himself in this pod= ,ton no one could say with authority; but storlesif dissipation and gaming were put about. Now the ruthless ordeal of the Bankruptcy Court has brought out the whole vulgar story, and there is much shak- ing of heads and uplifting of hands. Personally, whether in appearance, manner, or conversation, .• Mr. Borlase was the last person in the world to be suspected of such a liaison. He was just the kind of man to be righteously shocked when London society trembled with indignation when some con- spicuous sinner against morals was convicted of the crowning crime of being found out.

Dr. SEPHTON reported that the number of births for ' the month ending *November 30th was, males 14,, females 12; deaths, males 7, females 11. The death rate was equal to 15.6 per 1,000 against 10.8 in the corresponding month of last year.--Hospitat Accomnuxlatibn : In his re- ,,port the inspector referred to,a small-pox case having occurred in/ Liverpool-road, hi the Authority's dis- trict, and it was stated that efforts had been made to get the patient into the 'infectious diseases hospital belong- ing to the Warrington Corporation. Dr. Sherratt had brought the case under the notice of Dr. Goma.. the medical officer for the borough, and the latter gentleman had communicated with the Town Clerk. The Town Clerk had in consequence witten as follows to Dr. Gornall : "I have seen the chairman of the Sanitary- Committee respecting the small-pox case in rural district, and I am instructed to inform you that as our accommodation is at present very much strained, we cannot accept any cases from a district which does not codtribute to the support of the Hospital."—Mr. Jolley said a sufficient reason for that letter was that the hospital was at preSent full, and the tents outside that were used were also full.—The CHAIRMAN said that affairs;showed how incumbent it was upon that Authority to have some resources of their own within the walls of the work- house. It was agreed that the medical officer (Dr. Sepli- ton)should visit the case, and take such measures with regard to it as he thought best.

div.head: FIRES NEAR WARRINGTON AND RUNCORN,
div.p: FIRES NEAR WARRINGTON AND RUNCORN,

. At about ten o'clock r.oll Sunday morning informa- tion was receiv IA the Warrington Fire Brigade Station th.C4 ft fire had broken out at Parkside Farm, Aston, hi the occupation of Messrs. G. and J. Percival. Messages were also sent to Runcorn and Preston Brook, and in a very short space of time the respective brigades were on the spot, the Warring- ton contingent being under the charge of Superin- tendent Turner. It appears that between eight and nine o'clock in the morning it was discovered that the shippon was on fire, and steps were then taken to summon the aid of the fire brigades in the dis- trict. The fire had broken out at the west end of the shippon, and, as there was a strong wind blow- ing at the time, the flames were carried along with great rapidity, the consequence being that the whole of the shippon, which is of considerable length, was soon well alight. The combined bri- gades played on the flames, but two or three hours elapsed before the conflagation showed any signs of being checked. Near the shippon is a large wooden erection, in which was a valuable lot of cows, and steps were at once taken to remove them from their place of danger. This was successfully accom- plished, and by this means the loss was to no incon- siderable extent minimised. The shipper' was com- pletely gutted, the lofts being burnt out, and all that remains are the boundary walls. It contained at the time of the outbreak a valuable collection of agricultural produce, all of which has either been consumed or rendered useless. With reference to the cause of the outbreak nothing definite is known. The damage done amounts to nearly £l.ooo. It is understood that the loss is covered by insurance in the Globe Society, for which Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, of Frodsham, are local agents. Shortly before eleven o'clock on Thursday even- ing an alarm of fire was received at the Warrington fire station, and it was found that an outbreak had occurred at Orford, a haystack belonging to Mr. Ashbrook having by some means, at present un- known, become ignited. The brigade, with Captain , Turner in charge, at once proceeded to the place, , and succeeded, after three hours' work, in saving about half the stack. Damage to the amount of about £25 was sustained.

Tus TRAFALOAR DISTURBANCES.—Mr. Cunninghamo Graham, M.P., and Mr. John Burns were again before the Magistrate at Bow-street, on Thursday, charged with obstructing and assulting the police in Trafalgar- square, on Sunday, November 13th. The case for the prosecution having been closed by Mr. Poland, evidence was brought fori.vard by Mr. Asquith, M.P. who re- presented Mr. Graham, to show there had been an un- interrupted right of public meeting in the square since 1844. Among the witnesses were Sir E. J. Reed, M.P., and Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P. At the close of the case for tho defence, Mr. Vaughan said that in a matter invol- ving such a difficult point of law he could do nothing but commit the defendants for trial at the Central Criminal Court. They were accordingly so committed, bail being allowed in both cases. HOME AND CLOtHES. as Sweet as a Rose when Hudson's Dry Soap is used. Try a Penny Packet. Softens water.— Add EXTRAORDINAY POSTPONEMENT OF A MARRIAGH : DISAP- PEARANCE OF A Noncs.—On Thursday forenoon a large number of persons gathered in the vicinity of the Con- gregational Chapel, Orinskirk-street, to witness the mar- riage of Mr. Samuel Glover. manager of the St. Helens Corporation Gasworks, and Miss Annie Brown Sharpies- the eldest daughter of Mr. Christopher Sharpies, draper, St. Helens, but through an extraordinary reason the in- teresting ceremony had to be postponed. Notice of the intended marriage was given to Mr. Welsh, deputy, ' registrar, in St. Helens' on the 22nd of October, and it was Mr. Welsh's duty to forward such notice to Mr. Hartley, superintendent registrar at Pres- cot, in whose office the notice should lie for twenty-two days. All arrangements were made for the wedding, but upon inquiry on Wednesday night it was found that the certificate had not been received by either Mr. Welsh or Mr. Chorley, the deputies in St. Helens,and on further inquiry at Prescot it was foundthat the notice had not been received there, it having in some extraor- dinary manner disappeared after leaving Mr. Welsh's hands. An intimation was given that the marriage could not take place without the statutory time being complied with, and it was decided to take out a special licence, which only requires twenty-four hours' notice, so that the marriage might take place as soon as pos- sible. The people commenced to arrive at the Congrega- tional Chapel an hour before the time fixed for the cere- mony. and hundreds went away disappoimed. CHAPTER XII. A GLEAM OF LIGHT.

There could be no question of bail this time.l Martin Derrick had been spared imprisonment before, but there was no escape -for him now. Just n little time was allowed him to glVe some directions to- Richards about the farm, and to write a letter to Mr. Harrison, a lawyer at Tavistock,.. while! Watkins mounted guard over his prisoner, sitting in a chair close to the door of the smoking-room where Martin was writing. Anne, meanwhile, was in her brother's bedroom packing a portmantead with some of his clothes; her niind was quite clear and collected, and she thought of everything he would be likely to requite. Presently she came • downstairs again, and went into the smoking4oom, Watkins rising respectfully as she entered. Martin rose too, fastening down the envelope of his letter as he-did so. "This is to Mr. Harrison, the lawyer, Anne; he'll do the best he can for me no doubt; and now I am just ready to start." , Then, as lie looked into her face, which was white with anguish, he held out both his hands to her, and for a moment she hid her face on his shoulder,,whilst Watkins went to the window at the other side of the room, put his head out as far as it Woilkl go, and appeared to be dceply interested in the domestic aflairs of the fowls in the farmyard without. " If, it were ric4 for the thought of that poor girl upstairs, Lunt still more of you, Anne I should go away cheerfully enough this time," said ilartin. And indeed it seemed to his sister that Martin was , like another man. At the former coroner's inquest, , which was held after the death of Dick Lawson; Martin had seemed stunned with misery. He had scarcely thanked the two gentlemen—his landlord and the vicar—who had :lone him the friendly office of becoming bail for him; he had, ap- peared indifferent as to what became of him. Now he was alert, vigorous, self-reliant; , his eyes were bright, the colour had come back tu his face; he looked like a men ready to make a gallant tight for his libeaty and life. "Keep up a good heart, Anne, and don't worry about me more than you can help. You and Richards between you will be able to entry on thefaim allright this winter, and by the end of January this matter Will be settled one way or. %another." "01i; Martin, if there is any justice in Heaven or earth, you'll be cleared of this at 'once 1" "Well, something fresh may be found out at any moment.' Ever so many things came into my head to-day as I listened to the witnesses. There's some- thing mixed up in thib that people haven't gOt any notion of as yet. The Coroner said Susan had notan enemy in the world. What does he know abinit it —what do we know—her own family ? "and then : Martin's voice lowesed. "Don't waste your time, Anne, in looking too near home—you know what, • I mean—though there's something that puzzles ! me even in that quarter. What did Stambridge tifean by saying I had had a quarrel with Susan ? ' ' Then Martin addressed the policeman, who at once • turned round from the window—" Watkins, I am going upstairs to see my sister Susan—for the last time. • _ .

They went upstairs, Anne first, then Martin, with Watkins keeping close behind him, and entered a, little room, where the blinds were drawn down over the casement windows,and there was a faint fragrance of flowers.. Susan, white, cold, and placid, lay on her little white bed, some white chrysanthemums and sprays of rosemary were strewed on her bosom, and on the pillow. Her beautiful dark hair was brought a little over her forehead, and hid the ghastly bullet. wound. The brothdr and sister remained for a minute in silence, their heads bowed down, on each side of the bed. Watkins stood at the door, his helmet in his hand. Then Martin stooped, and kissed Susan's cold lips without a word. After that he walked firmly across the room. "Your prisoner is ready," said he to the policeman. r ("And if 'twa,s the last word I had to speak," so Watkins remarked teNhie wife that evening, 'l'd fake my Bible oath that 'Martin Derrick isan innocent , Martin was gone, carried off to the police-station at Tavistock ; and Anne went to her own room, threw herself down on the bed, and turned her face to the wall. For a Hine she lay half conscious, feeling as though her life was ebbing away from her. An hour passed; there came a gentle knock at the door, but She made no a-newer ; then the doer was opened, and Mrs. Richards entered with a tray, I've brought ye a drop of het soup, Miss Derrick, and ,a,bit of chicken." Then, as Anne feebly shook her head; the woman Went on "Ma dear soul, do ye now take automat to keep up your strength. You'll have to go up before the magistrates at Tavistock to-morrow you know, and you'll see the master again, and hear how he's getting on." ' "I know—l know ! " and Anne started up, reused by the acute pang of remembrance that a. further ordeal awaited her brother and herself to-morrow. "Yes, I must keep up till that is over. , Oh, Mrs. Richards, think of all my brother has gone through in the-last two years, doesn't it seem as thouglithere was no pity in all Heaven or earth for'us ? " Mrs. Richards had no gift for uttering , words of consolation; her kindly nature could express itself , only in acts. "I'm come to stop a bit with you, Miss Derrick, and send Eliza home. She's no use at all now; she does nothing but cry and holler, because her father's been, telling of hp that she's been and swore the master's life away -with her tales; and she can't abide the thought of being had up before the magis- trates to-morrow as witness, and then there is the Exeter 'sizes to come after. But what's the girl to do, when she's put upon her oath? The treth's bound to come out, and so I says to her father." "Eliza did perfectly right," said Anne, who, revived by the food Mrs. Richards had prevailed upon her to take, seemed to have become more like her energetic self again. "Where is the girl? I want to see her." "She's in such a taking; Miss Derrick, fit to cry her eyes out." "Never mind, tell her to come to me, and say I am not angry with her, not in the least." So the mother presently led the daughter into the room ; the girl's eyes were all inflamed with crying, and her hands were plucking convulsively at her apron. She was a comely, honest-looking girl of seventeen, and Anne, who had known her from her childhood, had perfect reliance upon her truthfulness. "Come here, Eliza, and don't cry so; you have done nothing but what is perfectly right. Come tell me all about it, there's a good girl,' said Anne very kindly; _" tell me all over again what happened on Friday afternoon and evening whilst I was out. Begin at the beginning, and tell me what time it was When Miss Susan asked you to go to the dressmaker's." " It was close upon four o'clock as far as I can mind," began Eliza a little consoled by her mis- tress's sympathy. "It, began to get duskish early, be- cause of the fog, and I know I lighted that there lamp in the hall as you found put out, miss, before I went away." " Well,did Miss Susan seem very anxious about your going to the dressmaker's? Because, you know, Miss Taylor had promised to come the next morning, and there could be no such great hurry about the lace." "That's just what Miss' Taylor said, miss. She hadn't cut out the body of the dress even, and says she to me, 'Whatever put it into Miss Susan's head to send you along here bothering about the lace trimming to-night,when she knows quite well I've never had no time to puta scissors into that brown silk of hers, and its done up in the paper now, just as it came from the shop." Anne's eyes brightened as the girl went on. These trivial remarks had a bearing on the case far more important than Eliza could imagine. I Well, Eliza, I am pleased you remember all that so clearly. Now go on, what did Miss Susan isay to you about not hurrying back? I want to hear all about that again." "She said to me two or three times over, so I couldn't but take particular notice of it,for you know, miss, if you'll please to excuse my goyim-,t' of it—Miss Susan wasn't one in general to think about a pool girl's having a bit of pleasure--she says, says she, You needn't hurry home again Eliza, you can go and see your friends in the village and have a cup of tea. You won't be wanted here till Miss Derrick comes home from Tavistock, and that won't.' be much before six o'clock, I know. P'raps I shall lock up the house, and take a bit of a walk this evening,' says she, so you'd better not come back just yet, or you won't get in." " Wake a walk in that fog, and getting dark tool"
Ann was almost werwhelmed. Everything that Eliza told her confirmed the vague suspicion floating through her mind. The curtain was beginning to lift —but then what a dark, mysterious vista was being
revealed beyond! "Well then, Eliza, did you go and see any of yolif

Mends in the village'?" - "Yes, miss. I stopped and had a cup of tea with Mrs. Westlake, and then I thought Ifd go and Si with mother a bit on the way home. Iltnowed bow 'I should hear you driving home in the trap, and then I could run out and be here as soon as ever you

wanted me." "And. • then "—Anne's voice faltered and a deadlY . pallor came aver her face, but she forced herself to go on. "Then, Eliza, as you were just going into ' your mother's house you heard—tell me what it wee, you heard." But nere Eliza burst into loud sobbing, and it was' ' some minutes before she was able to go on. "I heard something—Something as now I krerf what 'twas—l shall never get over—never." • "Try to tell me, my poor girl," said Anne, Yer7 „ gently. • . "'was like this here, Miss Susan, she gave OM. Awful screeches—' Martin, Martin 1' she boilers twice over, and then in a minute came a little bang;., and ~• I was skeered, and I runs into mother's house. "And did Eliza tell you, Mrs. Richards, what she had heard?" - 4 Yes, she did,. Miss Derrick," replied the woman sorrowfully; "and I was busy washing up the tett things, arid didn't pay much heed to the girl, worse, - luck. 'Don't come here with your foolish tales, Eliza; says I to her ; if you (lid hear Miss Susan a-screecbin,, out, what's that to you? She's one • as'll screech if she sees a spider. (You'll forgive mY saying that now, please, Miss Dervick.) like as not there's been a rat about, and the master's been and- shot it'; lie will shoot the rats sometimes when he sees 'em, as you. know, Miss Derrick." "And, of course, you and Eliza both took it for granted that Mr. Derrick tiLturasti',, "Why, yes, miss," said Mrs. Richards, reluctantlY; "'twas only nateral as we should. But now we know the rights of it. The poor soul was calling out for help in her last Moments, hoping as the master would hear and come to her." Anne sighed bitterly. These honest kindly folk might put perfect trust in the young master they had always served so faithfully, but would the rest of the world accept this explanation of poor Susan'' death-cry? • ' There was no more information to be gleaned from Eliza, so Anne dismissed her for the present, with feiv words of praise for having stated so clearly el i l she knew. This one vitally mporfant fact had• been established by her evidence. Susan had' sone strong inaive for wishing to, get rid of the girl for an hour or two that afternoon and for • being left entirely alone in the house. Anne remembered bow ill and worried and fretful—as if with the pressure of some great anxiety—her naturally good: tempered sister had seemed on the morning of that fatal Friday. - " Susan knew the day before that Martin would he out on the moor all that afternoon, and she knew that I was going to TaviStock market, and that all would be left in the house with only Eliza. 'at four o'clock that afternoon she sent out 'Viz' . with the excuse of a message—for it wo.s clearil nothing but, an excuse—to Miss Taylor; and she said all she could to prevent the girl from coming back before I was expected home. : Now why did Susan take such great care to be in the' house alone -- what was she going to do, or whom was she expecting to see ? Surely not James Stambridge, her honest and respectable lover, who was going to make her his wife in a few days' time." It. appeared never to have occurred to the Coroner to inquire who* Stambridge was all that Friday evening. " Stambridge is a man above sus; picion," thought Anne, rather bitterly; then her Just and candid nature re-asserted itself. "I own I inclined to be unfair to him; he's an honest man he's a hard one, and it's ridiculous, because a man is' vulgar in his looks and ways, and because he is stuck- up, and talks sometimes hike a book, its ridiculous because I can't abide him, to suppose that he 158.1 murderer I Besides, what would his motive be 1 It could only be because he was mad with rage he; cause of her threatening to jilt him' and I sliouh` neVer have thought that Stambridge was a hasty', violeat sort of man. By-the-by, how is it that Susan told me they had had a great quarrel, and then he denies it on his oath, and says it was she and Martill who had quarrelled? Now, we know that fiat is a lie.' And so Anne racked her weary brains with con' lectures, until at last she. fell asleep from sheer 0. haustion.
(To be continued,)

['HE CRISIS 1N PRANCE.-THE PRESI-

PARIS, MONDAY NIGUT:—II is not unnatural that 8012Ie 1 loubts should still prevail whether M. Grevy's latest stir- tender is final or not. This time, however, it is thought .lbat there is no prospect of the President backing out of tis announced intention, and that reason for this opinion s that his. own raper, La Pais, which throughout the mists has been most accurately posted up as to M. %ivy's intentions, to-day, for the first time, announces at lit will resign on Thursday, and that the Congress will take place on Friday, which happens to be the anni- rersary of Napoleon's coup d'itat. The nmes Paris correspondent, discussing the chence.s 3f the candidates for the Presidency, says that M. de Freyeinet will win if M. Jules Ferry is not elected at the krst ballot. Nevertheless, everybody distrusts M. de Freycinet. The Catholics dread his • accession, as in- fallibly involving separation of Church and State, and as an immense dancer for their Church. Id. de Freycinet t-eing a Prole 'ant, his accession requires a modification af that part o. the Concordant which empowers the Chief Magistrate to present bishops and cardinals. He IS aware of this, and for some days has been negotiating the modification. This, however, must be submitted m Parliament, and the present Chamber will repeal the Concordant as soon as it requires touching. "As M. Clemenceau will be the fir,st Premier, and as separation of Church and State Ii in his programme, it will be a settled thing. This involves the abolition of the Budget of Worship, which is 50,000,000 f., and to make up for it the Catholics will have t 3 find i00,000,000r. for lawsuits with the parishes, and the cost of new build- ings will fall upon them. It is madness to think that they can do this. As for the Royalists, M. de Freycinet is the man who banished their Princes. To contribute directly or indirectly to his election seems monstrous. In the eyes of financiers he is the man who expended the milliard on public works which ruined the Treasury. He will give Paris a central Mayoralty and trust affairs to the Radicals, agree to the progressive income tax, and gradually instal Socialism in power. For men of peace, he means the passible return of General Boulanger, and the accession of the Radicals who want war." Penis, Tarresnar.—President Grevy did not resign after all. As soon as the President of the Chamber of Deputies had taken his seat M.Rouvier rose and informed the House that President Grevy—who had announced his intention of sending a message to the Chamber—had reconsidered his determination. Under these circum- stances, the Premier declared that he and his colleagues again tendered their resignations. The sitting was suspended, as was also a sitting of the Senate. THE EUROPEAN SITUATION.-RUSSIA AND GERMANY.-- --IMPROVED RELA-
TIONS.

BERLIN, SUNDAY 14itoirr.—The Czar 11:19 lIMAP the first move towards fulfilling his promise to help to detect the plot of the forged despatches. Immediately after his arrival at St. Petersburg he sent copies of them to the Berlin Foreign Office, where they arrived on Friday. We may therefore shortly expect the publication of some particulars clearing up this mysterious affair. In any case, this prompted ion on the part of the Czar is one proof more that. Prince Bismarck eompletely succeeded in convincing, him that he had been de- ceived. At the Russian Embassy here, much satis- faction Li felt at the effect produced lw the Czar's visit, as the Russian representative at Berlin has always done his utmost to maintain friendlyreta• tions between the two caintries. The alleged speech of General Gourko in Polandis partly sneered at and/partly discredited. The general coricensus of opinion seems to be that it has been inisrepmented. It is pointed out that in the speech. as it is reported, there is an allusion to the old age of General °mirk°, who in reality is a man of about 50. The Russian press, which a few days ago pretended not to believe in the forged despatches at all, now begins to attach some credit to the matter. In short, it would seem that Russia is inclined to take ad- vantage of this affair to cover her diplomatic retreat in the Bulgarian question, and to surrender a policy which has only led her from fiasco to fiasco. On the other side, we may expect that the allied Powers will smooth the path of Russia as much as possible.

THE EMIN BEY RELIEF EXPEDITION.— MR. STANLEY IN DIFFICULTIES. BRUNDLS, SUNDAY NIGHT...—A despatch addressed to the Independance Beige, from Leopoldville, in the Congo Free State. says that when the last mail left, Tippo who was recently appointed Governor of Stanley Fall, has not yet sent the promised carriers to Mr.l7. M. Stan- ley at Yambuya for the carriag,,c of ammunition and stores intended by Mr. Stanley for Emin Pasha. The mem- bers ot Mr. Stanley's rearguard were powerless to carry the stores forward alone, and the expedition, therefore, proceeded without the requisite means of relief. It is asserted that Mr. Stanley's expedition ha q latterly suffered afresh from famine, and that manyof its members have died. The action,.or rather the inaction, of Tippn lib has strengthened tin) suspicion that he is not loyal to the State. THE RAILWAY FATALITY AT LATCH-
FORD.

-- - • Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, on Saturday held an en- quiry at the Dog and Dart Dm, Grappenhall, on view of the body of Alice Appleby, (24) a domestic servant, who was killed on the railway at Latchford station on the previous Wednesday evening, under circumstances reported in Our last issue.---Amy As- tall, wife of Jesse Astall, Wash-lane, Latchford, said that the deceased was her sister. Deceased was twenty-four years of age, and was in service at Bowdon. Her home was at Bilstone-stre et, Wolver- hampton. About eight o'clock on Wednesday even- ing deceased came to see witness. After remaining about an hour she went away with the intention of goingto Broadheath station by the-l 2 train from Latchford station. She was then apparently in her usual health and in good spirits. Witness was told next morning that her sister had been killed.— Joseph , Harrison, station master at Latch- ford, said that at about 9-11 on the night of the day in question' he was at the station, when he heard someone at the other end of the platform call out for the stationmaster. Ile and a porter went to a spot about 20 yards from the end of the plat- form, and there found the body of the deceased ly- ing in the "four-foot," on the down line. One of her legs was against the metals, with the foot Crushed off. She was removed to the platform, and a policeman sent for. There was a footpath running parallel with the line for the convenience of passen- gers. It was fenced off with a wire fencing. There was a gate at the end of the platform. No one saw the accident. Deceased had been knocked down by the Buxton lime train„which was rather late on the night in question. Both trains were registered as arriving at 9-14. She had not taken a ticket; and his impression was that she was watching the train by which she intended to travel, and intended, by passing the line at the back of the train, to get in one of the last carriages, when she was knocked down by the Buxton lime train.—P.C. Millington said that on the morning after the accident occurred he found a purse containing £3 ss, on the line, and Mr. Harrison, recalled, said that in his opinion the driver of the train could not possibly have seen the deceased on the line, however sharp a look-out he might have kept. -This was all the evidence taken. —The jury found that the deceased accidentally Met her death.

KAY'S COMPOLIND.—AMRIDa and Bronchitis are immediately relieved by it. Of all Chemists.—Advt. THt DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.—The two prisoners, Thos. Collan, alias Scott, and Michael Harkins, were brought up on remand at Bow-street Police Court, London, on Monday, charged with being concerned in the dynamite conspiracy.—Mr. Poland, for the prosecution, said it would be proved that the prisoners had been in com- munication with two other men Cohen and Melville, or nn Morony, of whom thekrst-named recently died in Lam- beth-road, London ; that they had been traced from America and were in communication with General Mil- ler, or Millen, in Paris. Revolvers of American make had been found in the prisoners' possession. Sergeant Downs, of the City Police, proved arresting Callan in Queen-street, Cheapside. He produced a small tin trunk and Gladstone bag found in his lodgings, as also a loaded revolver and ten loose cartridges. 'Mrs. Maria Bright, landlady of the house where Callan lodged in Islington, said he told her he was a travellor in the tea trade. ,On October the 29th, finding the closet pan choked,, she cleared out about half a bushel of substance like cement or lime, and threw it on the dust bin. The prisoner said it was samples he had thrown away. He received letters addressed "Scott." On the day of his arrest, Detective Wlntyre came and examined the dust bin. Mary Ann Johns, living in the next house, deposed to finding seine substance like cement in her back garden. Her son brought some of it in and put it in the oven. This caused a loud explosion and cracked the oven door. The court adjourned fer a week. JAPANESE GOODS at London Prices, MAYOR and Co., 175 Oxford-street, Manchester.— N.B.
