GREAT UNIDNIsT IEMoisTIATIu
IN DUBLIN.

The Marquis of Hartington and the Chancellor of the Exchequer were the principal speakers at a mass meet- ing of Liberal Unionists. held in the Leinster He; Dublin, last evening. Mr. J. R. Wigham, hon. secretar of the Dublin Chamber of Commerce, Presided, am' amongst those present were the Duke of Leinster, Mak, of Abercom, Professor Dicey, Dor& Stalbridge. Powers court, and Ardelaun. Sir Rowland Blennerhasset. Lot Edward Cavendish, .M.P., Lord Gough, Lord Howth, Mr T. W. Russell. M.P., Lord Fin,gall, Sir Robert Kane, an' Sir Robert Heron. Letters of regret for inability to attend tbe meeting were announced from Mr. John Bright, Sir Hy. James. Lord Selborne, the Duke ef, Westminster, the Duke Argyll, Professor Leckr, Professor Tyndall, Sir Win Thompson, Mr. Craig Sella]., M.P.. Mr. J. H. Tuke, Mt Finlay, M.P., Lord Monk, and others. On entering the hall a few minutes after eight o'clock. Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen were received with great enthusiasm. The CRATRIKAN presented the Unionist leaders with address of welcoinc on behalf of the Dublin Cham- ber of Commerce.

Sir EDWARD SULLIVAN, Bart., moved—" That we hereby declare our unalterable determination to resist by all lawful means every attempt to dissolve the legislative Union between Ireland and Great Britain, end we tender our most hearty thanks to the Right Hon. the Marquis of Hartington and to the Right Hon. George J. Goschen, Chancellor of the Exchequer, for their firm and con- eistent conduct in the defence of the Union, and of our rights a/5 citizens of the United Kingdom." Lord Ilairrisoros, who on rising to address the meet- ing was received with cheers, said he never had the honour of addressing a larger or more enthusiastic meeting than that before which he stood. He knew that the reception accorded to him a Mr. Goschen was in- tended ,to testify to the serviZtfi which the Liberal Unionists generally have rendered to Ireland, and not merely to those which he and his colleague personally had been able to render, and he felt that the importance of the meeting was greater than could be attached to any speeches which he or Mr. Goschen could deliver. A great service had been rendered to the Unionist cause by the speeches which Mr. Chamberlain had recently delivered in Ulster. Mr. Chamberlain had brought before the people of the United Kingdom the importaziee of the loyalist element in Ulster, and the meeting now assembled demonstrated the existence of an infinential minority in Dublin, which altogether repudiated and protested against the assertion that Ireland, as a nation, was determined to abolish the legislative union. (Cheers.) He had had some difficulty in considering upon what points of the Irish question he should address them. It had been said that the question of Home Rule was not that at present before the country, and it might he true that more interest attached to the struggle going on between those who were endeavouring to carry out the 18W in Ireland and those who were endeavouring to break it. He did not underrate the importance of that struggle, and perhaps that was the subject upon which he ought to address them. But he had thought that upon the whole Cis conflict was only a phase in a larger and greater struggle, and that he should do better by attempting to enlist their attention upon the larger subject which underlay all these temporary phases of the Irish question, upon the question which, though ~it might for a moment, be slumbering, would un- doubtedly at shine not distant period, be revived; ,which appeared in all probability likely to be the ques- tion which would be the dividing one between parties in the Parliament of Great Britain; and which for Ire- land and for Irishmen had larger, and wider, and greater, and `deeper issues at slake than any which belonged to a 'merely political or party question. (Cheers.) Therefore he proposed to speak on the government of Ireland, on that question which was known as the Home Rule question. They must look on this question first and foremost, and mainly as it would affect the destinies and progress of Ireland. He did not admit that the majority in favour of Home Rule in Ireland was so large as it appeared to be according to the Parliamentary repre- sentation. Undoubtedly, it was possible, under our present system of Parliamentary representa- tion, that a very large minority should be without Parliamentary representation at all, and but for the accident that a considerable proportion of the Unionist population of Ireland was concentrated in a few coun- ties in the north, the fact would be that the Unionist minority in Ireland, although it might approach in num- bers very nearly to the Separatist majosity might find itself without a representative in Parliament at all. But acknowledging that there was a majority in favour of the Separatist policy proposed in the last Parliament, were the English Home Rulers prepared to grant any- thing which the Irish majority might ask for ? They bad distinctly repudiated any such suggestion, and it devolved upon them to prove that the Home Rule which they were willing to grant was the Home Rule which the Irish were asking for—a thing that would satisfy their desires. To his mind all the indications were in the contrary direction. If they looked at the speeches which had recently been delivered on the sub- ject in America it would be seen that the real object striven for was not for any limited subordinate Parliament, such as was offered to them, but for national independence and complete separation from Great Britain. And again, if they looked at the course of the struggle taking place in Ireland they would see that it partook more of an agrarian struggle for possession of the land than of any reform or change in the system of the Government of Ireland. (Cheers.) He denied that the Irish land question could be satisfatoril,y settled by the intervention of the Irish Parlia- ment; and in reference to the existing depression in agriculture in Ireland he asked whether there was any remedy which had been proposed to Par- liament by the Irish members which Parliament was un- willing to consider. Did they suppose there was any remedy, either for the agricultural depression which per- vaded the whole of Ireland, or for those more intensified forms of agricultural depression which pervaded portions of Ireland, which the Imperial Parliament would not be ready to take up and ,grapple with if any suggestion of a practical character could be made? Were they to suppose that Mr. Parnell and his followers had got some specific for the removal of thee* evils in their pockets which they were unable, or refused to produce to & British Parliament, but which they were going to produce at once for the acceptance of an Irish ' Parliament, and which was going , at once to produce a different state of affairs. He believed that it was doing the people of Ireland the greatest injustice to induce them to believe that evils which were of a purely economical character could be redressed by the action of any political changes. What- ever might have been the case in the past, he believed that the present democratic Parliament of Great Britain was ready, and only too anxious, to listen to arty pro- posal which might be made which could have the effect of improving the condition of any part of Ireland, and it was idle for the Separatist members to persuade the people of Ireland or Great Britain that they had reme- dies which could be adopted by an Irish Parliament which a British Parliament was unwilling to consider. Ile maintained that in the minority which opposed the Home Rule policy were largely included those classes upon which the future prosperity of Ire- land mainly depended. Wherever industry and trade could find an expression, that expression was given by an. overwhelming voice against the policy which was being pressed upon them in the name of the people of Ireland. He did not assert that the industrial classes were unanimously opposed to Home Rule, but he firmly believed ,that the vast majority of those classes were opposed to it, and he maintained that a strong prima facie case had been estab- lished in support of his contention. He had been accused of ignoring Irish national sentiment, but those who made this accusation had either not taken the trouble to read what he had said on the subject, or had wilfully misrepresented it. (Cheers.) In conclusion, having contrasted the position of things in Scotland with that in Ireland, his lordship said that if Irishmen had been allowed to have leas in- fluence over the administration of their own affairs than Scotchmen it had arisen mainly from the fact that Irish- men had, in times past, siiown their unwillingness to conform to the law of Parliament, even when it was a just law, or to respect the authority of the Imperial Executive Goverement, but whatever might have been their influence in the past, he believed that now the democracy of Great Britain was fully and fairly represented in the Imperial Parliament, and that , no other desire existed in the mind of any subject of Great Britain than to do full and equal justice to Ireland. It was in the power of Irish- men to , obtain for themselves equal attention to their grievances. Not by means of rebellion, of forcible resistance to the law, but by simply acknow- ledging the existence of irrevocable facts, could they have that full measure of confidence which they' (the Unionists) on their part would always be willing and ready to extend in full measure to the people of Ireland. (Loud cheers.)

Mr. Goscntur said every flattery and cajolery and misrepresentation had been used in order to mislead the English people and suborn them as accomplices for the Borne Rule cause. Referring to the charges made against Mr. Balfour in the Irish press, he said that if ever a Minister had the sympathy of his colleagues for the gallant execution of the policy placed in his hands, Mr. Balfour was that man. (Cheers) Mr. John Morley had said that he (Mr: Got:schen) and Lord Hartington were coming to Ireland to nurse a force and breathe new life into the spirit of dissension which had been the bane of Ireland. He (Mr. Goschen) would like to know who was responsible for the dissension 'that existed? He should have thought that Mr. was the last man looking to Ks a.hhies to have said what he did. Sir William ilansim up the commerce of Dublin as simply con- sisting of brewing and the whisky trade. This joke, on the lips of 31. merry roysterer such as Sir William Harcourt., became an outrage when it was ac- cepted by a serious po!itician such as Mr. Morley. (Groans.) lie bad been under the impression that Mr. Morley, the austere St. Just of the Gladstonian party, had but small respect for Sir Witham

Harcourt, the Falstaff of polities. (Laughter.) That made his endorsement all the more remarkable. Had Mr. Morley been so absorbed while he was in Dublin with hie Home Rule dreams that he had no time to dis- cover what Dublin commerce, industry, and learning meant? Mr. Morley treated the loyalists and landlords as identical; but there were loyalists outside Belfast and the landlords' class. (Cheers.) Attempts were made to throw opprobrium upon the pro- fessional, mercantile, and industrial classes. It was significant that in Ireland these classes threw their whole influence on the side' of 1. the integrity of the Empire. (Cheers.) Sir George Trevelyan and others spoke of the unparalleled unanimity of the Home Rule movement, but such a phrase was unwarrantable. Neither in Italy nor Hungary, which were alluded to by him could they have got together such a meeting in opposition to what were there truly described as national movements, and he defied the picturesque •Trevelyan, the didactic Morley, or the profound Histoncua to cite any analogous meetings in either Milan or resth to this one in Dublin. It was a bastard Nationalism at which the Home Rulers were aiming. (Loud and prolonged cheers.) It was a Nationalism that could never satisfy, but could only irritate and produce unendurable friction. It could not satisfy, it could not settle this question, and if it could not settle this question, would it increase the resources of Ireland, would it minister to its development? The Government sympathised with the poverty of the i Irish tenants, and they would do what n them lay to meet the difficulties of the case. There was no measure connected with Ireland in which he did not take the Irish view till Home Rule broke loose from what might be considered the doc- trines of loyalty. The rebel party had claimed to annex a noble phrase as a monopoly of their own. But, uttered with as deep a devotion to this fair portion of the Britiah Empire, and inspired by as profound a hope that peace and plenty and every coveted national blessing might revisit that, troubled land, there rang from the hearts of the British Unionists and of loyal Irishmen that common cry, "Cod Save Ireland." (Cheers.) Both Lord Harrington and Mr. tioschen subsequently addressed an overflow meeting, and they were the recipients of thanks for their speeches.

Lord Harlington presided at a great Unionist banquet in Dublin on IN ednesday night, Mr. Goschen being one of the guests. Mr. Goschen replied to the toast of the Unionist cause, and in the course of his speech dealt with the charges made against Lord Hartington and himself of having ignored Mr. O'Brien in their speeches of the previous night. Their experience in England and Scot- land had proved that as large and as representative meet- ings could be gathered in support of the Unionist cause as could be pointed to by the other side, who were fond of declaring that the majority of opinion was in favour of Home Rule. A conference of the leaders of the Liberal Union was held on Thursday, at the residence of the Right Hon. W. F. Cogan, formerly M.P. for Kildare. Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen were present. The proceedings were private. Lord Harlington returned to England on Thurs- day everting.
IR.ELAND.

It is stated that the legality of the conviction of the Ennis nevrsven or, for selling United Ireland. will be tested, and that thousands of the same impression were sold at Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son's branch establish- ment in Dublin.

..... On Monday. the Queen's Bench, Dublin, refused to change from the City of Cork the trial of Dr. Croy, for the murder of his wife by poisoning her, the Court not being satisfied that there.was reasonable ground to allege he would not get a fair trial. It is stated that Mr. O'Brien has lost eleven pounds in weight since his imprisonment. Mr. Mandeville has been on bread and water; and on Monday evening a writ was served, at his instance, on tlwi governor (Mr. Feather- stonehaugh) for assault in taking away his clothes. A letter is published from Mr. Dillon, in reference to the strictures by Nationalists on the conduct of members who have evaded arrest. He says that they offered to avoid capture, if he thought they could thus •serve the cause. He considered they were actuated by the highest patriotism, and they have done excellent service since the warrants were issued.

On Monday various members of Boards of Poor-Law Guardians visited Mr. Pyne, M.P., at Lisfinny Castle, and presented him with an address congratulatory of his pluck in resisting arrest. Mr. Fyne, who was lowered by ropes from the top of the castle, thanked the Guardians for their address, and, amidst their cheering and shout- ing of "God save Ireland," he was again hoisted aloft to his quarters. On Sunday there was a Nationalist demonstration at Waterford to protest lining the conduct of the Govern- ment in suppres.sine the Limerick demonstration com- memorative of the execution of the " Manchester martyrs." Bands paraded the principal streets, followed by thousands of person wearing mourning badges. The Mayor of Waterford presided at the meeting, which was addressed by aldermen. councillors. and Roman Catholic priests. The proceedings passed off quietly. On Monday, while the steamship Thetis was swing- ing from one berth to another in the Belfast Docks, a boat containing two men, named McAllister and Thomp- son, was caught between the vessel and a schooner, Mc.Allister being crushed to death. Thompson had a miraculous escape, diving when he saw the two vessels coming into collision.—The schooner Anne Jones, of Aberystwith, which went ashore in Belfast Lough during Sunday's gale, has become a total wreck. A deputation ot Liberal members of Parliament, headed by Mr. Illingworth, visited the Ponsonby estate on Monday, it being the anniversery of the plan of cam- paign being adopted by the tenants. The deputation was met at Killeagli by .Mr. Lane, M.P., and Canon Keller. After an inspection of some of the barricaded farmhouses, a meeting was held at Inchiquin, at which Mr. Illingworth and other members spoke. The party then drove to Youghal, and addressed another meeting at the Town HalL A Government reporter and a num- ber of police were present at Inchiquin.

A convention of delegates from all the branches of the National League in Lord Dillon's Mayo estates was held on Tuesday at, Aghamore, near Ballyhaunis. The Rev. Fr. Me. Alpine presided, and amongst those present were Mr. Cully, M.P., and Mr. Conway, M.P.—The Chairman an- nounced that Lord Dillon had consented to give all the tenants a reduction of thirty per cent on the judicial rents, and the offer was accepted unanimously amid great enthusiasm. This decision puts an end to a long- standing and acrimonious dispute. A brutal murder took place in Dublin on Sunday after- noon. Eliza Hynes, an old woman of 60, was found dead in the house in which she and a woman, named Fraser, lived, in a lane in Leeson-street. Fraser states that she left the house at seven o'clock on Saturday morning, and on returning in the evening, and, not being able to get in, she supppsed Hynes had gone out, and she went and passed the night in a neighbour's house. llynes's house was broken into on Sunday afternoon, and the old woman was found lying dead on the floor in a pool of blood, with her skull broken. It is believed that robbery was th motive of the murder, as the deceased was reported to be well off. Her trunk had been broken open.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF THE EARL OF
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF THE EARL OF
DALHOUSIE, K.T.

The Earl of Dalhousie died unexpectedly at Havre on Friday morning, he having outlived his wife, the countess, only a few hours- It appears that he retired to bed at 11 o'clock on Thursday night, in apparently his usual health, and a few hours afterwards was seized by an apoplectic fit, and although medical aid was at hand, he never rallied, but died about nine o'clock on Friday morning. The deceased, John Williarn Ramsay, Earl of Dalhousie, Baron Ramsay, of Dalhousie, and Baron Ramsay and Caryngtoun, in the Peerage of Scotland, and Baron Ramsay, of Glenmark, County Forfar, in the Peer- age of the United Kingdom, was the Meet son of George Maule, 12th Earl of Dalhousie, and Sarah Frances, only daughter of the late Mr. W. Robertson, of Logan House, and was born June 29th, 1847. He formerly served in the Royal Navy, was appointed lieutenant in 1867, and promoted to the rank of commander in 1874, but retired from the service after having served on board the Britannia up to 1879. He then went to Oxford, and was for some time at Balliol College. He unsuccessfully con- tested Liverpool in the Liberal interest on the death of Mr. Torr, in February, 1:40, hut was returned at the general election held shortly afterwards. He had, how- ever, to vacate his seat in July the same year owing to his accession to the peerage. For some years he held an appointment in the household of the Duke of Edinburgh, and ass Equerry to his Royal Highness from 1874 to 1876, when he was appointed extra equerry. He succeeded to the earldom and other honours on the death of his father, July 218 t,, 1880. In September, 1880, he was appointed a Lord-in-Waiting to the Queen, and was made a Knight of the Thistle in 1881, in place of the late Earl of Airlie. On the resignation of Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan, he was appointed Secretary of State for Scotland, which post he held till the breaking up of Mr. Gladstone's Government The deceased earl married December 6th, 1877, the Lady Ida Louise Bennet, youngest daughter of the Earl of Tankerville, and they leave issue five sons, the eldest Arthur George Maule, Lord Ramsay, born in September, 1878. The deceased I peer has an only brother living, the Hon. Charles Maule Ramsey, formerly a lieutenant lathe Royal Artillery.

The remains of the late Lord and Lady:Dalhousie were received at Dalhousie Castle, near Edinburgh, from Lon- don, on Thursday morning, and interred in Cockpen churchyard. The coffins were met it the entrance to the castle by a deputation of the tenantry. • They were covered with immortelles from the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Buceleuch, the Earl of Dalkeith, the Earl and Countess of Aberdeen, Lord and Lady Rosebery, the Dowager Countess of Dalhousie, Lady Claud Hamilton, Dr. Herbert Spencer, and others. At noon service was conducted in the Established Church. The service was of short duration, and the coffins were laid in the same grave, side by side. The funeral was numerously attended, those present includ- ing deputations from Lord Dalhousie's Forfarshire tenantry and the Earl of Tankerville's Northumberland tenants.

div.head: Mil. JOHN BRIGHT ON "FAIR TRADE."
div.p: Mil. JOHN BRIGHT ON "FAIR TRADE."

A Yorkshire correspondent, having written Mr. John Bright. pointing out that there was a growing leaning towards Fair Trade; that, apart from politics, it was becoming a question of work and bread; that some of the Sheffield workmen said they had been subjected to repeated reductions in wages owing to the imposition of foreign tariffs on their masters' goods, and that some of these working-men were under he impression that he (Mr. Bright) had modified his opinions with respect to Free Trade; Mr. Bright has replied:—

'One Ash, Rochdale, November 25th, 1887. "Dear Sir,—l cannot be more in favour of Free Trade than I have been in time past; nor am I, nor can I be, less in favour of it than heretofore. the depression of trade of some recent years has afforded additional proof of the wisdom of our policy, and I believe we have suf- fered less than 'the countries which still adhere to the protective system. Doubtless you will have observed that the Fair 1 raders are in an amusing confusion as to what they want. Some would tax corn, as in old days; others would not tax corn. Some would only tax manu- factured goods, but they do not tell us which, or how much they would tax them. Some, would have Free Trade only with the colonies, not appearing to know that our principal colonies, say Canada and Victoria, have heavy tariffs against English goods. Our chief depression is in the farming industry. Our farmers, as a rule, • ve had farms twice too large for the capital employed upon them. Under the Corn Laws land was made to grow corn Which should not have grown tt, and now, with low prices, must cease to grow it. With Free Trade in 'corn land must depend on its own quality, and on the capacity of those who posse.ss it, or who cultivam it. The question of rent must, depend on what tenants are willing and able to pay. You cannot ask that a rate in aid shall he levied on the breakfast table of every workman's family to enable a tenant farmer to pay a rent, which the land he tills is not able to yield or to hear. The rent must settle itself, and pro- duce and prices will enable the farmer to determine what, he can undertake to pay. And if these Fair Traders, in their silly and childish dreams. impose again to raise the price of. food by the partial exclusion of foreign corn, how do they propose to ,protect the crowds of mm end women working in the cotton and woollen trades of Lancashire and Yorkshire, and to compensate them for the various basses which the Fair Traders are anxious to see re-imposed upon food and goods of various kinds which we import from abroad? T should like to see a carefully drawn tariff of the Fair Traders and trotectionists and monopolists who are now asking for public support. It would be an amusing exhibition of ignorance and folly and confusion. It would show the impossibility of going hack to tlat system which Sir Robert Peel attacked in the year 1242, and which he utterly demolished in the year 1846. Since that time there is abundant evidence of the im- proved condition of the millions who work for their daily bread. Wages are generally hi-her; in many em- ployments they are nearly or quite doubled, and the cost of almost everything the millions buy and consume .is greatly reduced, and their general condition is comfort- able beyond anything that has been known in the country during the last hundred years. There Sri! ex- ceptions to this picture, as there have always been seasons of depression in some or in special trades and industries; hut the picture, as it whole, is not over- t-olotired. If, as you perhaps fear, the working men will he persuaded to co hack to the errors and mischief of 50 ream ago, it will only show, notwithstanding efforts tor their education, how far they are from 0-imprehereline t heir own true interaits. You have observed .what the Conservatives have been saying at Oxford—they return, shall I say, like a dog to his vomit.? They very slowly accept new teaching and new opinions, and the old de- lusions still attach to them; hut they are all eunfusin. and know not what they ask.—You.s very respectfully, "JOlOl Butonr."

div.head: GREAT NATIONALIST GATHERING.
div.p: GREAT NATIONALIST GATHERING.

The largest and most representative Nationalist meet- ing ever held in Queenstown took place on Sunday in the new schools. The building, which is capable of holding 3,000 persons, was crowded, hundreds of people being refused admission. The meeting was presided over by a Roman Catholic administnator, and the following Eng- lish and Irish members of Parliament were present:— Messrs. Illingworth, Priestley, Woodhead, Lane, O'Hea, and Elynn. The three English members were met at the terminus by the chairman and members of the Town Commissioners Board and by about' a thousand persons, accompanied by the local band, and received a most enthusiastic welcome. At the meeting resolutions were passed protesting against the arrest, trial, and treatment of Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., denouncing the entire policy of the Government as pursued in the country at present, and especially manifested in the strained enforcement of the Coercion Act, and resolving to adopt the Plan of Campaign in all cases where land- lords will not give fair reductions in rent commensurate with the fall in prices, and likewise to prevent hunting until Mr. O'Brien is released from gaol. Messrs. Illing- worth, Woodhead, Priestley, Lane, and O'Hea, M.P.'s, addressed the meeting.
A LIVELY EVICTION SCENE.-FIRE-ENGINE AND BATTERING RAM EMPLOYED.

The Central News correspondent at New ROBS tele- graphs :—One hundred and fifteen police, commanded by Col. Miller, R.M., accompanied the Sheriff, on Tues- day morning, to carry out the eviction of David Foley, of Rallykerogne, on the estate of Colonel Tottenham. The force had with them a battering ram, consisting of a long and heavy pole, capped with iron' and they also took to the scene of action a military fire-engine for the purpose, if necessary, of drenching out the inmates of the house. The evicting party arrived at Foley's dwelling, and, after cautioning those inside, Col. Miller gave orders for the removal of the large crowd, which had gathered, to a distance, whence they could offer no opposition to the course of the proceedings, this being done amid a scene of some excite- ment, ,but without serious resistance. Possession of the tenancy was demanded from the inmates. No reply being given the emergency men began vigorously to work the ram, which, in about five minutes, had brought down nearly the whole of one nd of the house. The besieged then brought their forces into play, ejecting hot water and injurious liquids through garden syringes. They tried to drive back the emergency men, and followed up this action by a volley OF stones. The sheriff's men, however, were protected by wicker shields covered with canvas, and sustained little injury. The fire engine was then brought into play, and poured a deluge or cold water into the building, until very corner was soaked by the powerful stream. Drenched to the skin, and apparently bewildered by con- tinued torrents of water, in less than an hour ten men who occupied the building surrendered, and were forth- with placed uncler arrest and marched into New Ross. CONFLICT WITH THE POLICE.

A scene of great exnitement, which ended in a serious collision with the police, occurred on Saturday night at Limerick, on the occasion of the arrival there of Dr. John M'lnerney, of New York. Dr. M`lnerney was formerly a citizen of Limerick, and is prominently identified with advanced Nationalism, the object of his visit being to deliver an oration at the unveiling of the memorial cross to Allen, Larkin, and O'Brien. About two hundred police occupied the railway terminus, the High Sheriff and a few members of the Corporation were on the plat- form, which was thronged with people. On Dr. Wlnerney making his appearance there was tremendous cheering, and he was conveyed to his hotel in a close carriage amidst a scene of excited enthusiasm. In view of the Government proclamation of meetings on this occasion, the police charged the people, using batons freely. On reaching his hotel Dr. Wlnerney was about to address the crowd, when the police again charged, scattering the people in all directions. Several persons received severe blows on the hoed. Replying to an address from the memorial committee, Dr. M'lnerney urged his hearers to keep on the old path, and see the question out. Nationalists ahould take all they could net, but never say they were satisfied until they had the full measure of independence which they demanded. (Cheers.) The speaker was interrupted by the arrival of a constable to serve upon him a copy of a proclamation. The Mayor, who was present at the proceedings, issued, in the course of the evening, a proclamation calling upon the people not to collect in the streets on Sunday, nor to approach St. Lawrence's Cemetery where the memorial is erected. In this respect the Mayor was aided by the committee who had the management of Dr. M'lnerney's reception. Public-houses were compulsorily closed, and the town during Sunday was comparatively quiet. Every ar- rangement was made by the authorities to prevent the proposed meeting being held. Allen,Larkin, and O'Brien were prayed for in the Roman Catholic churches. The town was guarded by 300 extra police and about 200 of the llrarwickshire Regiment, in addition to the troops in the g trrison. At night, however, the streets were again in commotion, and the police were busy dispersing the crowds, who purposely harrassed them by throwing stones. Some boys groaned, and whistled "Harvey Duff," when about 200 police issued from the barracks with rifles and batons, and cleared the thoroughfare. Several people were batoned, and great indignation was expressed nt the conduct of the constabulary. At a late hour the town was in a terrible state of excitement. The police were charging through the streets, batoning right and left. The windows of the barracks in William- street and the temporary police lodgings in Denmark- street were previously smashed with stones. Several arrests were made, and a number of petiole were ad- milted to Barrington's Hospital. The Mayor, High Sheriff, amid a local magistrate had an interview on Monday with Capt. Stokes (Divisional Magistrate), the County Inspector, and the District Inspector, when, on the Mayor guaranteeing the peace of the city, the 500 extra police were promised to be with- drawn

SERIOUS ILLNESS OF LORD LYO.IS : PARALYTIC STROKE. —Earl Lyons, the British AIM iovzsador to France. was at breakfast time on Monday seized with a serious and dangerous illness at Norfolk House, London, and remains In a critical condition, Dr. Edward Tegart was imme- diately summoned, and later Sir William Jenner was called m. _

During the present week many notices have been served upon tenantry- in North Wales, demanding pay- ment of tithe rent-charge due and owing. It is stated that the clergy are making a firmer stand against the increasing demands for reductions. The authorities doubt whether, if distraints are TT, 'e, they will be able to maintain law and order unless supported by the military. -

FAILDRR OF A CONTRACTOR ! LIABITATIKS, £675,000. —At London Bankruptcy Court., on Monday, Registrar Linklater, upon the application of Messrs. Mason, Phil- lips, and Cotton, rr- 'e a recPiving order under a petition presented by William Douglas, of Queen's Gate, South Kensington, and elsewhere, builder and contractor. The liabilities are stated at £675,000, of which £lOO,OOO is unsecured. The trade liabilities are stated at .£17,000. 'The assets are at present unestimated.

THB RAID ON HIGHLAND Da FORESTS.—A detachment of Royal Scots and the extra police who have arrived from the mainland are still in Stornoway, the authorities having deferred sending the force into the interior in order to allow of a voluntary surrender of the raiders Five of the latter who had given themselves up were brought up on Saturday before Sheriff-substitute Fraser. and charged with forming part, of a riotous mob armed with firearms, and with the illegal destruction of forest deer. The accused were remanded, bail being fixed at £4O each.

BRUTAL AFFRAY IN BIRMINGHAM.—A fatal affray of a most brutal character took place in Birmingham on Saturday evening. A man named John liagot, spring maker, well known to the police for his ruffianism. quarrelled with a woman named Roach, with whom he had cohabited, and who is also a violent character, in one of the side streets of the town. In the course of a fight he knocked the woman down and kicked heron the head, fracturing her skull. She was conveyed senseless to the hospital, and was found to be dead. Begot was after- wards arrested in a public-house.—On Monday the prisoner was remanded. REMISSION OF SENTENCE.—The Home Secretary has just remitted the remainder of a term of eight years' penal seryltude, rassed in 1885, on A man named James Metcalf, for an alleged criminal assault on a girl in the employment of his wife. The case excited a good deal of attention. It is believed that the girl's story was the result of hysteria, and several medical men and a Man- chester solicitor have recently fully investigated ,the case. They petitioned the Home Secretary for the man's release, and Mr. Matthews has ordered him to be set at liberty. THE BRIDORWATER TRUST SURPLUS.-011 Friday, Mr. Justice North sanctioned the appointment of Mr. T. H. Birch, of Manchester, to represent the ordinary share- holders in the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and Mr. G. H. Schofield, of Oldham, to represent the pre- ference shareholders, in the legal proceedings about to be taken to determine in what shares and proportions and according to what principles the balance of purchase money paid by the Manchester Ship Canal Company for the undertaking ought to be distributed. The amount in hand is £1,700,000, and after the payment of all claims there will be more than £1,000,000 available for distribution.

A MINERS' REPRESENTATIVE IN PARLIAMENT.—MT. U. Pickard, M.P., addressed a meeting of miners at Morley, and, referring to his visit to America, the hon. gent ieman said the "Knights of Labour" carried on the work in a similar way to the Trades Unions in this country, though not quite on the same lines. In this organisation about 35,000 miners were united, and in consequence of their unity they wore in a position to command higher wages than could be demanded in this country. Speaking of the legislation of the last Session of Parliament, Mr. Pickard denied that the whole of the credit was due to Mr. Matthews for the passing of the Mines Act. With regard to himself, if he found that his Parliamentary duties interfered with his Trade Union work, he would seek an early opportunity of resigning his position as a member. DEATH OF A PROMINENT SCIENTIST.—The death is an- flounced of Mr. John Benjamin Dancer, at his residence, Greenhill-street, Greenheys, Manchester. For some time Mr. Dancer had been in very delicate health, and to this suffering was added the terrible affliction of total blindness. Mr. Dancer was born in London on Oct. 8, 1812, and may be said to have bean born an optician, his father and grandfather having been makers of optical and scientific instruments. In 1818 his father, Mr. Josiah Dancer, removed to Liverpool, where he carried on ,the business of optician and philosophical instrument maker; he was also a public lecturer ~n science, and was an active pro. moter of the Mechanics' Institute and Literary and Philosophical Institution of Liverpool. The foundation of Mr. Dancer's optical knowledge was laid in his father's workshop. He also assisted his father in his lectures, and very early in life evflenced a strong bias for mechanical and scientific pursuits. In 1835 the father died, and the business was afterwards carried on by his son. et>

EXTRAORDINARY COLLIRRY AMIDE:RT.-340 MEN TOIIIB2D--A colliery accident happened at Abernant, Aber- dare, on Saturday morning, resulting in the entombment of 340 men. At eight o'clock on Saturday the winding gear broke, with the result that an ascending cage, laden with coal, was precipitated to the bottom of the shaft, whilst the upward cage was shot out. of the mouth of the shaft, and fell through the roof of the engine-house some dis- tance away. The winding rope having broken, commu- nication with the men in the pit was cut off. Alarming reports immediately spread. It was rumoured that an explosion had occurred, and the people from the neigh- bourhood flocked to the mouth of the pit in the wildest excitement. Food was lowered clown the shaft, and after being entombed for 45 hours some of the men found their way by au old working to another colliery, and were brought to the surface in this way. Two hundred and twenty men had been got out up to eight o'clock in the evening, but the remainder were inn part far removed from the old working. The colliery will have to be stopped for three weeks or a month, owing to the damage done. On Monday morning the remainder of the men were brought safely out.

IV CHEAP WINE FOR THE PEOPLE.—Sir Charles A. Cameron, ex-president of the Royal College of Surgeons, in the "Dublin Journal of Medical Science," remarks: "When people talk of the adulteration of claret and other wines, they must be ignorant of the fact that there is no material so abundant or so cheap to prepare wine from as the grape. It must not be inferred however from my remarks on the cheapness of claret that it is the only pure cheap wine in the market. In Spain and Por- tugal thd quantities of wine produced annually are enormous. We have now Port and Sherry which can be bought at a Shilling a bottle. Are they pure? Just as genuine as the dearest port and sherry, but containing somewhat less of added alcohol. A short time ago I pur- chased specimens of port and sherry at one of Messrs. W & A Gilbey's branch establishments in Dublin, and submitted them to analysis. They proved to be as genuine as the most expensive wines of the kind but, they contained a little less alcohol—a difference, to my mind, wholly in their favour.

Mr. Denne, a county magistrate, committed suicide, on Friday, by shooting himself at his residence, Under- hill. Hythe. A fire broke out early on Saturday, at the Royal Oak Railway Station, on the Metropolitan Line. The ticket office was gutted, and a portion of the platform roof was also destroyed. George Michael Graham. an American. who, it is alleged, was shot by another American named D. K Dorothy, in Woobume-place, London, last Monday even- ing, died in hospital on Sunday. '

SERIOUS RAILWAY Suastruorca,—A serious subsidence of land has occu-red on the Severn Valley Railway, between Bridgenorth and Shrewsbury. The subsidence, which is of the depth of thirty feet, is caused by the adjacent mining operations. - A despatch meeived at Portsmouth reports that Mr. Markham, late paymaster of her Majesty's ship Repoir, on the China station, has been tried at flung Kong on several charges of forgery and embezzlement, and sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude.

EAOLRS IN EN(ILAND.—A fine specitnen of the golden eagle was killed on Saturday afternoon at the shooting box of Colonel Pnuntain, on Matlock Moors. It appears that the keeper on duty was attracted by the bark of a spaniel, which had been struck by the eagle, which he at once shot. A shocking accident i reported from Cardiff. A Nova Scotian barque was being towed out to sea from New- port, and when off Lundy the tow rope suddenly parted, severely injuring 17 on board the barque. One man, named John M'Endy sustained compound fractures Of both legs, and died before he could be got ashore. - '

The -Queen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, and their children, arrived' at Windsor, on Saturday, shortly after 9 a.tn. by special train from Scotland. The railway station was kept private, only some metropolitan police and tho railway officials being present, and her Majesty, with the Prince and Princess Henry and the children, at once entered the Royal carriages which were in waiting, and drove to the Castle.

MORE THAN EVER 1 "HUMOR'S Dry Soap is used more than ever." Try a Packet.—Advt. Mr. Sheehy, M. P., against whom a warrant issued under the Crimes Act had been out for \ several weeks, was arrested on Wednesday near Limerick Junction.

div.head: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.
div.p: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.

" Yule Tide" is the title of Cassell's Christmag - Annual. It is a wonderful shilling's-worth, includ- ing as it does, in addition to the complete story by R. L. Stevenson, a large and beautifully-coloured nresentation plate entitled, "Nelson's first farewell," .o coloured pictures, and two fine tinted plates— ye. well worth framing. "Nelson's Farewell" ;7 ,1_the famous painting by George Joy ;itis a " -Met) at once appeals to the heart of young pictsre „ and eid, ems has been executed with the greatest being pri,:ite.d in is in than fourteen colours care, tory is in his strongly characteris- Mr. Stevenson's tal Christmas reading, as it is tic style; it is cisini "Yule Tide from beginning to end. ng exce..dingly interests. besides, a number of char- " containe ades, puzzles, Sze., and ere is a nice bit of verse th, by George Weatherly. I. Messrs. Macmillan and C. ."ve provided a ions by Mr. A. charming Christmas book mums: poem of "The Brook," with by •suipg Tennyson's Woodruff. The artist seems to have worked, not only with a skilful, but a loving hand, .for these vignettes are of the daintiest kind. The colt:mince is in the highest style of the art of the ehrotoo- lithographer. The views are on toned paper, and the little volume is neatly bound. There are, in all, no less than twenty illustrations, and they are altogether executed in a style of which the laureate himself might well be proud. This issue of "The Brook will be hailed with pleasure by those who are on the look out for an artistic gift book. "Little Miss Peggy—only a nursery story" is written by Miss Molesworth, and is also published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. Although "only a nursery story,' it is a substantial volume of which neither author nor illustrator need be ashamed. Mrs Molesworth thoroughly understands child life, and • has a most attractive way of blending fact and fancy in her narrations. "Miss Peggy" is a dear little child—

A creature not too bright and good For human nature's daily food. and she is sure to become a favourite with the reader. The power of imagination which she dis- plays will seem extraordinary to some, but not to those who ,ire most familiar with the inner life of children. The illnqraLions are from the pencil of Mr. Walter Crane; and they are distinguished by his usual breadth and freedom of style.

The English Illustrated Magaiine, ordinarily six- pence, is issued for December as a double Christmas number at the price of one shilling. "The Sea of Galilee," by Laurence Oliphant, is abundantly illus- trated; and the letterpress is of a kind to make the reader fully realise the characteristics of the scenery. "Ornithology at South Kensington," by R. B. Sharpe, is beautifully illustrated from draw- ings by Maud M. Clarke, the engravings throughout being really fine. "The Story of Jael " is concluded, and another story,- "That Girl in Black," is com- menced by Mrs. Molesworth. Mr. J. Fitzgerald Molloy contributes a very interesting paper with the title of "What Players are they? " It is illus- trated by as many as four full page engravings, with portraits of Garrick, Peg Woffington, Mrs. 11 Yates, and Mrs. Abington. Mr. Hugh Thompson and Mr. Herbert Railton as illustrators keep pace with Mr. Outram Tristram, whose racy papers on "Coaching Days and Coaching Ways" are being read each month with great interest. Amongst other full page engravings niay be mentioned "Por- trait of Rembrandt, by himself; " " Study of a Head,' from a drawing by Sir F. Leighton, and "St senen Cove," from a painting by C. Napier Henry. "The Graphic Christmas Number," is equal as heretofore to the highest anticipations. The large presentation plate which accompanies this year's issue is a reproduction of Mr. Barton Barber's pain ti nz of "The Mischievous Puppy." A little girl who has been enjoying dessert whilst sitting on a buf- fet is being pulled over by the mischievous puppy, whe is giving a good tug at her sash. With her feet going up and her head going down, the situa- tion becomes an exciting one. Another large pic- ture. called "A very, very great Secret," from the painting by Fred. Morgan. This picture—a little girl whispering to her granny—is sure to be we]- corned; it tells its own tale so well. Then we have as full page coloured plates—" The Squire's Christ- mas Box," "Our Reindeer Sleigh," "Seizing an Op.. portunity," and "A Story of the Sea." There are besides, many other coloured pictures—most of them illustrative or suggestive of Christmas. The principal story is by Mr. W. E. Norris, and bears the title of "Robinson's Friend." The other, "Paleface and Redskin "—a comedy-story for boys and girls— is by Mr. F. Anstey. The Christmas number of "All the Year Round," conducted by Mr. Charles Dickens, is a complete story with the title of " tell thee, Dick. where I have been." It is from the pen of Mr. Arthur Pater- son, and is edited by Mr. Walter Besant. "Mike Alison" would have been, we think, a better title for the story, as most of the adventures are rela- ted to the personality of ti-is extraordinary indivi- dual. The character is drawn with a firm, careful hand, and, from the first introduction, the reader is interested in the doings of "Mike Alison." The story furnishes a vivid picture of life in the back- woods of America. and it abounds in thrilling inci- dents.

"Clarkson'! Musical Pictures," published by Mr. John Heywood, is a novel way of making boys and girls familiar with musical terms without feeling that they are going to the trouble of learning them._ The pictures are cleverly designed and brilliantly coloured. and they are sure to prove a great attrac- tion to children.

Mrs. Leach's Children's and Young Ladies' Dress— maker is issuedsas a double Christmas number. It is profusely illustrated, and there is, besides, a coloured picture and paper pattern. Part 37 of "Ward and Lock's Technical Journal contains, among other things, articles on students introduction to mechanics, the steelmaker, the fac— tory worker, building and machine elraughtsmen the cabinet maker, the farmer, &c. The articles, it should be added, are amply illustrated.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. H. H. McMINNIES.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. H. H. McMINNIES.

Yesterday week, the remains of Mr. Henry Hew- itson McMinnies, aged 38 years, of 3, East-cliff, Preston, were interred in the new burial ground connected with Leyland Parish Church. The de- ceased, who died on the Tuesday, was the nephew of our respected townsman, Mr. J. G. McMinnies. The funeral was of a strictly private character, one, mourners present only including his Widow; Mr. and Mrs. Wm. McMinnies, The Cottage, Faringten, and other near relatives. The obsequies were conducted by the Rev. Father Cardwell. S.J.. of St Wilfrid's, Preston, assisted by the Rev. Father W. A. Bulheck, of Leyland. The deceased, after acting for five years as mariaging partner in the firm or Messrs. Merman, Xing, and Co., merchants, Shangai, left China in 1879, he having decided to adopt agriculture as his profession, and in order to make himself thorotivhly et-quainter' with it he resided on different farms in Yorkshire,the Isle of Mart_Glouces- tershire, and Cornwall. He also went threnth full course of training at the Royal Agricultural College. Cirencester, as is married out student, and had the work of two farms under his view. Success so far attended his efforts that he obtained twenty- two certificates of lionmir and prizes for proficiency in different subjects. and in 1888 took his diploma as gold medalist the highest distinction procurable. He secured the first place at. Edinburgh in chemistry and veterinary scienee. Mr. Me.Minnies nulled for anti obtained the position of Professor or Agriculture of South Australia. one of his testimonials being from proreft,,,r Robert Wallace, in which it. was stated that. the appli- cant, had hail quite a distinguished career as a student at the Royal Agricultural College. Cirencester. few liar- inL, equalled Ilia position he took in the final examina- tions, and nri sic having surpassed him in earnest der- ti-in to all the work of the enurse, beth practical snit scientific. As :Ail ONOMOtOr for the Iiit:1.1411(1 Agricul- tural Society's tfplonia. he (Professor \Vali:tee) could say NTr. Nic.Mittilitv, took an exceptionally high position in the previous year's competition for that honour. Per- sonally, lie had a high opinion of Mr. Mc.Minnies and Ids ability. In IliFt application the deceased gentleman was successful. He went out to South Australia, hut, soon after his arrival a distressing and fatal disease manifested itself—catieer in the throat. Ile constiltewt the most eminent medical men, and they hold- ing out no hope for his recovery, he felt himself bound to resign his position. He re- turned. to England, and took' up his residence with his mother, at. No. 3, East-cliff. Preston, where the. painful complaint gradually developed itself, and caused his &Atli on the 22nR instant • At the annual distri- bution of prizes at. the Cirencester College, in August. lest, the Rev. .1. B Mc.flelland, Principal, referred to Mr. McMinnies in the higliet terms. He spoke of having received a letter from him, stating that he had resigned his Australian appointment. through a fatal disea.se4iav- ing seized him, and was bringing his wife home, with the saddest prospects bath for himself and for her. He ex- pressed his high sense of the courageous tone of the letter written under those circumstances, and said it led one to hope that their work and social intercourse at that College might have other effects than those they imagined at the time, in strengthening men's characters, and in fitting them for some of the harder duties of life which in God's providence they might some day have to face. Great sympathy is extended to the family in their bereavement, and regret is generally expressed at, So promising a career being cut short under such dis- tressing circumstances.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1887.

Loan °Boss allowed his light to shine before the Conservatives of Earlestown on Monday even. ing, and it proved, as heretofore, to be a light of the feeble and 'flickering kind. He is a simple- minded man, whose vanity has been tickled by ' having greatness thrust upon him. Having some- how found his way into a Cabinet, he never forgets that he is a Cabinet Minister, and he consequently puts on oracular airs in a way which is amusing to behold.' It will never be forgotten that he once solemnly announced that he intended to reply to Mr. GLADSTONE —jUSt as the Cuckoo might make it known that it meant to put itself in competition with the nightingale. There is, to be sure, some- thing of the cuckoo in the composition of Lord CROSS; he has always the same cry as to the virtue of the Government, and he never varies his note. The Government, he said, wanted to show the Irish that they were the real friends of the nation, and to expose their false friends. This may be their desire, but Irishmen will probably think they have a hateful way of giving expression to their kinaly feelings. ‘Lord SALISBURY intimates that not only is Home Rule to be denied them, they are not even to be favoured with such reform in local government as is promised to England, until they submit to the yoke which the Tories would put upon them. admitting, for the sake of argu- ment, that there is such a thing as oppression by the National League, is it not reasonable to ask why the nation should, on that account, be pun- ished with defective government? Can we regard Lord Cnoss as sincere, in view of such a glaring distinction, when he talks of showing the Irish that thefare the real friends of the Irish nation, or shall we not say that he is mocking Irishmen with verbiage of the most offensive kind? The great ory of the Tories at the last election was that there should be equal laws for the United Kingdom; but they have already so far outraged their professions that they are putting men in pri- son for offences (so-called) which are no offences at all in this country. More than that, they now talk of extending self-government to England, and denying it to Ireland—thus increasing the dispar- ity, while ,at the same time politicians of the maudlin type, like Lord CROSS, speak unctuously of their friendly feeling to Ireland We are told that what is wanted to ensure the prosperity of Ireland, to foster and encourage commercial enter- prise, is "a strong Government which knows its own mind ? " But does the Salisbury Govern- ment answer to this description? Is it to be re- garded as strong when, Jiotwithstanding procla- mations of the National League, in certain dis- tricts, meetings are held in these very districts week by week, and openly reported in the Irish newspapers? Is it to be regarded as knowing its own mind when, after opposing the proposal to revise judicial rents, as something dishonourable and di:honest, it comes forward next session with a measure to accomplish this very object? But Lord CROSS says, the Tories were "returned to power by a vast majority." Analysed however, the voting strength of "the vast majority" is found to be something under 80,006 more votes than were obtained by the Liberal candidates a figure so small, compared with the total number of voters that, as Mr. GLADSTONE has demonstrated, it has already vanished into thin air—judging by the polling results of the bye-elections. Nobody knows this better than Lord SALISBURY, for did he not pitifully ap- peal to his supporters to swallow a Land Bill , based upon principles which he had denounced as dishonourable and dishonest rather than incur the risk of going before the country? Lord CROSS takes some credit for the foreign policy of the Governments and as to its main lines it is satisfac- tory to be able to say that, thanks to fear of the loss of the Liberal Unionist vote, it is in the right direction. If Jingoism is not dead, it dare not at any rate show its head in a Government, which , Lord HARTINGTON can at any moment overthrow. His Lordship is a Gladstonian as to foreign affairs; and Lord SALISBURY has succeeded in foreign ; affairs just in so far as he has taken Mr. GLAD- stoics as his model.

THE People of St. Helens seem to be as much in earnest about the projected new railway as the inhabitants of Warrington and Runcorn are about the Ship Canal. There was a large attendance at a town's meeting in St. Helens the other evening, at which resolutions were adopted in support of

the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway. It ' is open to question whether it is wise to hold Town's Meetings in aid of what are, strictly speaking, private undertakings ; bub the preceilent has been , established in the matter of the Ship Canal scheme, and we need not be surprised that it should be followed when a local railway, is con- cerned. No great harm can, of course, be done so long as there is no intention to apply the money of the ratepayers to the support of the undertaking, and it is due to the promo- ters of the Company, and of the 'meeting, to say that they have no thought of anything of the kind. They have confidence iri their scheme; and, they believe that the more it is inquired into . the more the inhabitants of the district, as a whole, will be likely to support it by investing their money in shares. St. Helens is a rapidly thriving town, and the need of better railway communica- tion is being strongly felt. In 1871 the population of the town was a little over 4.5,000 inhabitants; it is now over 60,000; and it is steadily increasing. It is proposed to carry the new line from Lowton, ' through HaYdock to St. Helens, and forward to Liverpool by Knowsley and West Derby. Any person who will take the trouble to look at a rail- way map will see that, although South-West Lan- cashire is pretty well intersected with railways, there is quite an open country in the line which it is proposed to follow. It is more than ten years /since the project of a second railway was first mooted, and meantime the trade of St. Helens has considerably developed, and there has been an addition to the population of at least ten thousand inhabitants. The Haydock coalfield will be directly tapped by the new line, and, as it con- tains some three or four hundred millions of tons of coal, it will be seen as to this section that there is a good prospect of a dividend. The cost of the carriage of raw material and of manufactured goods has come to be a factor of some importance now-a-days, when competition in every branch of industry is so remarkably keen. St. Helens is not so favourably situated as it might be in this re- spect, or as it will be when the new line 'is brought into operation. Mr. J. Lths, one of the speakers at the meeting, said the lowest rate at which they could get raw material into their works at present was 5.1 d. per ton; but he ventured to predict that the competition of a new railway would bring the cost down to 3d. per ton. It may be said that "it's always rash to prophecy unless you know 7; but Mr. LEITH is HOt Withollt data for his conclu- elusion. Comparing Widnes with St. Helens, he .said that the rate for the carriage of limestone was less in Widnes by sd. per ton. It is obvious that a difference of this kind is likely in the long run to affect trade. Capital flows into those channels where profits are largest, and it is a matter of , course to say that they are largest where the cost of production is smallest. St. Helens is not alone in being handicapped by heavy rates for carriage; the nation as a whole is suffering, having to com- pete with countries where railway charges are ex- ceedingly hiw. The great railway companies are not themselves sufficiently subject to that law of competition which brings down prices; but it is satisfactory to think that something is being done to mend matters. St. Helens will profit by the construction of a new railway; and the whole. of Lancashire and Cheshire by the making of, the Ship Canal.

WARRINGTON SS a barracks town has been pretty well to the front when questions have been raised as to the qualification for the franchise of military men. Mr. HENRY ROBERTS, the Liberal agent or the borough, has all along had a strong opinion that army men broke their qualification when away from their usual residence under the QUEEN'S regulations; and it has been found that he was right in his contention. This year the point was raised as to whether eleven non-com- missioned officers and six bandsmen of the Liver- pool Regiment of Militia hail not lost their qualifi- cation by reason of their being absent at Altsar for the annual training. The Revising Barrister took the view that, as the men "were in no sense domiciled at or resident , inhabitants of Altcar," their title to a vote as residents at Warring- ton held good, and he therefore allowed the names to remain on the lists of voters. An appeal against this decision was ea_ cordingly made on behalf of the Liberals. The ease was gone into, on Wednesday, by her Majesty's judges, at the High Court of Justice, i and the result is that the decision of the Revising Barrister is reversed. The names of the Militia- men are to be struck off the lists on the ground that, as they could not leave the camp without permission, they thereby broke their residence. We can sympathise with the Revising Barrister in allowing the names to stand so long as there was a doubt in the case; but on the other hand it was the plain duty of the Liberal Agent to take the I necessary steps to have them removed so long as I he believed their title to exercise the franchise was not sound in law. The vigilance which Mr. ROBERTS has exercised during the past two years in keeping military men off the list whose title to remain on was not proved to be good will make a difference to the Liberal party of fully one hundred votes, :and he is therefore to be congratulated on the success he has achieved. The Tories are already saying that it is unfair for the Liberals to. disfranchise inhabi- tants in this way; but the unfairness, if there be any, is in the law, and as to this We shall be glad to assist them in remedying the defects of our registration system; it is a part of the Liberal programme.
make people moral by act of Parliament, we may at least make the fear of the law a beginning of wisdom.

A criminal named Job Alrarburton, who com- mitted suicid3 in a Bolton police cell, was buried like a dog, on Saturlay night, in the Cemetery, a verdict of .felo do se having been passed by the jury. Is it not time that the law stepped in and removed such a remnant of barbarism- and, super- stitution ? Self-preservation is the. first law of nature ; it is the basis of sanity. The man who vicilates this law by taking' his own • life is no longer a sane man, and should be adjudged accord- What is, the use of being vindictive With a strangled corpse? . • '

The lot of the baillf is not. always a happy one when County Court "duty to be done." A case was heard at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satur- day, in which a collier named Williams was sum- moned for assaulting a bailiff namCd Burrows whilst in the act of. levying an execution for four shillings. We don't know what the collier Would have done if the amount demanded had been 1.'4%, he would perhaps have murdered the bailiff. Hew- ever, he found his little game didn't pay; he 'Was fined 20s. and costs, and the execution wasleVied after all.

The revelations arising out of the examination , in connection With the Greenway Bank, Warwick, are ol the most startling kind. Mr. Kelynge Greenway admitted that his deficiency on his farming account represented .a loss of £1,660 a year on a farm of 1,000 acres,.for which he paid no rent. How suggestive! Talk about ordinary agricultural depression, it is not in it. The manageinent of the bank seems to have been bad, and then worse, and worse. _

The breach, though small at first, soon opening wide, ' Ins rushes folly with a full-moon tide. It has been very pleasant for the Tories 't,(3 see how Mr. John 'Bright could pitch into tromp Rulers; but, oh! how unhappy they would be when they read his letter on Fair Trade. He smites them hip and thigh; they are "childish and silly" dreamers who "know not what they ask." The, severest punishment would be to let them have their own way; but, unhappily, they cannot injure themselves without injuring the rest of the community. They must, therefore, be dealt with as people who are childish and silly.

Lord Salisbury is known to be a Free Trader; but there was a hope that, after the resolution in favour of Fair Trade passed at the Conservative Conference at Oxford, he would give the Protec- tionists a pat on the back. But he did nothing 'of the kind; be put them off in a very unceremonious fashion, and gave them to iniderstand that there was something else to do than indulge in academic speculations. Lord Salisbury is not to be led into this particular bog; he blows that. the Liberal Unionists would leave him to his fate, if he made a single fiscal change in the direction of Protection.

Mr. T. W. Legh, the member for Newton, had not a little to say, on Monday evening, abont the Irish question. He was quite merry about the Irish members who were "dodging the police," and about the fiasco of Mr. W. O'Brien and his prison clothes. But he did not describe the figure he himself recently cut when he "took up a strategic position behind a tree," while his guides made terms with, those who were "after him." He did not, of course, want to fall into the hands of brigands, and he was just as ready to dodge them as the Irish M.P's. are to dodge Balfour and his brigade.

The people of Widnes must mend their ways, or they will acquire an evil repute for violent assaults. Three cases of this kind were under con- sideration, on Monday, which revealed a ourious variety in thdb mode of attack. In the first case the offender—a woman—had -taken off her clog and laid open the head of another woman with it. In the second cue a labourer had enforced an argument with a tea can, inflicting such injuries that his opponent was unfit to appear in court. In the third case, a Pole had plunged a fork into another man's nose, and caused a dangerous wound. Variety is said to be charming; but there is no charm in various modes of brutality.

The London "Times" has a craze in the matter of Mr. Parnell. This was shown in the publica- tion of the articles on "Parnellism and Crime," which, by-the-by, damaged the (mis)leading jour- nal more than the leader of the Nationalists. The latest move of the "Times" has been to track Mr. Parnell to' the privacy he has sought, under an assumed name, for the benefit of his health. He has been living at Brockley as "Mr. Preston." Several of the Tory paper; show themselves dis- gusted with the action of the "Times," which the London " Observer " says, "labours under the im- putation of having disregarded the sanctity of private life in order to damage a political op- ponent."

It is seldom that one reads anything so sad, either in history or fiction, as the account of the deaths, within a few hours of each other, of Lord and Lady Dalhousie. They were both in the prime of life; they loved each other dearly, and were beloved by all who knew them. Lord Dal- housie will be long remembered as a politician who was amongst the first to show himself favourable to an inquiry into Home Rule. He was assisted in his candidature, in Liverpool, in 1880, by Mr. Crosfield, and when, in 1885, Mr. W. Cros- field became the Liberal candidate for War- rington he did not forget the obligation. The Liberals of Warrington will have a vivid recollec- tion of his frank, genial manner, and of the excel- , lent speech he made in the Public Hall.

LORD DERBY ON FAIR TRIDE.—Lord Derby, writing from St. James's-square, Loudon, to a Lan- cashire gentleman on the question of Fair Trade, says he quite agrees that a return to Protection would be a mistake and a misfortune It is, how- ever, not easy to suppose that the people of our towns will consent to tax imported corn or meat, or other articles of food produced abroad; but if they decline to do so, what interest have the agri- cultural classes in conceding protection to British manufacturers? Loif Derby conceives that the present partial reaction against Free Trade arises from the disappointment of exaggerated expecta- tions. FENDERS, Fire Brasses, Curbs, Tile Hearths, I. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Eariestown.—widvt. SINGULAR SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch, and C, Pilkington, Gilbert Dean, of Southworth-with- Croft, was summoned at the instance of John Dain- teth, School Attendance Officer, for negletAing to send his child to school. The defendant's wife ap- peared, and produced a medical certificate stating that the child was not fit to attend school regularly. She added that she would promise to send the child to school every time she was fit to go. Mr. Pain- teth said he must ask the Bench to record a convic- tion in that case, as it was the very worst case they had. Mr. Gillespie, J.P., remarked that they could not do so in face of the medical certifilate that the child was not fit to attend regularly. The Bench said Mrs. Dean must send her child to school at least one half day daily, or she would be finedif she did not do so. WEDDING AT Ruxconx.—On Monday' the marriage of Mr. Henry John de Korte, son of the late Honourable G. T. de Korte' J.P., Mayor of Cape TOWD, South Africa, and Miss Tessie Buchanan, daughter of Mr. Chas. Buchanan, late pilot of the port of Runcorn, was solem- nized at the Parish Church, Runcorn. The service was conducted by the Rev. A. Tindall. The bride was charmingly attired in a dresk of blue plush, trimmed with Valenciennes lam, with hat to match, and was given away by Mr. Tomlinson. The bridesmaid, Miss Rose Pearle, wore a gold coloured dress, with Ilat to match. Mr. Samuel Tomlinson officiated as best man. A DISHONEST RUSSIAN AT WIDNES.—At, Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Teresa Mackales, a Russian Pole, was charged with having, on Saturday morning, stolen a pillow worth 35., the property of Charles Stevens, also a Pole, who lives at 24, Barns-street. It was 01e...ad that the prisoner entered Stevens' house on Saturday morning, and after some conversation with regard to a coat,dook up the pillow, and rushed out of the house.— Several witnesses were examined, and an interpreter had to be employed.—The prisoner contended that Steven had a coat belonging to her, and she took the pillow in its place.—The prisoner, who had been pre- viously convicted of theft, was sentenced to a mouth's 'hard labour.

'SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT WIDNES.—A serious accident occurred on Wednesday at the Widnes Foundry. A boy named John Thomas, an orphan, who resides with kis sister, at 11, Church-street, was assisting an engine driver to oid an engine, when his foot slipned, and stum- bling:. the left sleeve of hjs jacket caught in one of the cogwheels, his arm being entangled in the machinery. As soon as possible the engine was 'stopped, and the in- jured limb being extricated Thomas was taken to the Accident Hospital, where it was found that his arm was severely lacerated above the elbow, the bone being com- pletely bared and partially splintered. It was at first feared that .amputation would be necessary. but Dr., McDonnell and his assistant, Mr. RichardS, ATP trying to effect a recovery without resorting to this extreme measure. •

FOREIGN MISSIONARY MEETINGS AT WIDNES AND DIT- TON.—On Tuesday evening the annual meeting in con- nection with the Wesleyan Methodist Foreign Missions was held in Victoria-road Chapel, Widnes. There was a good attendance, Mr. E. Hutchinson, of Liverpool, pre- siding. The annual report, which was read by the Rev. J. Bryant, showed that £l4B 8s 24 had been raised in the ! Widnes circuit, the Victoria-road district raising £57 9s 104 of this sum. Interesting addresses were delivered by the Rev. T. Choate, late missionary in the West Indies, and the Rey. Edward Strutt from Ceylon.—On Wednesday evening a meeting under the same auspices Was held in Ditton Wesleyan Chapel. Mr. Roger Fog.- pre- siding. The report showed that £l5 2s 104 had been colleated in that district. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. R. Yeatman (Baptist minister), who attended as a deputation, and the Rev. J. Bryant.
