CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY AT RUNCORN.—In connec- tion with the Church of St. Michaels and All Angels, the annual congregational tea party was held in the school- room, Shaw-street, on Tuesday evening, and there was a capital attendance. Afterwards an entertainment was given under the presidency of the, Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., the vicar, and the room was crowded.—Mr. G. Summerfielcl, in the course of a speech, said the collec- tion at the church so far had amounted to £B3, hut when they had paid away what was required for certain organizations. there was only £...14 left for the warming, cleaning. &c., of the church. He appealed to the congregation to be more generous in their contributions. The Chairman said he. had been asked whether it was his intention to make St. Michaels and All Angels the centre, of a parish, and appoint a clergyman as incumbent. The first diffi- culty was that before a separate parish could be made there must he a population of not, less than 4,000, and this number could only be reached by adding the township of Weston, to which the people did not agree. Then the Ecclesiastical Commissicners were not willing to find any money to support a church unless there were 8.000 people in the neighbourhood, and they could not get a clergyman to live upon LSO a year, as had been suggested. He could assure them that the clergy of the Parish Church would do all they could on Sundays to conduct the services at the church,,which must remain at present a part of the parish of Runcorn. (Anplause.)—The entertainment, which was of an agreeable character, was taken part in by Miss Simkin. MSS Ainsworth. and Mrs. W. B. Kay; Messrs. J. Wood, T. H. Annett, R. Moore. R. Morris, J. Little, W. Pownall, T. Sharrocks, and Ma,ster W. Cook. Mr. W. Pownall ably acted as accompanist. INDIGusTION CURED by one box of Howell's Golden Herb TDB WIDNES LIME-TRROWING CASE—At the Liverpool ASSiZni, before Mr. Justice Grantham, Frank Kelly, a youth about fourteen years of age, pleaded not guilty to haying, at Widnes, on the 21st September, maliciously inflicted grievous bodily harm upon a girl named Eliza- beth Evans, sixteen years of age. Mr. Shand prosecuted and Dr. Conimins, M.P.. defended. The proseeutrix, in company of two of her companions, were on the above date on a piece of waste land in Albert-road, Widnes. where there were some swingboats. The prisoner was there also, with one or two others, and it is alle,red that while the prosecutrix was there prisoner occupied him- self in teasing her. He took her hat from her, and after this had been restored the prisoner, it was alleged, fol.. lowed Evans. took some lime from an adjacent lime pit. and threw it in her face. A portion went into her leff eye, which was very seriously burned, and there was a probability she would finally lose the sight of the eve. After the injury was sustained, the girl was taken to the Eye and 'Ear Infirmary in Myrtle-street, Liverpool. where she was an in-patient for some time, and Dr. Williams, of that institution, said the eye was very much damaged. At present she saw next to nothing with it, but with an operation she might yet have sufficient sight with it. to go • about. The Other eye was all right. The injured eye was greatly disfigured, and the disfigurement would be permanent. When taken into custody and charged with , the offence, the prisoner replied, in answer to the charge, that he did not do it, and that was now the defence set up on his behalf. The prisoner was found guilty and re- commended to mercy. Dr. Commins produced certifi- mtes, showing that betetofore he had been a very good lad, and the constable in the case said there was nothing else against him. He worked for his father, who was a rag gatherer. The father having entered into his recog- . nizances to bring him up for judgment when called upon, the prisoner was discharged.

• INTO THE LION'S DEN AT RUNCOHN.—reux akmonn was brought before the 'Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with damaging the police cell. On Saturday night the pri- soner went to the police station in a state of -drunken- ness and made a great disturbance. He refused to quit when requested by Supt. Hollingsworth, and, he was therefore taken into the cells below, where he committed damage to the extent of 2s 6d. The prisoner was ordered to pay £1 14s 10d, or go to gaol for a month. ALLEGEp ASSAULT ON A DOMESTIC SEILVANT, George Wharton, who is in business as a photographer at Man- chester, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on ' Monday charged with assaulting Sarah Bronwiek a do- mestic servant. It appeared that Wharton who is mar- ried was on a visit to his parents at Weston with whom his wife lives.. On the 19th November, he desirol to leave the house early in the morning and he ordered his breakfast to be provided accordingly. The servant taunted him with living upon his father ; said he was not her master ; and that 3 o'clock was early enough for ' his breakfast. It was alleged that Wharton "struck her and pushed her with the intention of putting her from the house.—Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, was for the, de- fence. The Bench characterised the case as a paltry one and dismissed the summons. • ALLEGED PEraunit AT RUNCORN.—On the sth Novem- ber, John Shelton, a bricklayer, and Phillip Handley, of no settled-occupation, were each fined 40s and-costs, on a charge of having poached upon the preserves of Sir Richard Brookes, at Halton, on the sth October. Shel- ton Paid the fine; but Handley was obliged to take the alternative of-a month's - imprisonment.---On ;Monday, Mr: .T.•lV.'KnowleS, solicitor, Widnes, applied for a sum- mons against George Rigby, gamekeeper, and William Fitfon; gardener, on the charge Of perjury: Mr. Knowles saki he had numerous witnesses to prove that the state- ments made by these men, and which led to the convic- tion of the defendants, were nottrue. The Bench granted the summons.

.... • ASSAULT ON TUE. POLICE AT RUNCOUN.-77-At RUOOOIII Police Court bri. Monday., Samuel Anderson ,an army pensioner, was charged with having on Saturday night, in Church-street, been drunk and disorderly, and also assaulted P.C. Kettle; The prisoner was very drunk and creating a disturbance in Chuirh-street, and as he would I not go away the constable ar&ted him. The prisoner ! struggled violently, kicked the officer, several times, and ! bit his hand. A civilian who assisted in . taking the prisoner to the police station was also assaulted. For the drunkenness a fine of as and costs, 6s 4d, or 14 days' hard labour, was imposed; and for the assault the pri soner was Sentenced to it month's hard labour without the optiOn of a fine. YOUNG HMI RIPPERS AT WIONF.S.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Michael. McPartland,. 12 years of age, whose home is at 14, Brvrme-street, Simm's Cross, was charged with having on the 3.Bth November, stolen three pounds of grapes, the property of Charles Clifton, fruiterer, Waterloo-road. Ile was .also charged with having stolen eight oranges and two pounds of apples, also the property of Clifton. On each occasion the pri- soner took the fruit from a cart, which was in charge of a boy named Patrick Mitchell, who lived in Sankey-st.— Clifton said the prisoner had a lot of " pals" with him, and if Mitchell irad attempted to stop tlamn from taking, the fruit thev would have "clouted him."—The pri- soner was oßlered to receive twelve strokes with the birch rod. . . _

ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Police , Court, on Monday, William Burns, of no 'settled resid- ence • was charged with haying assaulted. P.C. Davy On gaturday night Davy and P.C. Forster werein Anne-st West, when they heard a, disturbance in the. Victoria ITautts. The officers entered the place, and at once com- menced to separate two men who were fighting. The prisoner, who had been standing in the street, then rushed into the vaults, and, seizing Davy by the throat. he struck him in the face, and kicked him furiously. The prisoner's grip upon Davy's throat was with diffi- culty released.--Superintendent Johnston said the pri- , soner had been before.the magistrates on 24. occasions, and had been threetimes convicted for assaulting the The Bench now sentenced him to sixweekslard labour.

STEALING FROM A RUN'CORN P-kWNSHOP.—At Runcorn, on Thursday, a man named Frank Bayliss was charged, Janremand, on suspicion of laying lea a coat, a vest, and two pairs of trousers from Mr. William Craddock's pawnshop in Church-street, Runcorn, ori the 17th ulthno. Prisoner, it appears, was seen loitering with two other men near the prosecutor's shop shortly before the articles were missed, and consequently suspicion fell upon him. It was also ascertained by the police that the prisoner had pawned a coat at Widnes on the night of, the alleged theft, and he was arrested on the following Monday, as he was unable to give a satisfactory account as to 116 w lie became possessed of it. The only explanation ten- dered was that it belonged to one of the men who were with him in Church-street on the 17th ult, That man, however, had not been found, and as there was a doubt about the case prisoner was given the benefit of it and was discharged. BRUTAL TREATIMENT OF AN OLD WOMAN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mary Jane Keegan, wife of a labourer who lives in Water-street, was charged with having caused grievous bodily harm to Ellen Godfrey, a widow, sixty-two years of age. Mrs Godfrey lodged with the prisoner, and on the 12th November she was sitting lin the house when the prisoner came home in a state of drunkenness and commenced to be abusive and to use threats. Becoming alarmed, Mrs Godfrey ran into the street followed by the prisoner, who, upon reaching her, knocked her down, and kicked and struck her upon vari- ous parts of her body. Mrs Godfrey screamed that her , arm was broken but the prisoner gave no heed to her cries and jumped upon her. The prisoner was wearing clogs at the time. Besides being severely bruised, Mrs Godfrey's shoulder was dislocated. Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, having addressed the Bench for the defence the , prisoner Was committed to the assizes for trial. THE RUNCORN BARBER AND His ArermiTtor.--George Bebbington, barber, Church-street, on Monday asked the magistrates to Make an order compelling his apprentice William Ford, to fulfil the terms of his indentures.-.--Mr. Knowles appeared for Bebbington, and Mr. Barton was for the defendant. It appeared that Ford had been em- ployed by Bebbington for twelve months' and was ap- prenticed to him for five years in July last. Lately the boy had shown signs of discontent, and in the opinion of his master had broken articles wilfully to induce Bebbing- to send him away. A fortnight ago the' boy absconded, and obtained work under Charley Hedgecock, barbel; Bridge-street, at higher wages.—lt was contended that the boy had run away because Bebbington had fre- quently illtreated him and had threatened to break his neck and to cut his throat.—Thomas Foulkes, a bailiff, said a few days before the last election he went into Beb- bington's shop for a shave and found Bebbington in a beastly state of drunkenness and not fit for his business. He saw Bebbington strike Ford on that occasion.—The Bench declined to gra.nt the order asked for. Low. LAW CASE.—Smrrx v. Gussr.—This was an action brought before Mr. Justice Chitty, in the Chan- cery Division of the High Court of Justice by the plain- tiff, Mr. Mark Smith, a contractor, carrying on business at Widnes, and residing at Helsby, seeking to compel the defendant, Mr. William Guest, quarry proprietor, Runcorn, to restore the level of a road at Helsby, called the Quarry-road, which bounded some property belong- ing.to the plaintiff, and over which he had a right of way, and which road the defendant was alleged to have wrongfully lowered. On the third day of the hear- ing, and after the evidence of several witnesses had been taken, the defendant submitted to give an undertaking to restore the road to the original level, as indicated on the plan produced in court, prepared by the plaintiff's surveyor, and to pay the costs of the action. Mr. Mac- lean, Q.C. and Mr. George enders on, instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies, Sharp and Kirkconnel, solicitors, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Romer, Q.C. and Mr. Farwell, instructed by Messrs. W. and A. Linaker, solicitors, Runcorn, appeared for the defendant. . .
, . lIATNER'S WINTER STOCK OF BooTs AND SHOES just arrtved, at 42 and 44, Horsemarket-street.—Adut. _ _

INTERESTING GIFT TO THE BRITISH MUSEUX.— That most ancient and interesting historical relic, the throne-chair of Queen llatasu (xviri. Egyptian Dynasty, p.c. 1600). exhibited at the Royal Jubilee Exhibition at Manchester, has been presented to the British Museum by the owner, Mr. Jesse Haworth, of Bowdon, Cheshire. This throne-chair is the only extant specimen of ancient royal Egyptian furniture, and is the most venerable piece of dated cabinet- makers' work in the world. The national collection is much enriched by this additiontoits treasures,and the nation has reason to be grateful to the munifi- cent donor. COVENTRY AND THE PREscoT WATCH FACTORY SCHEMIL—A Coventry correspondent writes : —The intended establishment of a watch factory at Pres- cot is causing a good deal of discussion at Coven- try, where last week manufacturers and workmen formed an association to prosecute for infringe- ments of certain clauses of the Merchandise Marks Act, 1887. The watch trade in Coventry has been depressed of late—due, manufacturers think, partly to the transition state of the type of watch to be produced. In an interview on the position and prospects of the industry, a local manufacturer of standing states that the same genius which enabled Coventry to take the trade from Liverpool and London and concentrate it in the "city of the three spires' is going to give back, on new lines, the old suprem- acy. Asked as to what would come of the Prescot scheme, the opinion was expressed that the factory system must be established, as against the old way of" garret" working, so much adopted at Coventry. The Prescot scheme is regarded as a retaliation on Coventry for making its own movements, or, at any rate, for ceasing 'to rely entirely on Prescot for them. The gentleman in question had a distinct hope for the future of Coventry watchmakers. Gauged by the progress in the article produced, Coventry's advance during the past five years is greater than that of either Switzerland or America; and he says that should that be continued, a new future for Coventry, based on the new type of watch, the keyless and going barrel, and the im- proved method of manufacture—the highly organ- ised factory system--may fairly be predicted. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The high rippers of Liverpool and elsewhere are warned that the ", eat ". is stirring at Walton Gaol; they must mind what they are about, or they will be scratched—and serve them right too.

The trial of Most, the Anarchist, on a charge of inciting to violence, was concluded in New York on Tuesday, the jury returning a verdict of guilty. Sentence will be delivered on December 5. Wonder how Most likes lying in goal, and if he is ready to say with "Othello "—"lf it were now to die, 'twere now to be Most happy"?

Professor Elmslie, discussing the first chapter of Genesis in the "Contemporary," puts his case very simply, and, as many people will think, very sensibly. He says :—" If the order of Genesis was meant as science, then geology and Genesis are at issue; but if, on the other hand, the sequence was never meant to be physical, the wrong lies with ourselves, who have searched for geology where we should have looked for religion."

No one who is in the habit of attending a Police Court can fail to be struck with the flatly contra- dictory evidence which is often given. Alderman Hanrison remarked as to the evidence of one wit- ness in a Warrington police case, on Monday, that "there was no doubt he had committed perjury." 'But when the perjury is beyond doubt, why not follow it up with a prosecution? If we cannot

div.p: • PROPOSED NEW CHESHIRE LINE.-- At a crowded meeting of Cheshire farmers at Tarvin on Thursday night, it was unanimously resolved to request the London and North-Western Railway to construct a new line from Tattenhall, on the Chester and Shrewsbury line, to Helsby or Halton, on the Ches- ter and Manchester line. The undertaking would be only eight miles, long, but would shorten the route of the South Wiles traffic to Liverpool and Manchester, and develop that part of Cheshire. The petition was numerously. signed. A committee was appointed to approach tne railway company. • TEE Ho= Inos TRADE.—The English iron mar- ket presents a decidedly more cheerful aspect this week. _ The improvement is, perhaps, most marked . . .

in pig iron, which has advanced between 3d and Is per ton. The demand for finished iron has improved, and quotations are more firmly adhered to by man- 4acturers. There is still a very go-id ,inquiry for steel, and prices are stronger and higher. The pig- iron market is steady, with an advancing tendency, and a better business doing. The Glasgow warrant market has been very strong this week, and prices have risen over Is per ton. The stocks of iron, how- ever, continue very large, and are daily increasing. But the prospects are more favourable. There is more inquiry for Scotch makers' iron, and prices are firmer. Closing quotadons of warrants on Wed- nesday were 41s Id cash and 41s 34d a month with layers, sellers id per ton more.—lron. DELAY OF AN INQUEST.—An inquest on the body of Henry Dabney, the well-known flag steward, who died suddenly at Newton-le-Willows, was de- layed under singular circumstances at Newton on Thursday afternoon'. The jury, witnesses, &c, were summoned. for a quarter-past one by order of Mr T. W. Husband, the deputy coroner, but that gentleman did not arrive until a quarter-past four, when he apologised for having kept them waiting. He said until he arrived there he had not the slightest idea that the inquest had been fixed for the hour it was; he thought it was quarter-past four. He had in error fixed two inquests—one at St. Helens and that at Newton—for the same time, and he was extremely sorry. Several jurors pointed out the great inconvenience to which they had been .put, and.suggested that the Deputy Coroner or the Coroner should bring before the county authorities the advisability of paying jurors. The Deputy Coroner promised to do what he could in the matter. DISTRICT LODGE OF GOOD TENIPLARS : QUAR- TERLY SESSION. —The quarterly session of the South-West District Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Mission Room, Banks-road, Garston, on Saturday. Brother J. B. Collings, D.0.T., of Liver- pool. presided, and was supported by nearly all the district officers and a strong muster of representa- tives from Warrington, Widnes, Rarlectown, St. Helens, Liverpool, &c. The D.C.T. presented his report on the state of the Order in the district, and steps to be taken to incrutse their numbers. The W.D.Sec (Brother Morris Jones) reported the number of members in good standing on the books to be about 2,100, being .anincrease of about 140 on the quarter. He also gave the report of the Exec:Wive, showing that an active work had been carried on during the quarter, and they were pleased to report that the increase in the membershin had not been merely local, but of a general character.—The W. Treas. (Bro. Kirkus) re- ported that the finances were in a satisfactory con- dition, and the D.S.J.T. (Bro. R. Anders) reported that the juvenile section of the order was increasing, and the various Temples were• ;in an encouraging condition. A vote of condolence was unanimously passed. and di- directed to be forwarded to the widow and family of the late Hon. J. B. Finch, the chief presiding officer of the order in America. After the business of the session had been concluded Brother R. W. Kirkits read an instructive paper on "The juvenile order," which gave rise to a discussion It was de- cided to hold the next quarterly session at Liver- pool. The company then adjourned for tea, after which a public meeting was held, Brother J. B. Col- lings presiding. Addresses were given by Brother M. Jones, Sister A. M. Green, P.G.W.V.T., and the Rev. Dr, Oliver, of Garston. SUDDEN DEATH OF A COURSING FLAG STEWARD. —Henry Dabnev. the well-known coursing flag - steward, died suddenly at New ton-le-Willows about eight o'clock on Monday night. The deceased arrived by train from his home, Ashbury, Berk- shire, at 6-30 o'clock, to attend the Haydock Park coursing during the present week, and proceeded to his lodgings in Newton, where he partook of tea apparently in his usual health. He retired at a few minutes before eight o'clock, and he was shortly afterwards found quite dead in an outbuilding. Many sporting men in the district, who were well acquainted with the deceased, were saddened on hearing of the sad occurrence. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, at the Blue Lion Hotel, en Thursday afternoon. Sarah Ann Dabney, of Ash- bury, Berkshire, said the deceased was her husband, and he was 56 years of age. He was a labourer by business, and left home on Monday for Newton. For some years his chest had been had and he had suf- fered from asthma and bronchitis.—Richard Wilkin- son, gardener, Mercer-street. Newton, said the de- ceased had lodged with him on two former occa- sions. He did not look so well when Ile came to witness's house on Monday night and he coughed. After having his tea he went out and on returning he went into the yard. Witness found him in the* closet as if he was asleep. but it was found that he was dead. Doctor , Watkins was sent for, and Dr. Overton appeared ' directly afterwards.—P.C. Spencer said he was sent , for, and found deceased in the closet. He had the body removed to the Blue Lion Hotel.—Police Ser- geant Commins reported that a telegram had been received from the deceased's doctor stating that death had probably resulted from heart disease.— The jury returned a verdict of death from" Natu.ral; causes," probably heart disease.

div.head: WIDNES CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CRICKET CLUB.

The annual meeting of the members of this club was held at the Central Hotel, on Tuesday evening. Mr. James White presides!, and there was a good attendance. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., the tree- Surer, read the statement of the accounts, which I showed a deficit of about £2O. The total receipts amounted to £137 19s Bd. The subscriptions had increased by £2 over last year, but the gate money had decreased from £4 5s to £3 us Bd. One of the chief items of expenditure was £2O 15s, upon the Mr. Deacon observed that the only way to keep the club ' in existence was for the members to exert themselves ; and to get some extraneous help, or reduce the expendi- ture very considerably. He moved the adoption of the report.—Mr. R. H. Colquitt seconded the motion, which was carried, the Chairman observing that Mr. Deacon had taken too desponding a tone, and all that was needed was that the members should make an extra effort.—Mr. W. E. Oakden, the secretary, read the report, which stated that the number of members was now 175, being an increase of 40 over last year. During the season the club had played 17 matches, and had won 4, lost 5, and drawn 8. Although they had played stronger clubs, one more match had been won than last year. The great , fault in the players, the report stated, was that they did not turn up to take part in the matches out of town, and regret was expressed that the club nights were not taken advantage of to the extent they should be. The lawn tennis courts were well patronised by the ladies, and the bowling green by the gentlemen. A proposal had been made to the committee to hold athletic sports conjointly with the Football Club, but the scheme was considered unpracticable. The committee were also asked that they would allow the Athletic Club the use of their field at a reasonable rent, the Cricket Club to find fixtures, which would cost about £3OO. The committee declined this proposal, but stated that the Athletic Club could use the field if they would provide the fix- tures. The Athletic Club, however, 'would not accept this suggestion. During the discussion that ensued it was stated that the subscriptions were £lO in arrear.—The report was adopted.—During the even- ing several suggestions were made for promoting the greater success of the club, and it was decided that the club colours should be white and blue. Mr. F. H. Gos- sage, J.P., was elected president, and the vice-presidents were Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., Major Cross, Major Williams, Captain Wareing, Rev. G. Bond. Mr. J. L. - • and Mr. E. Carey.. Mr. W. E. Oakclen and Aluspratt9 ; Mr. Neild were appointed putt secretaries, Mr. H. Wade Deacon treasurer, and the committee was com- posed as follows :—Messrs. I. Carr, G. E. Sayce, Upward, R. Scott, J. Cannon, sen., F. Young, G. Ashall, El. IL Colquitt, W. Atherton, W. S. Callender, J. A. Brown, J. White, S. Beasley, and J. J. Latham. The post of cap- tain of the first eleven was awarded to Mr R H ColqUitt, sub-captain Mr. W. E. Oakden ; and Messrs. S. Beasley and R. Scott were appointed captain and sub-captain re spectively of the second team. A bat were presented ' Mr. Cullen and Mr. Colquitt, who had made the high batting and bowling averages respectively. est

div.head: AND SOUL. AN INTERESTING STORY.
div.p: AND SOUL. AN INTERESTING STORY.

Diversified character of soil, a large part of which is barren and utterly useless,together with an overcrow- ded and rapidly increasing pop u lationdi as done much to cause misery and poverty in the fair Green Isle, and Ireland to-day is attracting more sympathetic attention from the world at large than any country ever did in the history of nations. Health and educa- tion are alike neglected in the fierce struggle for bread, and to gain this is often an impossibility, many calls being made on the charity of other coun- tries to assist the needy. It is in Ireland that Minister or priest finds his work like that of the Master more thin in any other land. Here he not only has to nay pastoral calls and minister to a ' hungry and thirsty soul, but often he is compelled to look to the physical well-being of his parishioners. Com- bining the physician, minister, and alms-giver in the oneperson,he is brought intostrange contact with all phases of life and society, and the story told us a short time since by the Rev. M. B. Hogg, of the Rectory, at Keady, County Armagh, was not at all peculiar, yet thoroughly interesting. The Rectory is a beautiful little place, standing back from the road in the shadow of a clump of grand old • trees, and is such a place as the tourist or passer-by will look at with longing for the restful, quiet, and home-like - comforts, that its every appearance indicates it to have. It was in the library of the Rectory that Mr. Hogg made his wonderful statements, only a portion of which can be given here, but enough is repeated to let the pub- lic know something of those things which the reverend gentleman considers useful and beneficial to mankind. He said Some months months ago I became interested in a gentleman who had suffered for a considerable period from albu- minuria, which so seriously affected his health that he was incapable of bearing the slightest exertion. His water was examined by heat and acid tests, and dis- played one-fourth of alfmmen. I purchased and save him some Warner's SAFE Cure. After taking 'two bottles, another test was made, which showed only a small percentage of albumen. He has now taken four bottles, and feels himself perfectly well and capable of 'any exertion. The benefit in this case was so great and, so rapid that I have used the Sara Cure in other cases among my parishioners, and always with the same good

. - results. "At first I regarded the SAFE Remedies as of a piece with otherpatent medicines,but I am now convinced by actual and severe tests that they are wonderful medicines, whatever be their nature, and cannot fail, under Providence, to efect a radical cure in 'every case in which they are applied. I have tried it, and never found any medicine to secure as-much good result in a short time." After listening to the Rev. Mr. Hogg, we could not help thinking that if the thousands of our people who are suffering from diseases of th., liver andkidneys would only take his experience as a guide, and would use the SAFE Cure, how much physical agd mental misery they would escape, and how much btirter would it be for the community at large to have strong, healthy ditizens than to have so many invalids and chronic alters. The remedy mentioned by the Rev. Mr. Hogg can be procured of all chemists. at 4s. 6d. per bottle.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAT.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr. R. Garnett.

Afisc'Estm.mocs.—Ellen Elliott, last from 'Manchester, -was fined 5s and costs for drunkenness, and John Thos. Warburton, a labourer, was se& to prison for seven days for begging. THEFf.—ThomaA Ratcliffe, carter, 225, Howley-lane, was sent to prison for fourteen days for having stolen a horse cloth, the property of Edward Lunt. Greening- DRITNEENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Ellen Mason, in Buttermarket-street, fined ss, including costs; Elizabeth Allman, in Irlam- street, fined ss, including costs; Philip Buxton, in Wil- derspool-road, fined 5s and costs; William Butler, in Tanners-lane, on the previous morning, fined ss, includ- ing costs. She wa.s remanded for further inquiries to be made. ALLEGED FURIOUS RIDING.—James Murphy was sum- moned for furiously riding a horse in Sankey-street, on the 22nd inst. He was dismissed with a caution. Smoot A'TTEICDANCE CASES.—Mr. G. Riley, school at- tendance officer,summoned John Rooney, Crossley-street, for neglecting to send his- two children regularly to sehool.—Mr. Riley stated that that was the defendant's 14th appearance, and although the children had tried nearly every school in the town, they were not sent regu- larly.—A line of lOs was imposed.—Thomass Hughes, forgeman, Pierpoint-street, was fined 5s for neglecting to send his child regularly to Heathside School, and Thos. Wright, glass blower, Bank Quay (who was represented by his wife) was let off with a caution, on Mrs. Wright promising not to offend again. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Piekmere, Councillor Fran- comb, and Mr. E. J. Guest. A Tiocurryss TRAVELLER.—JETne4 Brady. shoemaker, was fined ss. and costs for riding on the London and North-Western Railway from Ordsall-lane to Warring,ten on Monday, without having paid his fare. BEOGING.—John Masheter, labourer, and James Man- ning, labourer' were each fined ss. and costs for this offence, and a labourer named Walker was sent to prison for seven days. WEDNESDAY.—IIefore Mr. John Greening. DnumonslrEss,—James McAlister, a cripffie, who said that he came from Liverpool, was charged with this offence. He was dismissed with a caution. THITRSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster. Buoorso.—Winif red Cavanagh was charged with this offence. She was dismissed with a caution. ALLEGED THEFT.—Andrew Mackenzie Guthrie. and Sarah Guthrie, his wife, were charged with having stolen, or having received knowing it to have been stolen, 35 yards of flannel, of the value of 145., on the 25th ult., the property of Wm. Coates, woolen draper, Friar's-gate. They were remanded until Monday. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, and Aldermen • Harrison and Chandley. THREATS.—WiIIiam Wheelan was summoned by Lydia Smyth for having used threats towards her on the g6th ult. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the complainant. The matter was said to have arisen out of trade jealousy. Defendant, who denied the offence, was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour, and pay the costs, or, in default, to go to prison for a fortnight. A DESERTER.—George Bryce, a deserter from the 16th Lancers, stationed at Dublin, was remanded to Walton gaol to await escort. ASSAULTING A BROTHER-IN-LAW.—Elizabeth Monks, wife of John Monks, landlord of the Pocket House Inn, was summoned for having assaulted William Henry Monks, her brothet -in-law, in the Pocket House, on the 25th ult. Mr. A. Browne defended. After hearing evi- dence the Bench said that they thought Mrs. Monks had received great provocation, and dismissed the case on payment of costs. William Henry Monks, the complain- ant, then entered the defendant's box to answer a sum- mons charging him with having been drunk on the licensed premises of John Monks, his brother, on the same date, and with having refused to quit when re- quested. The Bench imposed a fine of 158 and costs. A YEAR OF MARRIED LlFE.—Patrick NOrton was summoned for having assaulted his wife, who said that she had been married twelve months, and during that time her husband had given her a dozen black eyes. He was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour for the next six months, and pay 95., the costs. CIIITELTY.—Peter Ryce, who did not appeal., was sum- moned for ill-treating a heifer at the cattle fair on Tues- day, by allowing it to be overcharged with milk. When being spoken to in regard to the condition of the cow by P.S. Cheney, the defendant said that if it was milked it would make £3 or £4 difference in the selling price. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed.

DARF.SBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Oreenal, W. Long, J. Marson, and Henry Neild. WRAA Setairs,—Frederick Chaplin, licensed publican -at Grappenhall, was summoned for having, on the 4th of November, unlawfully sold to Superintendent Hol- lingworth a quantity of whiskey which was not of the substance and nature demanded.—Constable Jackson, 'Runcorn, deposed to having bought a pint of whiskey, and Superintendent Hollingworth stated that the liquor had been analysed by Dr. Carter Bell, who certified that he had found 36 per cent. of water in it, being 11 per cent, more than allowed by statute.—Defendant, in replying to the Bench, said the which had been supplied was not for sale. His brother managed the business for him, and as he happened to be out at the time the girl had supplied the wrong whiskey. The whiskey intended for sale was in a decanter.—The Bench, taking into con- sideration the heavy- costs (£1 11s), only imposed a fine of ss. THE SONDAY'S DINNISIL—Jame% Smit'n, labourer, of Whitley Superior, was charged with having in his pos- session, on the morning of Sunday, the 9th October, a snare and two rabbits, and also with unlawfully being on the land of Mr. Henri Nield for the purpose of taking game.—Constable Harrison having proved the offence, and also produced the snare which he had taken from the defendant, the latter pleaded, guilty, urging that "he did it to get a Sunday's dinner for his wife and ' family, as he had not been getting much money be-. fore that."—A fine of 10s. and costs (17s. Bd. in all) was imposed, with the alternative of, 14 days' imprison- ment. DOG CASES.—Reginald Gordon Henry St. Clair Lindsay Williams was summoned for keeping a dog without a license at Appleton Thorn, on the 21st October, and was fined 5s and costs.—Peter Simpson, Appleton, was fined

Es 6d, and Robert Eyes, Dock-road, Leftwich, was or- dered to pay the costs for like olfenms. Ni7ISANCE AT ACTON GRAM:M.—Charles Leigh Williams, Acton Grange, was summoned at the instance of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, for permitting a nuisance to exist in the vicinity of his residence, and an order, with costs, was made to abate the nuisance.—A similar order was made with reference to a nuisance al- d to exist at Holly Hedge Farm. NEGLECT niP CHILDILEN.—John Hatton, a drayman, in the employ of Messrs Greenall, Whitley, and Co., and residing at Stockton Heath, was summoned, at the in- stance of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, for neglect- ing to support his three children—Mary Anne, Hannah, and Eheebe—with proper lodging and clothing.—Mr. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians.:—lt ap- peared from the evidence of Dr. Holbrook that he had visited the defendant's house and found the three 4161- ren named, who are all under 14 years of age, in a vary poorly-clad condition, especially with reference to their underclothing. There was only one bed in the house. and it was composed of an old mattress and a lot of rags.—the Chairman: Do these three girls sleep with their father ?—Dr. Holbrook: I cannot say for that.— Defendant: I have done the best I could, as I have been a widower for seven years, and my wages are not very high, but I will try to do better in future.—The Chair- man (to Dr. Holbrook) : Was there any food in the house P—Mr. Linaker : Oh, there is no complaint about • that.—Defendant was bound over in his own recogniz- . ances and one surety of £5, and discharged on promis- ing to attend to his children better in future. • Dntrxx AND DISORDERLY.—John Roberts, for being . drunk and disorderly, ss. and costs • Thomas Robinson (two occasions), laand costs; John Haddock, 5s and costs.

- NEGLECTING TO WEIGH BEAD. - William Welslip, 1 Stockton Heath, was summoned by Constable Harrison for selling two loaves of bread-without weighing them: , Defendant, in pleading guilty, explained that it was an oversight on the part of his wife, sl.s he was not present at the time. The Constable stated that one loaf was oz. light, and the other 2-ioz. He was ordered to pay the costs, 7.4.—Mary Tipping, Wilderspool, and Stephen Hindley, Wilderspool, were summoned by Constable Bennett for a like offence. In the former case the loaf purchased was a little over loz light, and in the second about loz. light. Defendants were ordered topay the costs.

D atom Awn Disorinalux.—Mary Crogan, Nelson-street; Ellen Coffey, Fryer-street; Mary and Ann Gough, High- street, were each fined for the offence of drunkenness. Constables Sutherland, Potts, and Kettle proved the cases.—For using obscene language, John Welsh, of Salkeld-square, was fined 10s. and costs on the evidence of P.C. Sutton.—Wm. Dova.ston, driver, of Weston, was fined ss. and costs, Bs. 6d., for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Runcorn. P.S. Woolley proved the case.--On the evidence of P.C. Sutherland, Kate Duffy was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk in High-street. FOOTBALL IN THE SrnErrs.—Freclerick Richardson and I Albert Mullen, boys, pleaded guilty to having played I football in Devonshire-square on the 25th November.— Superintendent Hollingsworth said he had no wish to take proceedings in such cases, but he was obliged to do so in consequence of the numerous complaints be re- ceived. A fine of is and costs, ets. 6d., was imposed upon each defendent,

BREACH OF THE PEACE.—John McCafferty, of 12. Catherine-street, and John Lawson. no residence, pleaded guilty to fighting in Lugsdale.road, on Saturday night, and each prisoner was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months or go to gaol for seven days.

WYCLIFFE V. FRODSILUI.—PIayed at Warrington on Saturday. Frodsham were defeated for the first time this season. Score—Wycliffe, 1 goal and 4 minors, to Frodsham 5 minors. RUNCORN FREE WANDERERS I. WIDNES BLUE STAR.— This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. Victory rested with the home team by 1 try and 4 minors to 1 minor.

RUNCORN (2ND) V. CHRETILtIst HILL (IST TEAM).— This match was played at Manchester on Saturday. The visitors were poorly represented, and the game resulted in a victory for Cheetham Hill by a goal and a try to a minor. _ _

HTINCORN HORNETS V. WIDNES TAN 0' SRANTERS This match was played on the ground Of the former and after a pleasant but hard-fought game, victory rested with the home team by 1 try and 7 minors to four minors.

WYCLIFFE V. FRODSRAM (21.r0 TEems).—Played at Frod- sham. The visitors soon showed themselves prominent in neat runs and passes, but scoring was stopped by the safe tackling of ,the home backs. At call of time the score stood—Froffaham, 3 minors; Wycliffe, 1 minor. Sr. jOHN'S (2ND) V. WARRINGTON STAR.—Played at Grange Park, St. Helens, on Saturday, in the presence of a number of spectators, resulting in a victory for Warrington Star, by one dropped goal (disputed), two tries, and five minors, to St. John's two minors. The visitors were a "smart and combined team, their play being much admired by the onlookers. The home team were but weakly represented, being with- out the services of Kay, Leyland, Chapman, and Billing- ton.

WARRIN¢TON WANDERERS v. DITTON.—The Wanderers visited Ditton with a weak team, and after a pleasant game of two 'thirties, the contest ended in a win for the visitors. During the first half nothing but minors was scored. After the change of ends Price got over for the visitors. Lawton took the place and kicked a neat goal. Nothing of importance was scored the rest of the game, and at the call of time the score was—Wanderers, 1 goal and 5 minors; Ditton, 3 minors. . .

WEST LtmcAsrunu RUGBY UNION .—The following ties in the third round of the West Lancashire Junior Com- petition were played on Saturday :—Widws Recreation beat Blundellsands by 5 points to 1. Si'vermeil Hornets beat nightield by 13 points to 2. Scott Lane beat Platt Bridge by 14 points to nill. Woodman Rovers beat Widnes St. Mary's by 6 points to nil. At a committee meeting of the onion, held on Saturday at the Goat Hotel, the draws for the fourth round and the semi-final round of the Junior Competion were made as follows : Fourth Round: Silverwell Hornets v. Scott Lane; Widnes Recreation a bye ; Woodman Rovers a bye; Poolstock or Altrincham a bye. Semi-finals: Widnes Recreation v. Silverwell Hornets or Scott Lane, at St. Helena ground; Altrincham or Poolstock v. Woodman Rovers, at Wigan Rovers Ground. To be played on Saturday, the 10th December. •

WARRINGTON V. WIGAN (" A" Tgams).—This fixture was played on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, be- fore a large number of spectators. There was a very strong wind, which greatly interfered with good back play. The home team were ably assisted at half back by Mr. Wells, of the "Silver King" Company; which had been playing at the Public Hall during the past week. This player officiated as captain of the Loadon United Hospitals during the season 1831-2, and also figured in the county team of Middlesex a few seasons back. It is needless to say that he justified his selection by playing in first-class style, and the spectators were not slow to accord him a hearty reception. The home captain won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. Halliwell kicked off for the visitors at 3-30, play settling down in the Wigan quarters. Barnes put in a short run, but Bithell kicked into touch. From a scrimmage, Whittle secured and passed to Barnes, who kicked, Bald- win sending the ball dead. Vilkington dropped out, and Parr dribbled to Warburton, who „punted to Marsden, this player being held befere he could make any return. Kearnes relieved from a kick into touch, and from a line- out Turner got possession and went away with a strong run, but fell when he seemed likely to score. On a scrimmage being formed, McNamara came through with the ball, but Barnes picking up smartly succeeded in grounding the ball over the line after a grand run, the same player kicking, a goal. Halliwell re-started, but the ball had to be scrimmaged in centre through the visitors getting off-side. Whittle next passed to Evans, who ran and passed to Appleton, the latter playez kick- sng to the visitors' full hick, who was held by Turner. Ryan passed to Yates, who kicked into touch, and from the lineout the iriganers worked tho ball into the War- rington 25, Jolley relieving by a splendid screw kick. For a short time play was now located near centre, until Barnes got hold and put in a long kick, the ball going dead. Wells returned the drop out, and a _kick by Barnes took operations to the Wigan quarters, where Whittle passed to Evans, this player making a good run in, Barnes being again successful at the place. Half time was called, with the score standing—Warrington, , two goals and two minors, to Wigan nothing. 1 On change of ends the home team started with a dribble, but Hazledon stopped their progress. Evans by a long kick took play to the Wigan quarter flag, the same player shortly afterwards making a strong run, be- ing pulled down by Pilkington close to the line. The visiting forwards broke away with the ball, Jolley sav- ing nicely near centre. Wells now got away with a strong run and passed to Barnes, who was stopped by Marsden. Whittle passed to Wells, this player making another good run, . and, when tackled by Marsden, passed to Barnes, the ball going into touch. Wells next got away from a scrimmage, and threw to Turner, who made a wide pass to Appleton, and this player putting on top speed ran round his opponents, gaining a try, Turner failing at goal from a difficult place. Halliwell kicked off, play resting near centre. Some good pass- ing took place between Whittle, Evans, and Barnes, the

last-named player being collared by Kearnes. The visitors now dribbled to the home line, and almost suc- ceeded in getting over. Appleton removed the danger by kicking to touch, and from the line-out broke away to centre. Wells, who was now playing a good game, got away from a scrimmage, and passed nicely to Evans, but he was pushed into touch. The Wigan forwards headed by Bibby Hilton, and Parr, dribbled to centre, Barnes staying their career. Whittle now passed toEvans, who made a beautiful run, and gained what was generally considered a well-merited and legitimate try, but the referee ordered a five-yards senmmng,e to be formed. The Wiganers broke away, and Hilton kicked to Jolley, who saved near midfield. Wells put in another fine run and looked like scoring, but he was pulled down near the line by Marsden. Whittle passed to Evans,. who transferred to Appleton, the latter player running in near the touch Bag. Warburton failing to improve the point. At the call of time the score stood :—Warring- ton, 2 eats 2 tries, and 2 minors; Wigan, nil. Teams —Warrington:; Full back, Jolley: threequarter backs., Barnes, Evans, and Appleton: half backs, Whittle (cap- tain), and Wells; forwards, Molvneux, Eyes, Thornley, Turner, Holmes, Warburton, Lloyd, Unsworth, and Danohue. Wigan: Full back, Baldwin; threequarter backs, Yates, Pilkington, and Marsden; half backs, Kearnes and Ryan: forwards, McNamara, Parr, Bithell, FlalliwclL Wells, Bibby, Batchelor, Hilton, and Hazlo- don.
WIDNES v. BIRCH.

Widnes journeyed to Birch on Saturday, with a very poor team, Hughes, Plumpton Barker, and G. Bing- ham being absent, but nevertheless the " Chemicals ' proved themselves superior to the Birchonians (who, however, lacked the services of Ferriman) to the extent of one goal, three tries, and seven minors to nothing. The visitors played down hill in the first half, and also had the wind in their favour. When half time was called the score stood—Widnes, one goal, three trios, and six minors, to nil. Throughout this half the home team never had the slighest chance of scoring, only taking the ball into the Widnes territory once. In the second half. , however, when they had the advantage of the wind and slope, they did better, and once or twice assailed their opponents' line. But the visitors were too good for them even now, and despite all disadvantages showed the better play. Only a armee minor was scored in the second half, and at the close the score was as above stated. Teams :--Widnes S. Bingham, back; Smith (captain), Parkinson, and Farrell, three-quarter backs; Wilkinson and Howard, half backs; Kiddie, Woods, Gandy, Barber, Hardman, Pennington, Wright,. Samp- son, and Williams, forwards. Birch: Edmunds, back; T. Higginbottom, H. D. Wheeler, and Eaves, three- quarters; E. Higgirrbottom and groteghton, half backs; Bambridge, Abbey, Warlc, Smith, K. Higginbottom, A. Wheeler, P. Estcourt, Heywood, and Hardman, for- wards. RUNCORN v. KENDAL, HORNETS.

The above teams met at Runcorn on Saturday, in fine but windy weather. Bbth sides were weak, Wood% Wright, and Broady being absent from the home side, while the visitors were- without Walker, Wilkinson, Reatham, and Fisher. The game- was very fast and well-contested, and furnished one of the' best encounters on the Irwell-road enclosure this season, Runcorn win- ning byone goal, one try, and two minors to a try and tyro manors. H. Hughes won the toss; and the Hornets kicked off against the wind, a series of exchanges taking piace- for the first fevrminutes, Cawley eventually kick- ing into touch slightly-in the Hbrnets' territory. From the line out " Parsons "'and Crass forgedahead, but Bra- zendale met the ball and dropped into, touch at the visiting 25 mark, where Speakman, being fed, took an abortive drop. Allen, runningthe-leather out, Brazen- dale, with a huge return, landed into touch near the visitors' lines, and from the line out the- saving clause was nebessitated. The drop-out was a failure, but the Hornets' forwards rushed grandly up-the field, danger being averted by a jirdicious flying kick by the Runcorn captain. Then Battersby got in a good run. Cawley stayed' his progress, Wainwright, Gatley, and Clarke came through the scrimmage, and the- Hornets retired precipitately to their 25 fia.z. Here Andrews passed nicely to Speakman, who dropped his first goal this sea- son amid loud cheers. The kick-off saw Battersby again prominent only to have-his effort spoiled by H. Hughes. but Runcorn had shortly to touch down. A beautiful passing movement by the Hornets' backs brought play in front of the Runcorn posts, where several tight scrim- mages took place, Andrews eventually relieving to mid- field. From here Baines ran strongly to the home 25, where soon after the same player essayed a. drop, which compelled Brazendale to again touch down. 'After the drop out Baines obtained a free kick in front of the Run- corn pasts, but nothing came of it. Even play followed, but lust prior to half time good passing by the Runcorn backs enabled Cawley to run to within a few yards of the visitors' lines, a touchdown ensuing. On crossing over, Runcorn pressed, Wainwright and' Andrews being conspicuous, and the visiting quarter flag was the scene. Armstrong, by a dashing run, relieved the pressure, Davies pulling him up in fine style, and the latter, after a period of even play, dodged through the opposing for- wards and kicked into touch near the- Hornets' line. From the line-out H. Hughes had the ball thrown to him, and, running splendidlyacross the field,placed the leather nicely into Cawley's hand, who dashed over the line, a maul ensuing, buttheßuncorn man eventually grounded. Brazendale was very unlucky in not registering a goal, the ball striking the post. ' For a time the-visitors were kept well within- their own territory, unt* nice passing between Crass, Baines, and Battersby caused Runcorn to retire, and Baines, taking a pass intended' fee Cawley' scrambled over and gained a try, Allen's attempt at goal from the difficult position only just missing. Nothing further was scored after this, and the game ended as above. Teams L—Runcorn—J. lb•azendate., back ;T. H. Davies, H. C. Speakman, and If. Cawley, three-quarter hacks; H. G. Andrews and H. Hughes, half backs; W. Hughes, P. Riley, W. S. Stubbs, J. Lewis, J. Clarke, J. Gatlev, W. Fauikner, G. T. Wainwright, and J. Barns, forwards. Kendal' Ffornets—J. Allen, back; G. Batters- by, T.G. Baines, and J. Armstrong, three-quarter backs; J. Berry and W. Cross, halfbacks; ham, W. "Parsons,"T. Cross, F. Heap, W. Whitehead, W. Franklin,?. Ireland, and E. Wilson, forwards.

Wigan harve several times been subjected to defeat by the Warrin,gtoinams, but on Satorday they evidently in- tended to retrieve their reputation as far as they possi- bly mulch and having a comparatively weak team to deal vrith•they nude use of the opportunity to achieve a fairly decisive victory over thmr opponents. This is a match which is looked for- ward to with some interest. ,The Het-nets are a strong lot, and arereputed to play a fine °pets game. Turner from the first team, and the Wigan contingent, although they plard with a gond , cleat of spirit, were, prevented from notating any tingi- bre points. CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRAMION AT EARLESTOWN. A, meeting of Conservatives and Unicniets of the Ne eton Division in support of the policy of the pre- sent Ceavernment, was held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on Monday evtming. There was a very large attendance, but there tease noticeable absence of any prominent Isiberern. whether so-called "Unionists" or otherwise.. Prier to the commence- ment of the proceedings- 311 r. George Wright, of Earlestown, excellently sang "'Rule Brittania," the audience joining in the'chorus.. Mr. M. Brown-Westheatis chairman of the Conserva- tive Association, presided, and he wa.4 supported by Lord Cross, Mr. T. W. Legbi.MtPsfor the Newtoni:Divi- : sion, Rev. W. H. Pugh, Rev: E £-Hlack, Captain With- ; ington, J.P., Messrs. R. Efonghtoni.J.P., W. F. Geoch, J.P. R. W. Francomb, 'B; Clover J. E. Pardey, B. d. F. Herron, George Clarke; EsStone,T. D. Grimke, R. H. Wright, R. Barton, T. Cooper;.W. H. Brook (War- rington), Dr. Handyside, Dr.,.Pattersen, anyl other gentle- men. Letters of apology fernornattendanee had been received from the Right Horn At.JL.Badfour, M.P., Baron de Worms, Mr. A. B. Forweedl./CP:, Sir James Fergu- son. M.P. Sir Gilbert Greenail. Mitt. M.P., Sir A. B. Walker, ion., M.P., Mr. T. B Rbyden; M.P., Mr. H. Beton Karr, M.P., Major Sandys; Rev; Canon Hopwood) Colonel George McCorquodale;J:P. and Mr. A. C. Me: Corquodale, J.P., the latter of.' Idiom: wrote regretting that he would be away from: home, and hoping they might have a good meeting of Urtionietss The Chairman remarked that-manrietters of apology ' had been received, including one from esgentleman who was highly esteemed in the neighbourhood, and who, when brought out as a candidate, ran. the present Lord Cross—then Sir Richard—a very narrowecontest. Col. George McCorquodale had written a letter hoping they would have a good meeting. and; continuing, 'I hope the strength of the Unionist party,will increase, in the intermte of Great Britain and our fellow subjects in Ire- land." (Applause.) The Chairman afterwards com- mented on the present state of political affairs, and said measures had been passed, and 'would continue to be passed, to make Ireland as contented as any portion of the kingdom. (Applause.) Lord Cross, who was well recei4d, said when the present Government came into .offiee they found them- selves in a very difficult position. They were returned, to power by a vast majority, and they were not a Con- servative but a Unionist party. (Hear, hear.) The diffi- culty of the Government consisted in their having to face an illegitimate opposition, for there never was in the history of Parliament such a determined and deliber- ate obstruction carried on as there was during the last session. (Applause.) This had been fostered and en- couraged and led by the leaders of what ought to be the' legitimate, butwhat he styled the illegitimate, Opposition. (Applause.) He proceeded to say that the present Gov- ernment had given pledges, which were borne out by its acts, that it was absolutely determined that law and order should be maintained, not alone in England, Scot- land, Ireland, or even in gallant little Wales, but through- out the whole of the United Kingdom. Touching upon foreign affairs, he said we had been passing through times of the greatest possible danger and disturbance all over Europe, but thanks to the prudence, wisdom, and forethought of Lord Salisbury, backed up by every single member of the Cabinet, the influence of England had pre- vailed throughout Europe in the maintenance of what constituted the highest interests of Great Britain—the maintenance of an honourable peace. (Hear, hear.) As to colonial matters, they might rest assured that it was the intention and the most earnest desire of the Govern- ment to draw together in the closest possible bonds of friendship and amity, not simply for the purposes of de- fence, but also for the purpose of commercial transac- tions, the whole of the colonies with the mother country, (Applause.) Dealing with the affairs of Ireland, the noble lord said he knew of no grander purpose for which men could be allied than that which now bound together the Conservatives and the Liberal Unionists. (Hear, hear.) They were determined to uphold law and order not only in Ireland, but in England as well. (Applause.) The proper way to deal with Ireland was to foster indus- tries throughout the country, and to do that the law must be maintained. It was quite impossible to let dis- turbances go on, and equally impossible to let the leaders' of those disturbances escape. The ill-doings of ',ears ' and years mist call forth patient, constant, and deter- mined energy in the path they had chalked out, but until the people said that path was wrong the Government would continue in it, believing it to Be the path of jus- tice, of honour, aiid of happiness, not for the English nation only, but for the Irish as a nation and for every individual in that country. (Loud applause.) • Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., who was received with cheers, moved "That this meeting cordially welcomes the late member of the constituency, the Right Hon. Lord Cross, . and desires to express its best thanks to his Lordship for , his address." They might, he said, extend a wider ap- plication to the resolution, and include in their welcome a vote of confidence in the Ministry to which he belongs —(applause)—for everyone there would agree with him. , that the Government, on the whole, emphatically de- served their confidence: In regard to foreign affairs, Lord Salisbury could, at any rate, claim three decided successes—the satisfactory' conclusion of the Suez Canal , Convention, the settlement with the French of the ex- ceedingly difficult question of the New Hebrides, and the . settlement with Russia of the Central Asian and Afghan. frontier question. Those services alone were sufficient to , entitle him totheir confidence, but foreign affairs had been overshadowed by what had taken place in these islands. , There was nothing in the result of the session which. . would strike one as possessing an exceptional. character. ; With the exception of the Irish measures the bills passed were of a modest nature, but at the same time theywere; .1 thoroughly useful measures. (Hear, hear.) Besides that they had to be passed in the face of the most per- sistent and shameless obstruction. He alluded to the Parnellite members SS the parents of obstruction, and , said their object was undisguised—it was to render all legislation in the country impossible; until their own do- mends were acceded to. But they must be shown that , the business of the country was not going to be delayed . solely on account of thedeterrnination of a certain num- ber of paid enemies of Great Iltitaini (Applause.) The ' measure by which ,the goverment would : stand or fall was the ; measure , which was , erroneously described as the Coercien BIM. It was only in consequence of persistent agitation of , Irish agitators, and after the ordinary law had failed, that the Government had recourse to exceptional i measures. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the recent dis- turbances in London, he remerkedthat it seemed' to him that tranquility and order were cheaply purchased if it „ was only at the expense of a few agitators' broken heads. He thought for the sake of the community they might well be put to a little temporary bodily inconveni- ence. (Cheers and laughter.) He believed that the peo- ple would realise and recognise the fact that to the party : of law and order, the great Unionist party, the duty Of : discharging the: government of this great empire might , most safely be confided. (Cheers.) Mr. E. Storey (late president of the Leigh Liberal 5 , Club) seconded the resolution, which. was supported by Captain Withington, J.P., and, carried. , Lord Cross having briefly replied, the following resolu- tion, on the motion of Mr. Catterall, seconded by Mr, • Francomb (Warrington), and supported by Mr. T. D. Grimke, was agreed to with: enthusiasm That this ; meeting of electors and others of the Newton division , desires to express its gratitude at the earnest and deter- mined endeavours of the Government to settle the , Irish question, and its high appreciation of the patriotic conduct of the Liberal Unionists in supporting what ap- pears to be the only line of policy likely to maintain the ; integrity of the empire. The meeting thinks the self- sacrificing efforts of the Conservative and Unionist mem- bers of Parliament worthy of the highest praise." The proceedings concluded with a Vote of thanks to the chairman. silos KAY'S TIC PILLS, a specific in Neuralgia, Faceache, 91-d. and 131 d. ; postage, hl. Of all Cheinnts.—Advt. L THE MI7RDER OP AN OLD MAN.—The itiag,isterial in- quiry into the barbarous murder of the old man Pickerill at Prees Lower Heath was concluded at Whitchurch on ' Thursday. Further important evidence was given of the ' prisoner, William Arrowsmith, having been in the vicinity of the old man's lonely cottage on the evening before the murder—a fact to which the accused man, who is a nephew of the deceased, gives a denial—and the magistrates sent the case for trial at the assizes. SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT CARHARTHEN.—Henry Jones, aged thirty-eight, milk vendor, living in Blue-street, Carmarthen, murdered his daughter, Annie Jane Jones, aged seven, on Thursday afternoon, by cutting her throat from ear to ear in such a way as to nearly sever the head from the body. When the police visited the house, Jones was fondling the dead body and saying, "It is my child; I did it with a razor." His face, hands, and clothes were covered with blood, and so was a razor which was shut up and in a case in his pocket. He had been drinking heavily. CHLORO-LINSPED " Cough Lozenges, post free, 7d.
