OPENING OF A SUNDAY SCHOOL AT GREAT SANKEY. The new Sunday school which' has just been erected in connectiim with St. Mary 'a Church, Great Sankey, was on Tuesday evening declared open by Sir Gilbert Greenall, M„P, For a considerable time past the need for an enlarged and improved Sunday , school has been strongly telt in the parish. of Great Sankey, the old building near the church: which had been condemned as so day school, getting less ' and less fit as time went ors for the uses to,which it was put. Consequently in Janmery of this year a corn- , mittee was formed, with the \ricer, the Rev., E. S. Jackson, as chairrnan. te endeavour to supply the pressing want of the parish for a suitable Sunday school. The labours of this committee in liaising the needful funds were singularlysuccessful, and as a result the commodious new schools were opened on Tuesday evening, it may be said free from 6bt, as SieGilbert Greenall generously promised to give a further donation of £25, so that all the antiCipated 'expenditure might be fully met. The architect of the school was Mr. W. Owen, of Warrington, and the builders. Messrs. Collin and Son, and it will "ile seen from therretnarks of Mr. Hughes, the secretary of the committee, that the architect and builders hems alike even satisfaction At the opening cere- mony there whoa very large attendance, the room' being crowded'. In addition to Sir Gilbert Greenall there were also, on the platform Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greener!, the Misses Greenall, theßev. E. S. Jackson, the Irev. S. Wilkinson, the Its-v. G. D. Wray, r.nd the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman T. H. Sutton;. The room was beautifully decorated with a variety of designs and mottoes. In the course of the evening Miss Monks sang in her ad- mirable manner, "There is a green hill far: away," and " O'rest in the Lord," the accompaniments be- ing played by Mr. Wersley. A short religimas cere- mony was 'cond ucted by the Rev. B. S. Jackson prior to the opening oereraony. Sir GILBIIRT.GREENXiM, Bart., M.P. on rising to disclare the schools open, waereceived with loud applause. Fisaid they would allew him to say in a very few words that it was a, great pleasureteehim to be there that evening, and that he gladly and sipcerely joined with Mr. .11ack- son in that service. H'-heartily hoped that God's bless- ing might rest on that Minot. (Hear, hear.) He was there but he had beerew very long time in coming. But it had not been the-faxik of his friend their clergy- man that he had not been- there sooner, because Me„ Jackson had most kindly-and courteously and very fre- quently indeed invited him to come. They might, however, believe him that there was no man in this world who had so much to do as he who had nothing to do. (Hear, hear; and'laughter.) People very frequently said" Oh, there is that Greenall, he has nothing to 40," I but Greet:mil found that he' heel a good many things to do, and he could not always appear when he was asked and expected. But he -was-there at last and he was thankful to be there as Mi. Jackson's guest. (Applause.) And if his presence there-on i that evening dould do any service he was teilthonsandtimes repaid for the little exertion it cost himi ,There-vrice no occasion in life upon which they might not usefully look around them, and if they looked upon the past that evening they were to be congratulated upon what they had done in that place. (Hear, hear.) Theirpastor, Mr. Jackson, had put his hand to the plough -and he-was not to look back. There was very much in that reamto,encourage him, there was nothing to deter hire; and-'might God's blessing rest upon him,, and might he be • useful and happy both to him- self and to others in that place: (Applause.) He (Sir Gilbert (/reenaLl) had known Sankey for more than half a century and he kneormost or the faces in Sankey though they-might not recognise 'ore know him, and he had a sincere affection forethe people of Sankey and he hoped that their friendship and affection might 'increase. (Ap- plause.) Haring formally declared the school open, Sir Gilbert remarked • that they had to thank those who , had obtained' that ached for them and they had to give al helping hand to those who carried it on. There was no person in the room who might not do a,•great deal to further the work of the school and to further the work of God's Kingdom in that place.' Let them allgo forward todo God's work a,ndif they all did that God's blessing wouldcorne. (Loud applause.) Mk: W. D. HUGIOIS , who was- greeted with applause, said he thought he might very fairly congratulate him- self upon the difference between his position that night and the position he occupied when on a former occasion he had to render some sort of statement as to the progress and prospects of their new Sunday school building scheme. The outlook at that time was somewhat gloomy, indeed they were in a very gloomy place, for they were at that time in the barn-like structure up , the road which had been condemned for day schoolwork, but which still had to serve for Sunday school and other parish purposes. But it was of coursetlaefinancial mist that he referred to more particularly. It- was his business at the former meeting to speak of 'work in front of them, 'of difficulties to be encountered, and obstacles to be re- moved, and of a large sunrof money to be raised. He had, so to speak, to give the -dimensions and to speak of the height of the hill of financial difficulty Which was in front of them, and which they had to scale. He might say that that hill -was, fairly, steep and tolerably high, in fa,et it was so high that its-top , might be said to have been -very much in the cloud§ at that time. However the Committee who had the matter in hand girded up their loins and the reetilt of their untiring efforts and of the warm and hearty co-operation of the parishioners generally, and/the liberal aid of their friends outside— in the forefront- oftwhom their chairman must stand—the result of all that was. that that night he was able to speak not of work in front of them but of work done, of strenuous effort carried out to, a successful issue, of a good work carried to its ultiinate conclusion, and, best of all, . of such a near approach to and equalisation of their liabilities and assets, that any little defieiency which might remain they might regard as a. mere bagatelle which they could meet with a, light heart. (Applause). For some years the old building had been creaking and groaning, and showing many signs of the infirmities which come with increasing age 4 and at last it got to such a pass that something must be dOne. Some-ten months ago they had their first meeting to consider what must be done, and they at once fOund themselves face to face with an ur- gent need for, a new site ancl new premises. In a parish which had barely- had breathing time to recover horn the severe-strain of metering its old but now beau- , tiful church,,it would not be surprising if some had 'felt inclined to. shrink from the new effort required, but they found that the only path of retreat was one which would' land them in the Still greater re- sponsibility of closing the-school. That was a responsi- bility they could not face ; they could not think of clos- ing a growing- school, and turning the scholars adrift. (Hear, heari and applause.) They preferred to meet their financial difficulties in the face, and they met them; the result being that they were there that night not very much worse for the trouble. Theirschools would cost them some £1,406;.0e nearly that amount, inclusive of the furniture, but not including the land. The site was free- hold, and had been given by a generous parishioner. (Loud applause.) That parishioner expressed a desire that his name should be kept secret, but the chairman said his name-was well known. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) And as lie did not like to keep a secret, he would tell them that the donor of the site was Mr. Jeans. (Loud applause-.) Towards the £1,400 they had raised Sams as follows_ From kind friends outside of the parish they-had received sums amounting in the total to £4OO. (Bear, hear.) They had a bazaar in the spring or summer which realised £200; they had a grant of £l3O from the Society for the Promotion of Christian Know- ledge, and also £l5 from King's College. By a concert which Mts. ilidgway—(applause)—was mainly instru- mental in getting up, some £lB was raised, and a Sun- day school concert, tender the management of Mr. Ray, re- alised £6. Therehad been raised in the parish itself, apart from the eifts of friends outside, a sum of between £6OO arid £7OOl whi'ch made up a total of £1,370 or there- abouts. They were short, therefore, to meet possibly outlay,. that they did not yet know of, no more than £2O or £25. (Applause.) That was the result of their labour since January last. (Applause.) He might mention, that so far as they knew, the work of the builders, Messrs. Coffin and Son, had been carried out in a thor- ough a,nd efficient manner, and with reference to their architect, Mr. W. Owen, of Warrington, he might say, and the committee would agree with him, that Mr. Owen had been more than a mere painstaking professional servant in that matter; he had acted like a friend, and the whole of the work had been carried out by him not as though ithad ,been a piece of business representing £ s. d., but as though it represented a labourof love, and the committee were left without that time-honoured annoyance which so frequently came in at the close of contracts—the ex- ' tras. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Mr. Owen had so managed matters that they had not a single charge in the- - shape of extras. (Applause.) There was one thing that he (Mr. Hughes) wished to mention, and which to him. was the most gratifying feature in connection with the work. They; had no millionaire in Sankey, or if they had he had not shown himself; but that large sum, of £6OO or £7OO was made up of subscriptions from all classes—from the well-to-do and from the poor, and he , believed there wasbardly a man or woman or child in Sankey who had not contributed something toward§ that sum. (Applause.) There was, therefore, no single in- dividual who could look at that school and say, "I did this." They could all say "We did this; we erected this place, and we will give it to the Lord." Might He bless it abundantly. (Loud applause.) The Rev. E. S. JACKSON said he had the honour to be the chairman of the building committee, and their wish was to offer their warmest gratitude and their heartiest thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenall. Lady Greenall, and all those who had come there to help them. (Applause.) Living as they did in an out-of-the-way place like San- key, they felt very much honoured to find Sir Gilbert Greenall present that evening to take the chair, and they thanked him for his kind words, which they hoped would be realised, and also for something more than words which he had shown to them. (Applause.) Hav- ing referred to the earlesteps taken towards the building of the school, Mr. Jackson remarked that nearly every person had given something towards the building fund, and at a public meeting like that the efforts and sacri- fices that had bog made should to be passed over

or overlooked. The rich had given of their abundance, but the poor had very often really given more than they were ablelagive, (Hear, hear.) Me thought, also, that the deepest gratitude of the people who lived there was due to the committee who put the schools up. (4- plause.) He had had the pleasure of working with a good many committeesi but he had never worked with one more competent for its work, more assiclimus in the at- tention which it gaveto that work, or more-harmonious in its meetings. Their gratitude was aleo)due to their hon. sec. for all the 'work he had done.- (Applause.) They had stood by him (Mr. Jackson) a considerable number of years, and they had helped him all they pos- sibly could. He thanked them for what they.lad done in the past, and he hoped tlitt would stand by hint once again. (Hear, hear.) There was another school and mission room he shouldillketa see on up in another part of the parish, and he thought the year 1888 would be a very suitable year for their building it. (Applasse).. The MAYOR OP Wernimaits (Alderman T. H. Sutton) , next gave an address. lieletui pleased, he said. to 'hear that they had been so verystmeessful in the building' of that school, and he thought great praise was due to everyone of them. It was ai great thing to havvilide- pendent schools of their own,im which a religious ediies- doh toitld be given, and especially when there were Roan/ schools in the parish which, gave nothing but a, secular education. He was oner of those who kad Been brought up, to believe that edirt.tion was not compitte' unless it was accompanied by a, refi„Motis educativm .:(Hear, hear:) The Mayor then spoke.? the importance -,of technical' education. The Rev'. S., WILKINSON next gave an address on Slaty)* day school work. Mr. J. C. RIDGWAY, in moving a lota of thanks to the chairman, said that he had been trying to find some formation abort the old school building. From some papers he had' been able to trace it basil. to theyear 1838, and it wa.s) curious that the first thing he found in the papers was that the people of San i key n 1838 were going to enlarge. the school. In 1839 they determined to have a day school, and advertised in the Manchester, Live ..el, and Chester papers for a schoolmaster. They wou • be rather surprised to hear of theterms on which this Schoolinaster was to be engaged. Ilk was to have the schoOl for nothing as a day school, he was to keep it in ordkr, and he must attend the Sunday school regu- larly, but he was to have no salary. (Ji.mghter.) It appeared from. a' minute that in 18401 he asked the trustees. if the,. could not help him, and they decided to allow Lim Ifive 'guineas per annum. (Laughter.) He seemed to hate been content with this, but' in 1844 the trustees decided to take the school in their,nwn hands,' and from that tingetill it was closed it had been in the hands of trustees. Mr. Ridgway next referred to the improvement that had taken place in Sankey in connec- tion with educatieru between 1838 and 1887; and con- cluded by moving the thanks of tie !need* to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall and their family for attending that night. (Applause.) Mr. JEANS, who )tv s warmly greeted, seconded the vote of thanks, which was.accorded with acclamation. In responding, Sir GILBSAT GRPANALL announced amid applause that he would give a further donation of £25, so that the whoa' might be clear of debt. The Rev. E.",&4014M050N heartily thanked Sir Gilbert for this gift, and the proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.
MISSIONARY MEETING AT WAR- RINGTON.

On Tuesday evening a public meeting was held in Wycliffe Congregational 'Church, in aid of the London Missionary Society. The chair was occu- pied by the pastor, the Rev. John Yonge, and earnest, addresses were made by the Rev. J. •Philips,•mis- sionary from Samoa South Seas, and Rev. W. J. Wilkins, late missionary at Calcutta.—The max said that it was his earnest desire that there ' should be awakened a much larger interest ir foreign missions than at present existed amongst them. He believed it to be true that a church that was thoroughly imbued with the missionary spirit was a church thaott was most likely to be prosperous and successful ia all the departments of its work. He believed,that the history of missions proved that those churches had been the most successful in gathering in totheir own borders those who stood without, who had felt a deep and lively interest in the extension of the work of Christ in all parts of the world. Many people said that the church at home had quiteas much as it could do to reach the heathenism in its own neighbourhood, but belied uBu4ly found that those who spoke in that way were not the most conspicuous examples of devo- tion to , home missionary enterprise. He be- lieved that home missions would succeed proportionahely as they took a deeper in- terest, in missions all over the world, The London Missionary Society,at present sent out to various parts of the mission field 150 English mis- sionaries, and there was also a bazukof 24 Christian ladies,,who had gone eut to various parts, especially I,ndia, to devote themselves to female missions. The society had a staff of 1.150 native ordained preachers of the gospel, as well as. 6,000 catechists and, preachers. For the support of the various missionaries, and the various agencies of the society, the income of the society last year ainoun- ted,to £122,000. Of this £72,430 was received from subscriptions, donations, and congregational col- lections, and the colonial and foreign auxiliaries had sent something like .C 4,700. The mission sta- tions themselves had raised, and in part contributed in their own locality, no less than £19,343, which was a sign of the interest they felt in promoting the gospel. The expenditure ot tile society balanced the income. In 1886 they in Warrington contributed to the society the sum of £9l 35 Id, which was con- siderably in excess of the sum sent from that church In the preceding yeall. This sum included .C 25 raised at a sale of work for the Zenan2 Missions. He was not .able to say ho* they would stand this year, but the ladies had not seen their way to having a sale of work for the Zeriana Missions. He believed, however, that the collections of Sunday were somewhat in excess of those of last year, and he thought that the contri- butions from the Sunday school would not be found behind those of last year, He hoped that they would be able to send a respectable offering, and that their interest would be renewed in that great and important Christian enterprise.—The Revs. W. J. WILKINS then spoke on the progress of mission work in India. They had every reason, he said, to be encouraged by the numerical success that had followed their missionary labours in that vast coun- try. H caste were only out. of the way, where their converts were counted by hundreds now, they would be counted by thousands. It was, however, gratifying to find that caste influence was decreas- ing..—The Rev. 0, Pamirs spoke of the work of Samoa, where mission work has been very success- ful, so much so that now the natives build their own churches and support their own pastors, as well as raising a considerable son of money.--The

addresses werelistened to with great attention, and a collecliun was subsequently made. On Sunday special sermons were preached in Wycliffe Church in aid of the sociey, in the ,morn- ing by the Rev. G. Philips,and in theeveni ng by the Rev. Wilkins. There were good congre- gations,

div.head: WANTON V. WIGAN.
div.p: WANTON V. WIGAN.

The first-named team journeyed to Wigan on Satur- day under disadvantageous circumstances, being with- out the services of Barnes, Jolley, Massey, W. Dillon, Rigby, and the brothers Turner. The home team mus- tered their full strength, and it was naturally expected that the Warringtonians would be- defeated; but, con- sidering the above-mentioned weakness, a grand game was witnessed, and at times they more than held their own against their heavy opponents. There was a fair attendance of spectators, and, consequent on the high wind which prevailed, four quarters were played. The visiting team having won the toss, Speakman de- cided to have the advantage of the wind, and Wardle set the ball in motion. No return havirr, been made, the first scrimmage was formed in Warrington territory, and from some loose play Daniels secured possession, and by a speedy run transferred operations to the Wigan lines, forcing Samuels to save. From the drop out Speakman "made his mark," and a splendid shot by Isherwood nearly reached its destination, Samuels again being forced to save. Again Wigan commenced, and play was taken to the Warrington lines. The visitors repulsed this effort by a neat dribble back to centre, in which Ashton, Povey, and Warren were prominent, but Bald- win and Mitchison threatened the Warrington goal, Davies checking the Wigan half back ia grand style. Speakman stopped a dangerous rush of' the Wigan for- wards, but Baldwin got away again, Daniels tackling him in, grand style. A neat dribble to mid-field by War- ren, Povey, and Ashton relieved the pressure. The Wigan men again threatened danger, forcing a minor, but Nevins, in stopping this rush, hurt his shoulder, and was of little use to his side for the remaining portion of the game. Play was taken to mid-field, where the first I quarter was reached with the score at two minors to one in favour of Warrington. Isherwood restarted, and the Wigan team, assisted by the wind, invaded the Warring- ton lines, but they playe I a grand defensive game, and by a neat dribble removed operations to the Wigan lines. A neat pass by Warren to Speakman took play in dan- gerous proximity to the Wigan citadel. The Warring- , tonians were now having the best of it, but the home I team rallied, and a mistake by one of the visiting backs let in Wigan, and play wag taken to the Warrington quarter flag. Mitchison got away from the pack, and passing at the right moment to Baldwin, the latter was enabled to Score at the corner flag. Atkinson failing at gsal. Half-time was now called, with the score—War- rington, two minors; to Wigan, one try and one minor. Wardle recommenced, and the first to show up WAS Mitchison who put in a sterling run to the Warrington lines. Ra:ndles relieved by a lucky kick to centre, and a neat pass by Warren to Speakman enabled tho latter to put in a good kick to the Wigan lines. Slevin shortly after got over, Wardle failing at goal. A combined rush by the visitors' forwards, soon after the drop out, forced the game on the Wigan lines, and from some loose play Littlewood got over, but this was disallowed, a minor only resulting. On changing ends Wardle re-started, and Daniels showed up with a good run to Wigan quar- ter flag, Hunter safely-holding him. Slovin was brought to grass by Nevins in grand style, but the Wigan team kept up the attack on the Warrington goal, and after a pleasantly-contested game Wigan retired victors by two tries, six minors, to Warrington three rainors.

On behalf of the Warringtonians, Daniels was by far the best of the backs, whilst Ashton' Craghan, Povey, and Littlewoorl worked hard to avert defeat. On the Wigan side, Mitchison, Slevin, Wardle, and Atkinson were the pick. .

The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full hack, Nevins; three-quarter backs, Bandies, Speakman (captain), and Daniels ; half backs, Warren and Davies; forwards, Ashton, Povey, Hayes Littlevrood, E. Dillon, Isherwood, Bate, W. Davies, anderaghan. Wigan: Full back, Abbott: three-quarter backs, Slevin (captain), Baldwin, and Samuels; half backs, Hunter and Mitchi- son ; forwards, Wardle, Atkinson, Holland, Carrington, Jolley, Hall, Hatton, Yates, and Swift. Referee, Mr. W. Higgin, Lancashire county.

LOCAL APPEAL CASE. In. the Queen's Bench Division, on WednesdaYr before the Lord Chief Justice, Mr. Baron Polltleb and Mir.. Justice Hawkins, the case of Dent:white in' Broohhcame up for argument on appeal from &deck:. sion of the Revising Barrister of the •borough 01' Warrington, who had placed on the list of .Parlia-• mentary voters eleven non-commissioned officers: and BM bandsmen of the Liverpool Regiment of; Militia;., now stationed at Warrington, who had' been objected to on the ground of non-occupation of the qualifying premises for the prescribed.Jperiod," owing to their itbsence at Altcar during the anima, ' traitungof the militia. In the- case of Brown, one of the non=ootareis:- sioned officers, it was skated that he was a marrien man, and.' rented a dwelling-house at Warrington 4.8 a weekly tenant, and by his wife, family, and fdriu' titre occupied the house during the full qualifying' year. Iltrwas away from Warrington with the regiment ivt Altcar for 26 days—viz., from July,l6tl to 3rd, and from 7th July to August Ist, all inclusive, He returned on July 3 on duty to Warrington and remained till the 7th, when he went back to the., camp at Alltcar, which was within 25 or 26 miles or Warrington. He returned on the Ist of August on duty, and subsequently went to sleep at his house at Warrington upon verbal leave given him by his superioroificer. Reasonable leave was always given as of course, and he has never been refused such leave. Ilb• believed that leave to return to Warring- ton would be granted every night upon personal aP"' plicationiff he needed it, and that no leave would be required to enable him to return home if lie were ready atliturar in the Morning to do his duty. 11e had no duties to perform at the camp at night, anctifAltcar had been nearer he should have re- turned each.night without leave. In regard to the bands- men the facts were embodied in the case of William Jolley, a file cutter, and a drummer in the band of the regiment. He also occupied a house with his wife and,, family during the whole of the qualifying year. He I'va"' away at Ancor for twenty-seven days, and return home on three occasions, once with written,' twice witn verbal permission, and twice in one week. He had no duties to pinforna in camp after twelve noon parade? though sometithes on Tuesday and Friday played officers' mess dinner. He had no quarters in barracks! and reCeived lodging money all the year round. He rent, and could remove to any other house he choose. WIT AND HUMOUR.

A restaurant waiter takes in the measure of a man from tip to tip. Talk is cheap. The man who talk too much gets so liberal that lie gives himself away. An exchange asks: "Does etiquette demand a vest on a hot day ?" If it does, it can have ours. It is strange! A woman who claims to have a mind of her own, takes every opportunity to give everybody a piece of it. The Indiana man who sold his wife had some trouble in collecting the money. Perhapsthe other fellow found that he was badly swindled in the trade. A Dakota woman is commended for her , courage in killing a wild cat. It does not take half as much courage for a woman to slay a wild cat as to kill a mouse. .

The man who can pass the warning notice, "paint," without testing the matter with his finger to see if it is dry, has sufficient will-power to give up drinking. Jones, he keeps a t42illlth's shop, `Fif' Poultry pen; Jo4es, he shoes the horse, And his wife, she shoos the hen. Nature is bound to keep up the average; when sho makes a man who can accumulate a fortune, she usually produces a family of spendthrifts to squander it. After running a lawn mower for an hour this morning he remarked that if ever he had said anything deroga- tory or unkind of the snow shovel he would most willingly take it back. "What in thunder did you put in that glass of soda ?" he gasped. "Whisky," replied the clerk "You winked." "I winked! My young friend, one of my eyes is made 4 of glass. I'm a temperance apostle." "My dear," said a gentleman to his wife, "where did all these books on astronomy on the library table come from? They are not ours.' "A pleasant little surprise for you," responded the lady. "You know you said this morning that we ought to study astronomy, and so I Went to a bookshop and bought everything I could find on the subject." It was some minutes before he spoke. "My dear, he then said slowly, his voice husky with emotion, "I never said we must study astronomy. I said that we must study economy." THINGS A BABY CAN Do.—lt can beat any alarm-clock ever invented for waking a family up in the morning. Give it a fair chance, and it can smash more dishes than the most industrious servant-girl in the country. It can fall down oftener and with less pro Vocation that the most expert tumbler in a circus ring. It can make more genuine fuss over a pin than its mother would over a broken leg. It can choke itself till it is black in the face with greater ease than the most accomplished wretch that ever was executed. It can keep a family in constant turmoil from morning till night and night till morning without once varying its tune. It can be relied upon to sleep peacefully all day when its father is at business t and cry all night when he is particularly sleepy. n may be the naughtiest, ugliest, most fretful baby in all the world; but you can never make its mother believe it, and you had better not try it. It can be a charming and model infant when no one is by; but when visitors are present it can exhibit more bad temper than both of its parents together. It can brighten up a house better than all the furniture ever made, make sweeter music than the finest orchestra organised, fill a larger space in its parents' breasts than they knew they had, and when it goes away it can cause a greater vacancy and leave a greater blank than 1 all tke rest of the world put together. HE KNEW THE DISTANCE.—A Boston citizen who was passing several days in the country soon discovered that every villager whom he was introduced to had a fond- ness for betting. They would bet on anything, from the colour of a horse on the bill a mile and a-half away to number of flies which would light on a pane of glass in a given time. The Bostonian kept clear of any wager for a day or two, and then "put up a job." He got a string and secretly measured the &Stance from the hotel steps to a certain hitching-post, and the next day, when the betting fever began to rage, he showed his hand. "Gentlemen," said he, "I am not a betting man; but, seeing that you are anxious for a bet of some sort, I'll lay twenty-five dollars that I can guess within a foot of the distance to that hitching-post." "Done !" 'cried the voice of the landlord, and the money was staked. "Now, what do you guess ?" "Ninety-seven feet." By his measurement it was six inches more. He had measured the string twice over with a rule' and he felt that he was twenty-five dollars ahead. One of the waiters ran for a tape-line, and the measure was taken in a manner no one could dispute. It was ninety-nine Ifeet, and the landlord had won. "I don't see how that is," muttered the Bostonian; but a second measure- ment verified the figures. It was a full hour before he recovered from the stunning blow. Then he walked over to the post and discovered that at some time during the previous night, and probably soon after his measurement, it had been moved a foot and a-half. THE REALLY IMPORTANT THING FOROOTTEN.—JuIes Bandeau, Gavarni, Henri Monnier, the Count de Gramont, Albedo Second, and some others received in September, 1839, a communication from Balsac the novelist, marked urgent, and inviting them to his house for the following Sunday. They were received by Lassally, Balzac's secretary, who looked as mysterious as his principal. Pumped with regard to the com- munication' Lassally refused to reveal the secret con- nected with It; all that he could say was that le maitre was going te make their fortunes. The announcement cast a chill on the spirits of the assembled guests. Henri 1 Monnier offered to sell his share beforehand for seven francs and a-half, money drawn; Lauren-Jan suggested I that Balzac had "struck diamonds" in the kitchen- garden, when Balzac himself appeared. "Diamonds !" he echoed, contemptuously shrugging his shoulders. "I have better than that. Diamond-mines get exhausted; I my mine will last as long as we live, and after that." The exodium was promising, and he was allowed to ex- pound his scheme. It was a simply a monopoly of the whole of the Paris and provincial theatres in collabora- tion with either one or two of the guests present in each department of theatrical production. Balzac spoke far two hours, almost succeeding in convincing his friends. When at last he stopped, they were as rich as any of the liothschilds, but as hungry as shipwrecked mariners on a raft. "What about a dinner ?" plain- tively asked Meunier. "Dinner !" repeated Balzac. "I'm glad you have reminded me; I forgot to order it." Fortunately there was a restaurant close to the gate of the domain. AN IRISHMAN'S CORNEE IN Com..—Dennis Reagan is living in lodgings overlooking some coal-sidings be- longing to one of the largerailway companies. Across the street lives an Italian who ekes out his wretched existence with the aid of a poor monkey and a worse hand-organ. To Garibaldi came Dennis one evening,and,after passing the time of day, warmed up to the subject in hand. "Av ye plaze, Misther Garibaldi," said Dennis, in his most unctuous and wheedling tone, " wud ye have any objections to loanin' me yer monkey for an hour or two ivry mornin' ?" " What-a for you want a munk ?" in- quired the count. " Niver ye mind," replied Dennis. "What wud ye charge a mornin' for the use av him ?" The count suggested that twopence an hour would be the proper figure, after vainly attempting to find out what Dennis was going to do with the monkey. Dennis haggled and tried to beat the Italian down, but Garibaldi wouldnot give in, and the deal was closed at his figure. Everything went delightfully for a week. The money was paid promptly, and the monkey was returned regularly in time not to interfere with the requirements of the Italian's profession. To be sure, the animal looked a little hollow-eyed and careworn, but in the main he was in good condition. Finally, however, the Italian's curiosity got the better of his avarice, and he told Dennis that the monkey would not be lent any more. This an- nouncement bad a most depressing effect upon Dennis. His intellect rose to the emergency, however, and he proceeded to effect one of those masterly financial coups which dazzle people who are not familiar with the workings of the capitalist mind. " Garibaldi, ' said Dennis, av yell promise to act square and not give me away, I'll be after takiia' ye into pardnership and gin ye half the profits for the use of the monkey." All-a right-a," said the Italian. On this the new partners shook hands, and each took another drink out of the pot of beer which Dennis had warily pro- vided to lubricate the negotiations. Then Dennis, in his customary lordly manner, put his arm within the Italian's, and together they sauntered over to the back-yard of the hcuse where Dennis lived. " D'ye see that ther pole, Garry ?" inquired Dennis, pointing to a pole some fifteen feet high surmounted by a cross- piece. The Italian could not very well help seeing it, and remarked that it was within range of his vision. "D'ye know phwat there is beyant the fence ?" said Dennis, " Thim's the railroad coal-sidings. Now, thin, Garry, this is the trick. Early in the mornin', whin the coal-trains begin to come in, I put the monkey on the pole. The brakesmin is all on the look-out, and ivry mother's son of thim fling two or three pieces of coal at the monkey. I've laid tin tons away in the cellar, and not wan o' them's hit the monkey yet !"

HISTORICAL PARALLELS.—A QUERY. Sir,—The singular frequency in which history repeats itself has often been commented upon, and everyone knows that there are many incidents in modern history of which parallels may be found in the records of by- gone times. There is a question I should like to ask through your columns purely as a matter of historical curiosity, and apart altogether from any consideration of current events or controversies, and that question is a this: Has any one ever read or heard of a patriot who sought to serve his country by sticking to a particular pair of breeches am, sir. QUERIST.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE LAND QUESTION. Sir,,--As a rule Englishmen love fair play, but I can scarcely think that anyone who attended Tuesday night's meeting, can say that fair play was accorded to me, especially as I was merely carrying out Mr. Howes' own _invitation to bring Mr. Chamberlain's speech in order to verify, if I could, my contention that he had been the means of misrepresenting Mr. Chavnberlain. He sent me two letters calling upon me to produce Mr. Chamberlain's speech, where he had said that he would- oppose Lord Salisbury if he brought in a bill dealing with land pur- chase on the same lines as Mr. Gladstone's. Mr. Howes wanted to infer that Mr. Chamberlain, although he had opposed Mr.-Gladstone's Land Purchase Scheme, because it pledged British credit, had not the courage to oppose Lord Salisbury if he attempted the same process. I con- tend that I was justified in giving it a fiat contradiction, and I know of no better system than the system of ques- tioning lecturers like Mr. Howes. On Tuesday night I fulfilled my promise to Mr. Howes to bring Mr. Chamber- lain's speech, which bore out my statement. What hap- pened? Why, Mr. Howes asked me to hand over to him Mr. Chamberlain's speech. He carefully read it aver to himself before rising to read it to the meeting. The result was he read over only half the sentence and commented largely, in his own way, upon that half sen- tence, and left the remaining half unread, thus gulling the audience at my expense. This was more than I could stand; hence I demanded to read the whole sentence myself, which was sternly refused, both on account of the Gladstonians being determined that fairplay should not be carried out, and also because Mr. Howes himself seemed to nudge the chairman when I made an attempt to read what he had read to himself, but not to the meet- ing. This was certainly unfair, and how anyone can condemn me for the eourse I took is surprising. But, al- though I was prevented from proving my statement in public meeting; I can resort, with your permission (which I think will be granted), to putting in print the whole sentence of Mr. Chamberlain's speech, and then leave the public to judge for themselves. Speaking in the House of Commons Mr. Chamberlain said:—" Ac- cording to the rules of this House we are not entitled to discuss matters which pass in another place' and, I ad- mit, fora very good reason, because the speakers .are not here to answer for themselves and to give the necessary . explanations' or corrections of what they may have been reported to have said. Well, sir, all I will Say in addi- tion at the present moment is that I also deprecate any attempt to transfer the loss which may fall upon the land- lords owing to circumstances of the seasons, or to other matters, to the pockets of the British taxpayer. I have deprecated it before. I will deprecate it again. Ido not believe the Government would be so foolish as to make any proposition of the kind. If ever they do, all I can say is that by whatsoever Government it may be made, and in whatsoever circumstances, I shall be bound by what I have said in the past and by my present opinions, to offer to it my most strenuous opposition." Mark you. it was the latter part of this sentence that all the conten- tion was about. Why did Mr. Howes omit to read the tatter part of this sentence and refuse me also who had the right to do SO? Yes, why? Let the reasoning pub- lic give the reason why.—Yours respectfully, L. SUTCLIFF.t.

THE NEW ARRANGEMENT IT TFIE LIBRARY. Sir, —I ventured last week to assert that so far from subscribers and persons who pay a penny for a book under the new arrangement at our rate-supported library being on an equal footing, there was as much difference between the positions of the two as there generally is between the position of the person who pays hi a way, and the person who, pauper-like, seeks the aid of public chhrity. To prove that I did not exaggerate when I said this I may perhaps be allowed to point out what it is that is regarded as constituting pauperism. Some people would say that the person who received any bene- fit that was paid for out of the public purse was thereby to some degree pauperised, but that is not so. In some of s our colonies education is entirely free to all, but the colo- nists who universally take advantage of this free educa- tion do not feel that they are—and nobody would for a moment pretend that they are—in any degree pauperised by doing so. But when we come to England the ease is different. Here it is the rule for people to pay the school fees of their own children, and anyone who is obliged to ask for the fees to be paid out of the rates feels keenly and bitterly that he is by that very act sub. jecting himself to some extent to the stigma of pauper- ism. Now, why is it that our Australian colonist loses sone of his self-respect when the whole cost of his children's education is paid by the State, while the Eng- lishman who has the same thing done for his children feels grieimuslv humiliated? is the simple explanation not this—that the colonist feels that he is still the equal of his fellows, while the Englishman is oppressed with the consciousness that he has lost caste,that he has taken a step in the direction of that state of pauperism which is the dread and horror of the self-respecting poor of England. Pauperism then does not consist in having benefits paid for out of Public funds, but in distinctions being made in the mode in which these benefits are con- ferred. Looked at in this light, what are we to say of the new arrangement at the library? Are there no dis tinctions in the mode of sharing the benefits of our rate- supported library amongst the ratepayers ? Clearly there are. There are two persons who are differ- ently treated, the sub:criber and he who goes with a penny. The penny device has been adopted professedly to accommodate those who find it difficult to pay a sub- scription, just as free school fee.' are to meet the case of these who cannot pay for their children's schooling. And the person who goes with a penny to the library stands in the same relation to a subscriber that the recipient of free school fees does to the person who pays for the schooling of his own children. It may be objected to this that the individual who applies for school fees has to submit to his circumstances beink inquired into by an officer, while the man who takes advantage of the new arrangement at the library is not subjected to anything of this kind. That is, of course, quite true, but on the other hand the would-be borrower of a book is subjected to an equal, or worse humiliation. Before he is ever al- lowed to take a volume home, he must get thesigna- tures of two burgesses to a voucher, and in the very act .(iif asking for these signatures he must cenfessto a degree of poverty verging upon that which compels people to plead for free school fees. I feel convinced, sir, that the more people think over this new arrangement the more indignant they will be at the odious distinctions which it introduces between Persons who really have equal claims to the use of the 4ibrary, and the more disposed they will be to reject such a mean and eleemosynary contrivance as a settlement of the free library question.—Yours, Warrington, Nov. 29, 1887. A RATEPAYER.

WHAT IRELAND IS, AND WHAT IT MIGHT YET BE. Sir —I know Northmen well and they are not so con- tented and prosperous as represented. But M.P's., and others that go there to lecture them, know their OW prejudice, and they play upon it, and tell them that Rome and Romanism Is going to be the predominating power, and that Home Rule means Rome Rule, so that these people will put up with any laws, however had they may be, so long as they come- from a Protestant community,—the very laws theywould not tolerate com- ing from a parliament in Dublin. The northmen resis- ted the Land Acts while they were being passed into law ; not because they were bad Acts, but because they were forced on them by the Catholies of the South. And when the Land Acts became Law, the Northman were the first to go into Court and claim the benefits of them. They also cried war to the knife against disestablishing the church. Now, I don't think there is a single indi- vidual in themorth would like ta see the church again established. I believe it would be the same with Home Rule ; the people would find that their great terror was as the working (if the night-mare. What danger to the State has there been in giving Home Rule to our colonies? None; but a much greater danger had we not done so. Had the great American Republic been granted Home Rule when struggling against our taxation, we would now have a united and powerful ally to depend on in time of war. To talk of a union of Ireland with England: it is no union in any sense of the word. So long as England governs Ire- land as she is doing at present, it will only be a danger to the State. If we were engaged in any great war it would require a large army to keep Ireland front- taking the side of the enemy; and a greater Ireland across the Atlantic that carry in their breasts their country's wrongs, will have to be settled with some day. To have a proper union with Ireland you must make the people feel that they cannot improve their position by going over to.the enemy, even if they had the (glance. Give them an interest in their hearths and homes, and they will defend them against your enemy and theirs. I would transfer the term Separatists from those it is gen- erally applied to (as they are the real Unionists), and I wonld apply it to those that call themselves Unionists. Their idea of a union forced with the bayonet is only a mockery and a snare, as they would find in the day of England's extremity. Now, I would suggest Home Rule for the four Pro- chives, each Province to legislate on all local matters. This to a great extent would settle the religious difficul- ty, as Northmen could manage their own affairsindepen- dent of the south and vice versa. I think if this had been the substance of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill. a Liberal Ministry would still have been in office. The Provincial Governments should have full power to settle all local matters, such as roads, rates, taxes, licensing, and police. The Queen to be represented by a Governor fter the manner of our Colonies; a certain number of avincial members to be summoned to the Imperial 'lament on Imperial matters only. Two Acts should ssed by the Imperial Parliament at once for Ire- a Land Purchase Act to do away with dual con-
Pt ' Par. be pa land

trol ; and Make the occupier, the owner of the land he I occupies, but to be strictly prohibited from sub-letting; as if this was allowed to be the case, the last state of the country would be worse than the first. The other Act to do away with all party processions in every shape or form, as this party work has been one of the curses of the country; for it creates strife and contention between class and class. It should be stipulated that these Acts should not be annulled by any Provincical Act or Acts. A basis for the purchase of the land could be made on the rents fixed by the Commissioners say, 15 or 16 years rents, which would be a fair value, taking hitto account , the price of farm produce. At the present time, owing to the tenants improvements, his interest is considered to be equal to the landlords. As regards separation from England, I don't believe the people would think of such a thing if they had laws suit- able to their wants. The best way would be to lep them make the greater part of their own laws- If they made bad laws,they could not blame the English Government, and it would save that body an enormous amount of time and trouble. At the present time Ireland might as well not be represented at Westminster, as its representa- tives are outvoted by a majority Of members that know nothing of the wants of the Irish people. L would re- commend the Irish M.P's. to stop at home; it is only a farce sitting at Westminster when their demands on be- half of the Irish are jeered at. I believe Ireland would be as loyal as any of our colonies and as peaceable as the Isle of Man if al- towed the same privileges. With Provincial Government, and the occupier made the owner of his land, I believe a great change would take place all over the country in respect of improved dwellings, and agriculture. I have no doubt when the people settled down to more peace- ful pursuits under good government, that capital would find its way into the coAntry, and mills, and manufac- tories would be erected where there is such splendid water power. This would find employment for the sur- plus population, and keep the Irish from flooding the Eng- lish labour market. It would also create a demand for their own produce. When the people could find profit- able employment, they would not be led about by agita- tors that prey upon society. A new era would set in when the country could be governed by one tenth of the soldiers and police that are employed there at pre- sent.—Yours, &c., JAMES McILWAINE. Knowsley, Lancashire.

A BOTHER ABEAWT CURBSTOOANS AT GOBURN. Sir,—lt's a gud whoile sin you heerd fro' me, an aw dassay yo are wantin' t' no heaw it is. Well, aw've bin lookin' after eawr Sal/nth, an' rnakkin cinder tay has bin moor i' moi loin than writin' for a noosTraper Yoa con tell yore misses us heaw th' twins are doom' yarry weel, un if hu's ony spare calico, or owd Sheets, they'l be very acceptable. Hu'l no wot aw want urn for. Sin aw rote yea last a greyt change ha taen place eawr heawse. Wayn aw joint th' church. Eawr Turn has bin made into a soidsmon (left-hond soide aw think Lit is) eawr Jack blows th' organ (fourpenslhaufßenny a wick he gets) eawr Mary sings (aw thia they cawn her a tenner singes) i' th' queer ; -eawr Dill rings th' un eawr Sayrah's husbant has bin bade into th' sexton. r Eawr Turn makes a gud soidmon, un if yoal ax ony- body heer they'll tell yoa us thare nare has bin a better mon for stonnin up for his own soide than he is. 'Mare are two soidesmen, owd Billy Bangum bein' at one soide un eawr Turn at t' other, un Sammy Durriplin th' middle fort see fare play dun if thare's ony feightin. But eawr Turn con lether booath on hum and his sot& allus wins. Just afoor way started o' gooin th' church aw'd a wary hondful, aw eon tell yea. Th' childees dooms wur not fit goea eavrt in on a Sunday ; eawr Turn's wur seedy, un aw'd nowt but mi linsey cooat, mi bedgeavrn un mi clogs gooa eawt in. Eawr Turn wanted us t' gooa way wur. "It's not th' adornment o'th' body, but a reet preparation o'th' heart us is necessary to profitable worship, he sod. " Eigh," aw sod, "that's quite true, but if theawl gooa owther t' church or th' chapel i' thoos cloog u.s thea,w has theawl hay a job t' conving onybody us thi heart is rest, un wets moor theavel have fort carry thi cup very level or thav'l turn thi eawt." Charity, they sen, cuvvers a multitood o' fauts. un so dus brass un foine clooas, un if aw'd ony munney to lay on a match aw shud back oather brass or foine cloos afoor charity." "Now, now," aw sed, "if way are fort goes t' church, way'l ha' summat dayant goes in," un th' next day aw °riled off th' Scotchman a soot o' does for eawr Turn, one apses for eawr Jack un Bill, un a puse un red merino dress un two bussels for mi un eawr Marv. Thi' bill coom to fourteen peawnd noin shillin un thrippuns haupenny, un way agreed pay it at a slain a wick. Way'n mist him tworce, un it's bin a gradely awkert job booath toimes. Eawr Scotchman is fust cuzzin o'th' faythees soide to Job. He's waited fur me three heawrs un a hauve at wons, whoile aw've bin sirrin upstairs wi' th' dur lock, un very neer starvint to th' deoth.

" hu in," he sed, one day us he dropt on us unawares. " Neaw," eawr Mary sed. "Where is hu? " sed th' Scotchmon lookin very feers. " Ha's th' cole hole," sed eawr Mary, forgerren hersel, un wi a pick hawm one bond no a flat iron th' t'other aw coor9 eawt, un towd him us heaw awd bin after a cat US had teen a peawnd o' black puedins off th' buttery shelf. He didn't bilenv me, aw cud see, but he geet his "shellun," an eawr Mary vet th' pick hawm midlin hondy when he'd gone. Awl bet th' cole hole dodge cums off next toime, an thail be no pick hayrms, cats, or flat irons requirt. Well, as aw towd yoa eawr Turn has bin made into a smdesmon, un he's th' best soidesmon thare's hare bin P Goburn. Tother day thay coom art towd him as heaw Billy Bangum, Vother soidemon, was havvin sum stooans put up th' soide o' th' church wauk. He'd nare axed him aheaut it, un eawr Turn lino into a pert (loom n to Billy, he sod, "Wot dust reckon thea,w'a bin dooin. If theawl mind thi own soide theawl hay enuf t' do. Aw reckon becose theawrt workin amung soft cole, yore middlin o' weshin, un yore Jane's i' full work, theaw thinks theaw con look after th' east sold, north soid,un th' west sold; but aw con tell thi if theaw dus- sant stop it awst fotch Sammy Duna:Ain un a warder, no ha thi put i' chancery." Owd Billy's blud wus up, use he sed to eawr Turn, "If theawl gooa ud pay th' Scuteh- mon wot theaw owes him, un tell yore Betty keep dur opoen un leoy off seyin her prayers upstairs un th' cole hole till he's bin fur his shillin, it'l look better on thi." " Theawt a noicc mon," sed eawr Turn, "to tawk abeawt onybody owin brass. Woi thare's nar a thing Us theaw stons in uv a Sunday—fm' th' thungs thi shooti to th' billycock o' thi ved—us paid fur un aw dunnot see wot differuns it makes wether th' mon us theaw geet hum off is Hoyrish, Scotch, or Welsh Us IMIX u.s theaw owes for horn. But wot aw owe, or wot theaw owes, has nowt do wi' thews stooans," sed Turn, "un if theaw dussant shift hum awat shift thee, un hourly too." un he was just gooint get out o' Owd Billy when th' pahron coom up. "Now what is the matter, Thomas," sed th' parson. "Whoi," serf eawr Turn," Owd Billy theer ba.s bin purrin thoos stooans deavrn heawt axing laof off me, un as lung Us awim a Sojdmon nouther him nor nobody else shall hinterfare wi moi soide beawt axing mi. Wot's gad o' ml bein soide-moinder if sundry else is fort' look after it. iln' besoides. thoos stooans arra fit pave th' rode to a pigcote, un if yoal sri th' word awl gona irn tack bonath Billy Tiungum un his stooans ilh' Bow Pits.". "Be calm, Thomas" sed th' parson. "Let brotherly love continue." " Brutherlv luv be hanged," sed eawr Turn, quoit hot. "Owd Bill Bloa,nmfs no brother o' mom, and hesoide, if he wus, wot':. brotherly luv gettun t' do wi skellart curb stooans un brickbats." "Thomas, Thomas, Thomas,' sed th' parson, "Calm thy troubled soul. Let peace reign supreme. Remembertfiat charity. love, and forbearance are due to thine office." " Eigh," eawr Turn sed, "its noyce tawkin abeawt charity un Owd Bungum grinnin at ml thro' rails therm bike a hyeener,un there ,To makkin faces us feaw us a wiz- sort, un us regards toy un forbearance, ony soidemon us con buy a mon us wants tack his soide off him, Am tells him abeawt his Seotehmon Sm wot he owes him til havt' hi made to erder. Aw eonnot heln batin Owd Billy Bungum, nn awm not gooint boss. Just then aw landed at th' church gates, and gerrin owt uv eawr Tum aw took him whoorn, no so th" squebble ended.— Yores, for ever,

FRODSHAM. TREFT or A Hxy.—At Mdisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ann Percival, of Frodsham, was charged with stealing, at Frodsham, a hen, valued at 2s, 64., on the sth November, the property of Arthur James Ashworth. —Prosecutor said he was a chemical manufacturer, and kept a number of hens. He trriFsed one of the fowls, and in consequence gave information to the police.—Sergeant Whalley deposed that he searched the prisoner's house and found the hen produced. When charged with the offence she at once denied it, but subsequently said that she killed the bird with a brush, and stowed it away. --Prosecutor said he did not wish to press the charge.— Fined ss. OPENING or A NEW WESLEYAN CRAPEL:—The handsome little chapel at Manley, near Frodsham, was formally opened for Divine worship on Thursday week. The chapel, which is capable of accommodating about 180 worshippers, is fitted up with pews in varnished pitch pine. The pulpit is of elegant design, and the windows 'of lattice glass in diamond pattern. The whole has been erected from plans and specifications prepared by Mr. Waring of Mouldsworth Hall, the building being erected by Mr. G. Johnson. The Rev. Charles Garnett officiated at the opening service, and the Rev. W. Wilson in the evening. The Solos were sung in a very efficient manner by Mr. Thomas Gleaves. The two services were well attended, the chapel being overcrowded, and the collect, ions realized about £3O. The trustees were well pleased with the result of the day's proceedings. and trusted that God's blessing may rest upon their labours. Tnt BONN-FIDE TRAVELLER QUESTION.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday. Elizabeth Potts was charged that she, being the landlady of the Robin Hood, Helsby, did keep the house open for the sale of intoxicating liquors on Stmday, the 13th November, at forty minutes past eleven in the•forenoon. Mr. J.H. Cooke defended. 0.0. Roberts stated the facts of the case.—Elizabeth Potts, daughter of the defendant, said the men who were in her house told her distinctly that they had come from Prndsham Bridge. She would not have supplied them with drink if they had not made that statement. —The case was dismissed on payment of costs, 45 6d,the Chair-

PICTuitE DEALER'S CLAIM.—WiII. Palin, of Clarence- street', who described himself as a picture dealer, sued Richard Houlbrook, grocer and provision dealer, Lord- street, for the sum of £2, being the balance of an account for photographs of the defendant's mother and mother- J. W. Knowles, of Widnes, was for the plaintiff and Mr. F. A. Lake was for the defendant. It was alleged that the order was for twolargephotographs with frames at £2 each, and that a sovereign had been paid, on each picture. Mrs. Patin and John Cliffe, of Pennington-row, corroborated the plaintiff's statement. —For the defence, Mr. Houlbrook, Miss Jessie Houlbrook, Mrs. Ogden, and Miss Beckett, of Caxton Vicarage, Lancaster, gave evidence that the plaintiff stated the price of the pictures was a guinea each, with 10 per cent. discount, and this amount was paid. No receipt was given, but when the plaintiff brought the pictures he arranged them on the walls of the sitting- room. He was left alone for some time, and on bis de- parture it was discovered that two cards had been left in a desk giving credit for the amounts paid, and showing that £2 was still owing.—His Honour gave judgment for the defendant, and said he was strengthened in this course by the manner in which the cards had been left at the house, and the confusion in the dates of the payment given by the plaintiff. A CLAIM FOR BEER.—H. Boddington and Co., Limited, brewers, Strangeways, Manchester, sued William Molyneaux, of Kingsley, for 153., the price of a barrel of beer. Mr. Burton defended.—Mr. Bardsley, collector to the plaintiffs, acknowledged that there was another per- son named Molyneaux in the village, and that the two accounts had been mixed. Tbe accounts had, however, been separated. The defendant took the oath that he had settled with Mr. Watson, the plaintiffs' agent, who took the order.—Judgment.for the defendant.

THE SHIP • CANAL. At the adjourned inquest, on Monday, on the body of John Forbes, an engineer enaployed at the Manchester Ship Canal work, who was killed at the Ilooton railway station on Wednesday last, by be- jug crushed between the buffers of some waggons which were being shunted, the jury, in returning a , verdict of "Accidental death," expressed an opinion I that sufficient precaution was not taken by the officials of the railway company in warning the de- ceased and his fellow-workmen to get out of the way of danger before the shunting took place. The jury added a suggestion that, in view of the large number of men employed at the canal works, a tem- porary or permanent hospital should be erected in the locality. Mr. Francis, solicitor (who watched the .case on behalf of the widow of the deceased), said that in all probability the contractor for the canal works would erect such a building.

div.p: DEEDS OF VIOLENCE AT WIDNES.

- - Bridget Brannen, an old woman, of 4, Elizabeth- street;was brought up at Widnes Police .Court, on Monday, charged. 4 with unlawfully and maliciously wounding Mary ;i Treacy, a. young woman, of 21, Barn-street. vlt.iippeared that about six o'clock on Saturday night the women had a quarrel in Eliza- beth-street, :mil the prisoner struck Mrs. Treacy cm the fa.ce:Wlth her clog. Mrs. Treacy, who was bleeding freely, Succeeded in, wresting the clog from the prisoner's hand, and at once took the ugly weapon to the -police station and made a complaint. Subsequently P.S. Strick- land apprehended the prisoner, who said, "May-be I did strike her on the forehead with a clog. That clog is mine. Some one took it away fr,om me." _ Dr. Hutchin- son deposed that Mrs. Treacy was stiffering froin a con- tused wound on the forehead which had teen inflicted by some blunt instrument. The wound not only pene- trated to the bone, but 4ad laid open a portion of the skull. There was great danger of erysipelas setting in. The prisoner' who stated that Mrs. Treacy- was the ag- kreaor, and had smashed her window, was remanded for a week. The magistrates refused to accept bail. _ . _

Thomas Price, a labourer, of 8, Regent-;treet. Run- corn, was charged with unlawfully assaulting Michael Lever' of 42, Princess-street, Runcorn.—Walter Davies, of 55, Reamont-street, Widnes, deposed that on Saturday evening the men had some angry words together in a vaults in Church-street, and upon going outside Price struck Lever on the head with a tea can which he car- ried.—P.S. Clarkson said Lever was bed fast, and Dr. Nealan certified that at the earliest he could not appear in court for a week.

Antony Antiskyesky, a Pole, was brought up on re- mand charged with wounding Adam Lanbinskas, also a Pole, who resided at 30, Water-street. The prisoner was a lodger, and during supper on Saturday night he made use of some offensive expressions towards the prosecu- tor's wife, He was tojil he would hive to seek. lodgings elsewhere, whereupon he plunged a fork into the prose- cutor's nose, inflicting a wound which Dr. Hutchinson stated was most dangerous. The prisoner was commit- ted to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr J. Dobson presided, and there were also present Messrs. Grice, Hankinson, Smith, Imison, Lightburn, Speakman. %Fisher, Pritchard, Taylor, Mellor, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Mar- shall (secretary), and IL Barker (surveyor). . HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. McDougall) reported that during November there were 30 deaths. Of these one was an inquest case, and of the remaining 29 deaths one was due to typhoid fever, four to misinteric disease, three to chronic bronchitis, two to rheumatism, four to premature birth, one to convulsions, two to acute bron- chitis' three to measles, one to natural decay, one to diarrlinea, one to heart disease, one to pernicious ancernia, one to cancer, one to erysipelas, one to inflam- mation of the lining of the membrane of the brain, and two to peritonitis. The above deaths showed an aver- age death-rate for the 12 months of a Mae over 21 per 1,000 dvf the estimated population, and exclusive of the inquest case of a fraction over 20 per 1,000.

div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA cllont

The -first-concert of the season under the auspices of this successful musical organisation, was given in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening, and, it is pleasing to record, was patronised' by a large and appreciative audience. The programme consisted of a choice selection of the mmitc ren- dered at the Crystal Palace Festival of Tonic-Sol-fa choirs. Mend'efssohnret 13th Psalm, and miscellane- ous items-. The choir, who were assisted* by Mr. Caldwell's orchestral band, of Warrington, per- formed ther tasks allotted to them in a manner that merits the warmest praise. Guided by the baton of Mr. J. llorfbrd, the conductor, the choir sang with excellent taste. judgment. and finish, and' the hearty ' plaudits testified to the appreciation of those pre- sent. The principals were Eos Mortals, t he celebrated Welsh tenor, and Miss Kate Meredith, of Liverpool. In the first part of the programme Ras Morlais contributedthe recita- tive, "Comfort ye,' fmm Flanders 4' Messiah,' and his robust, yet clear and expressive voice was heard to great advantage; He, however, shone with still greater ef- fect in the•second'part of the programme, when he con- tributed, "Only to love thee," and "Good company," an encore rewarding him for each effort. Of Miss Mere- dith it is ing.sy.-L-dble to speak in terms too flattering. Her 7ocalisatibn of the 13th psalm was characterised by great power and pathos, qualities which she also dis- played hr rendering "Daddy," and "Love in a dream." She was compelled to respond to the enthusiastic recalls of the audience on two occasions. It must not be over- looked-that Mr. Caldwell's band performed their work in a most skilful fashion, and caused much pleasure by their performance of the overture from Mlle's "Bohe- mian Girl." The duty of accompanist on the piano was ably undertaken by Mrs. W. R. Kay.

THE DULWICH ELEcriorr.—The nominations ,for the vacancy in the representation of the Dtawich Division of Camberwell, caused by the appointment of Mr. Morgan Howard, Q.C. (Conservative), to a County Court judge- ship, took place on Tuesday, when Mr. James Henderson (Gladstonian Liberal), and Mr. John Blundell Maple (Conservative) were duly put forward. The election took place on Thursday, and resulted in the return of Mr. Blundell Maple, 'Conservative, by a majority of 1,412 over Mr. Henderson, Liberal. There was no con- test at the last general election: but in 1885 Mr. Morgan Howard, Conservative, defeated his Liberal cpponent by a majority of 1,894. On Thursday there-was a small de- crease in the Liberal and a large falling off in the Conser- vative vote.

div.head: WARRINGTON SECTION.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SECTION.

The practical work of constructing the Ship Canal may now be said to have begun in right earnest in the locality of Warrington. On Wednesday the first sod of that section of the canal which lies between Norton Priory and Stockton Heath/was cut by Mrs. Squires, the wife of the engineer who has charge Of this section. The scene of this little ceremony, which was not accompanied by much pomp and circumstance, and was witnessed by few spectators, was in a field on Acton Grange farm, near to the village of Moore. After this formal beginning a contingent of about thirty nav- vies set about , the work of excavation, which has been continued since. A large quantity of material such as harrows, planks, spades, &c., is already on the ground, having been conveyed thither by means of the canal which runs parallel with the cutting and only a few hundred yards distant. It is intended, in the first instance, to make a trench about a dozen yards in width and as many deep, and in this will be placed a tine of rails and various other apparatus to facilitate further operations. For the purposes of an office a farm-house adjacent to the workings has been taken possession of by Mr. Walker, the contractor. The workmen engaged at Acton Grange have for the most part to come to Warrington to find accommodation but it is expected that this inconvenience will be remedied by the erection of huts. During yesterday and Thursday large numbers of people from Warrington visited the scene of operations, amongst whom were many workmen in search of em- ployment. As we mentioned last week, it is intended to lay a sid- ing from Latchford Station to the banks of the canal, in order to facilitate the removal of machinery and other. heavy material. It is probable . that the work of con- structing this siding will be commenced next week, and will, no cloubt,- be rapidly -completed': The section of the canal which extends from Stockton Heath to Lymm will be under the superintendence of Mr: Prirker; but AS it is not intended to begin with this section ,immediately Mr. Parker will superintend the laying of the siding.

THE SLIPPERY ROADS.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, John Taylor, of Newton, was summoned for obstructing the footpath by drawing his horse and i cart thereon, n Crow-lane, on the previous Monday afternoon. Police Sergeant Commins proved the ease, and stated that when he spoke to the defendant about the matter, the defendant said the roads were so slippery that he could not get along them.—The Bench fined the , defendant 2s 6d and costs. , FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE AT NEWTON : SINGULAR ' Casa.—On Sunday last the Newton police received in- formation of a supposed case of swine fever on the pre- mises of John Taylor, of Crow-tone, Newton, two Pigs, the property of William Robertson, collier, being the sufferers. rThe owner purchased them at St. Helens on the sth November, but last week they appeared unwell, apparently from swine fever. On Monday the animals were inspected by Superintendent Weir and Mr. Hewitt, veterinary inspector for the district, and they were found to be suffering from foot and mouth disease. The singular features of the case were reported to the authorities, and on Thursday morning Mr. William M. Smart, M.R.C.V.S., one of the Government Privy Coun- cil Inspectors visited the place and inspected the animals.
OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
EFROII OVR OWN CORRE-SPONDENT.] 23 Old Broad-street E C

There have been few features of special interest in the Stock Markets during the week. The fortnightly settle- ment which commenced on Monday absorbed attention for the first three days, and as a result no attention was given to further events beyond what was absolutely necessary. Copper mining, companies have claimed chief attention, the impulse given to copper being almost unprecedented. At the beginning of October copper was inkier £4O a ton ; Rio Tintos being under eight. Copper has now reached nearly £7O a ton, and Rio Tintos are over 14. Such an advance is so extra.erdinary that it requires something beyond the ordinary demands of the market to believe that the rise is bona fide; as a matter of fact there is little doubt that it is entirely the result of a rig worked by the French Syndicate, which undertook to send the price of copper t.to £7O a ton. Although this has very nicely been accom- plished, it has not quite succeeded, and there are signs that the beginning of the end has set in, as a slight re- action every now and again occurs which denotes a wavering and hesitancy that predicts a fall. The general tendency of the markets at the present time is on the vhole decidedly "bullish," and we look for a further rise in prices. 11l the American market East Tennessee Railway is deserving of attention; New York and Ontario Bonds is also a good speculative stock for a lock up, and which is likely to show a rise on present prices; both these lines are rapidly improving. We have lately called attention to the growing favour in which South African mining undertakings are regarded, and the rapid increase in value of the mining shares. Barberton, the centre of the gold-bearing district, is attracting special attention just now by the report of another com- pany adjoining the Sheba being about to be offered; the fame of the Sheba is world-wide, the Ll shares being to- day worth £2O. We are in a position to announce the almost immedi- ate issue of the prospectus of a company which has been formed by a highly influential board of directors, to pur- chase various properties in the Malay peninsula, and more especially to work the mining and planting proper- ties in the state of Pahang; the company will be known as the Pahang Corporation, and has been registered with a capital of £200,000 in shares of Ll each. The chief value of the property consists of the immense mineral resources which are knownto exist, the chief of which is tin. It is stated that the concession which extends over an area of about 2,000 square miles, probably comprises the largest and richest tin bearing property ever brought before the public. The vendors take all the interest, with the exception of £lO,OOO in shares of the company. This fact Is, perhaps more than any other, the best illustra- dela of their belief in the undertaking. The latest thing in the promoting world is the addition to it of a church dignitary. The company brought out by him is the New Canadian Crown Lands Syndicate, with a capital of £25,000. We have npthing to say against a canon of the church turning promoter, but it hardly adds to the dignity of his position or the credit of the church, even if the philanthropic motive is taken into account. We should advise -investors who may re- ceive the prospectus of the rev. canon's syndicate to view it from a purely business point of view and not from the philanthropic. In miscellaneous shares some business has been done in Music Hall Co's shares. Pavilions are considerably Over par, and Metropolitans, with a 20 percent dividend, considerably under. At the present time we should say to investors in these to sell the first and buy few of the seeprid.

When the ancient empire of Atahualpa existed in all its glory, and before its overthrow by the rapacious Pizarro, th. extraeecli.Wry Virtues of the " Pearl of South America " were as welt known to the then natives as to the Peruvians of the present day. Indeed, its great and admitted Worth led to its being used in all public ceremonies as an acceptable Dffering to their deity—the Sun God. The leaves of this marvellous shrub, when ready for market, are transported on mules up the steel me mtain sides, across the icy and desolate plateaux, and through the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many of them 13,000 and 14,000 feet above the level of the sqa,, then downwards on the othet tide d the mountains tnto Peru for shipment from ttz p6rt of cane° (Lin%) And so terrible is the icy -..*lrgatir or tile climate amidst the lifity heights of the 111°..ntaitis, especially of the icy plateaux of Lipes, that the Muleteers find the chewing of these leaves alone enables them to withstand the icy rarefied air, and to support the long night- watches to prevent the mules they are transporting to Peru from t4;raylng. Several natives, who, never allowing a day to Pass -without chewing the leaves of the "Pearl of South America" at least three times daily, attained the truly parrs arehal age of 130 years.

The condition of Lord Lyons remains unchanged. It is stated that he has joined the Roman Catholic Church. The Very ROT. Dr. Scott, Dean of Rochester, died on Friday morning. The venerable gentleman, who was 76 years of age, was appointed to the deanery in 1870. ARREST OF ANOTHER IRISH M.P.—Mr. T. Harrington, M.P., was arrested on Friday morning at the National League Offices, Dublin, for publishing in the "Kerry Sentinel" a report of a suppressed meeting. Mr. Harring- ton states that his connection with the," Kerry Sentinel" ceased five years ago. Mr. O'Sullivan has been lodged in Richmond Prison, Dublin. Great excitement prevails throughout the country. , SUICIDE FROM A BIRKE'NEEAD FERRY BOAT.—While the Woodside ferry boatwas crossing the Mersey on Thursday night to Birkenhead, a well-dressed young fellow, who was standing near the bow of the boat, suddenly moun- ted on the bulwarks and, leaped into the water. Great excitement prevailed, and the steamer was stepped, life buoys thrown, and a boat lowered, but all without avail. It was very dark at the time, and not a cry *as heard after the fatal leap. No trace of the body has yet been found. SENTENCE ON THE LORD MAYOR OF DUBLIN.—OR Fri- day, at We Dublin Police Court, the summonses against the Lord Mayor for publishing in the "Nation," of which he is the proprietor, reports of the meetings of the sup- pressed branches of the National League, came on for hearing before Mr. O'Donnell. Mr. Carson prosecuted, and Mr. D. B. Sullivan and Mr. Timothy Healy, M.P., defended. The evidence as to the meeting at Ramsgate was taken as given' and after Mr. Carson had made a short statement the case for the Crown closed. The magistrate, in giving judgment, said, hiving regard to the character and position of the defendant the case was one of a most painful character. He felt bound, how- ever, to convict, and he sentenced the defendant to two months' imprisonment with Jut hard labour. He also ordered that the defendant should be treated as a first- class misdemeanant. He would deliver concurrent sen- tences in the other summonses if they were gone on with. The Lord Mayor, in the course of a speech, thanked his worship for the manner in which he had dealt with the case. He would enter no appeal. RESIGNATION OF PRESIDENT GREVY. PARIS, FRIDAY, 2-25 P.m.—President Grevy;s message was read in the Chamber at the opening of the sitting this afternoon. M. Grey,- stated that he regards yester- day's votes of the Senate and Chamber as a decisive demonstration, necessitating his resignation. After re- calling the services rendered by him to the country assur- ing tranquility at home and peace abroad, M. Grevy declares that he leaves office with a feeling of sadness, at the same time declining any responsibility for further events. The President concludes by tendering his resignation. BALLOT FOR THE NEW PRESIDENT. Psuis,riunsy AFTERNOON.—A preliminary meeting of Republican deputies and senators was held this after- noon to select the candidate for presidency. At the ' final ballot M. de Freycinct received 190 votes, M. Bris- . son coming next with 83. M. de Freyeinct will therefore be the candidate at the primary conference at which the final selection will be made. There have been some riot- ous disturbances in the streets.
